i.x: Jesus and the apostles loved the book of Psalms—they quoted from it and lived out of it. These ancient prayers and praises of Israel provide a bridge between the Old Testament and the New Testament; the themes introduced in the psalms find further development in the New Testament. Where David’s dynasty failed, Jesus gives hope. Yet, certain expectations that emerge in the book of Psalms still remain for the future, namely that God’s people will completely fulfill his purposes and that all nations will submit to the Messiah.
Summary

The psalms, like all Scripture, are inspired and given by God (see [2 Tim 3:16](2Tim.3.16)). Yet each psalm originated with a human author as a prayer or praise to the Lord. The psalms are diverse: The Psalter includes laments, praise psalms, wisdom, thanksgiving, reflections on God’s actions, celebrations of God’s revelation, and worship.

The first two psalms serve as an introduction to the entire Psalter (the book of Psalms). [Psalm 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6) describes a godly person who delights in God, lives by divine instruction, and is not influenced by evildoers. [Psalm 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6) points to three questions: (1) Is there forgiveness for sins? (2) Why do the godly suffer? and (3) Why do the wicked prosper? The rest of the Psalter meditates on these questions.

[Psalm 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12) speaks of how the nations and the wicked are in rebellion against God’s rule. God judges the rebellious and protects the godly. [Psalm 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12) suggests two questions: (1) Why do the rebellious nations and the wicked prosper? and (2) Why were the kings of David’s line not victorious?

The psalmists largely wrestle with these questions. Some quietly accept their problems, while others question God or become exasperated. Meanwhile, new questions and issues develop out of their dialogues with God.
The Composition of the Psalms

For a thousand years, poets wrote these poems while people recited and collected them. The Temple liturgy encouraged both the writing and the collection of psalms. Gradually, editors incorporated smaller collections into larger collections, shaping five collections into the one book of Psalms. The process of editing the Psalter into one book took place over time and was completed following the exile to Babylon. There are several markers of this editorial activity:

1. The editors placed [Psalms 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6) and [2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12) as an introduction to the whole book of Psalms. Both psalms give idealized portraits: [Psalm 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6) portrays the ideal godly person who lives by God’s instruction. [Psalm 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12) portrays the Messiah, the ideal king of Israel. The rest of the Psalter develops and deepens these portraits, while at the same time exploring how neither the people of God nor their king were able to fulfill God’s ideals and bring about the happiness and peace of God’s kingdom.

2. Individual psalms were collected in groups. The editors arranged these groupings of psalms into five collections: Book One ([Pss 1–41](Ps.1.1-Ps.41.13), with a doxology in [41:13](Ps.41.13)), Book Two ([Pss 42–72](Ps.42.1-Ps.72.20), with a doxology in [72:19](Ps.72.19)), Book Three ([Pss 73–89](Ps.73.1-Ps.89.52), with a doxology in [89:52](Ps.89.52)), Book Four ([Pss 90–106](Ps.90.1-Ps.106.48), with a doxology in [106:48](Ps.106.48)), and Book Five ([Pss 107–150](Ps.107.1-Ps.150.6), without a doxology).

3. Books One ([Pss 1–41](Ps.1.1-Ps.41.13)) and Two ([Pss 42–72](Ps.42.1-Ps.72.20)) form the first stage of the collection. The shift from David in Book One ([Pss 3–32](Ps.3.1-Ps.32.11); [34–41](Ps.34.1-Ps.41.13)) to collections of psalms by various authors in Book Two (the descendants of Korah, [Pss 42–49](Ps.42.1-Ps.49.20); Asaph, [Ps 50](Ps.50.1-Ps.50.23); David, [Pss 51–65](Ps.51.1-Ps.65.13); [68–70](Ps.68.1-Ps.70.5); Solomon, [Ps 72](Ps.72.1-Ps.72.20)) reveals a thematic transition from David as the sole model and teacher to other perspectives. At the end of Book Two, the editor comments, “This ends the prayers of David son of Jesse” ([72:20](Ps.72.20)). This comment remained in place even when Books Three, Four, and Five (with additional psalms of David) were added to the collection.

4. Book Three ([Pss 73–89](Ps.73.1-Ps.89.52)) shares with Book Two its preference of the name *Elohim* for God ([Pss 42–83](Ps.42.1-Ps.83.18)) and its diversity of authors (Asaph, [Pss 73–83](Ps.73.1-Ps.83.18); the descendants of Korah, [Pss 84–85](Ps.84.1-Ps.85.13); [87–88](Ps.87.1-Ps.88.18); David, [Ps 86](Ps.86.1-Ps.86.17)). [Psalm 73](Ps.73.1-Ps.73.28), which opens Book Three, questions God’s justice and power, thus calling into doubt the magnificent vision of the messianic kingdom outlined in the final psalm of Book Two ([Ps 72](Ps.72.1-Ps.72.20)). This questioning returns in [Psalm 89](Ps.89.1-Ps.89.52), at the close of Book Three.

5. The psalms of Book Four ([Pss 90–106](Ps.90.1-Ps.106.48)) wrestle with questions raised at the time of the Exile, when it seemed that God’s covenant with David had been dissolved (see [Ps 89](Ps.89.1-Ps.89.52)). In response to this crisis, several psalms encourage individual growth in character and godliness (see [Pss 91–92](Ps.91.1-Ps.92.15)). Most psalms in this collection present God as the true and faithful king whose kingdom extends to every part of creation ([Pss 93–100](Ps.93.1-Ps.100.5)). He still loves his people, the flock of his pasture ([Ps 100](Ps.100.1-Ps.100.5)), but they have to listen to him ([Pss 95](Ps.95.1-Ps.95.11); [100](Ps.100.1-Ps.100.5)). God is the source of forgiveness, and his compassion assures his exiled people that he still cares for them. The review of redemption history from creation to the Exile ([Pss 104–106](Ps.104.1-Ps.106.48)) underscores both God’s wisdom and Israel’s folly as a framework for understanding the Exile.

6. The benediction of [Psalm 106:48](Ps.106.48) is also included in [1 Chronicles 16:36](1Chr.16.36) and might indicate that Book Four was completed in the postexilic era (when Chronicles was compiled).

7. Book Five ([Pss 107–150](Ps.107.1-Ps.150.6)) includes a number of smaller collections: the *Egyptian Hallel* ([Pss 113–118](Ps.113.1-Ps.118.29)); the *Torah Psalm* ([Ps 119](Ps.119.1-Ps.119.176)); the *Great Hallel* ([Pss 120–136](Ps.120.1-Ps.136.26)), which includes the *Songs of Ascents* ([Pss 120–134](Ps.120.1-Ps.134.3)); eight psalms of David ([Pss 138–145](Ps.138.1-Ps.145.21)); and five concluding hymns of praise ([Pss 146–150](Ps.146.1-Ps.150.6)). Book Five sets out the thematic progression of affliction, lament, God’s rescue, and praise. The opening psalm ([Ps 107](Ps.107.1-Ps.107.43)) begins this pattern, and its final verse ([107:43](Ps.107.43)) points to the importance of wisdom in discerning God’s ways. [Psalm 119](Ps.119.1-Ps.119.176), the longest psalm, celebrates the wisdom of God and the word of God. The psalms recounting the Lord’s historic care for Israel in the wilderness ([Pss 114–118](Ps.114.1-Ps.118.29); [135–136](Ps.135.1-Ps.136.26)) prepare exilic and postexilic Israel to read David’s final prayers ([Pss 138–145](Ps.138.1-Ps.145.21)) in a new light: David looked forward to God’s kingdom ([Ps 145](Ps.145.1-Ps.145.21)). The psalms of praise affirm this hope ([Pss 146–150](Ps.146.1-Ps.150.6)).

8. Additions appear to have been made to already-existing psalms. This may explain the prayer for the restoration of Zion ([51:18-19](Ps.51.18-Ps.51.19)) and for God’s blessing on Jerusalem ([69:34-36](Ps.69.34-Ps.69.36)). Changes in circumstances may have occasioned the addition of new stanzas.

9. The available manuscripts reveal some flexibility in the organization and titles of the psalms. Both the Hebrew and Greek editions of the Psalter contain 150 psalms, but with differing divisions and numbering as well as differences regarding which psalms have titles. The Greek text combines both [Psalms 9](Ps.9.1-Ps.9.20) and [10](Ps.10.1-Ps.10.18) and [Psalms 114](Ps.114.1-Ps.114.8) and [115](Ps.115.1-Ps.115.18) into one psalm each, but it splits both [Psalms 116](Ps.116.1-Ps.116.19) and [147](Ps.147.1-Ps.147.20) into two. Differences between the Hebrew and English numbering are indicated in the notes.

By the time of Jesus, the collected Psalter was well known (see [Luke 20:42](Luke.20.42); [Acts 1:20](Acts.1.20)). It was part of the third section of the Hebrew canon, called the Writings (see [Luke 24:44](Luke.24.44)).
Authorship

Many of the psalms are associated with David, but not all; in fact, less than half are explicitly connected with him. Others are connected with Asaph ([Pss 50](Ps.50.1-Ps.50.23); [73–83](Ps.73.1-Ps.83.18)), the descendants of Korah ([Pss 42–49](Ps.42.1-Ps.49.20); [84–85](Ps.84.1-Ps.85.13); [87](Ps.87.1-Ps.87.7)), Solomon ([Pss 72](Ps.72.1-Ps.72.20); [127](Ps.127.1-Ps.127.5)), Heman ([Ps 88](Ps.88.1-Ps.88.18)), Ethan ([Ps 89](Ps.89.1-Ps.89.52)), and Moses ([Ps 90](Ps.90.1-Ps.90.17)).

Of the 116 psalms with a title, most identify a person who is linked to that psalm. The person named may be the author, but not necessarily. The Hebrew preposition *le* before the name (often translated “of”) can also mean “for,” “dedicated to,” “concerning,” “to,” or “by.” So, *ledawid* (often translated “of David”) could be interpreted as “for David,” “dedicated to David,” “concerning David,” or “by David.” While many psalms “of David” may have been written by him, there are several reasons for caution. The titles occasionally have two names, such as David and Jeduthun or Asaph ([Pss 39](Ps.39.1-Ps.39.13), [62](Ps.62.1-Ps.62.12), [77](Ps.77.1-Ps.77.20)). It is possible that the other individual was the actual author of the psalm. Furthermore, the psalms whose titles connect them with an episode of David’s life ([Pss 3](Ps.3.1-Ps.3.8), [7](Ps.7.1-Ps.7.17), [18](Ps.18.1-Ps.18.50), [34](Ps.34.1-Ps.34.22), [51](Ps.51.1-Ps.51.19), [52](Ps.52.1-Ps.52.9), [54](Ps.54.1-Ps.54.7), [56](Ps.56.1-Ps.56.13), [57](Ps.57.1-Ps.57.11), [59](Ps.59.1-Ps.59.17), [60](Ps.60.1-Ps.60.12), [63](Ps.63.1-Ps.63.11), [142](Ps.142.1-Ps.142.7)) provide little or no specific connection with those episodes. For example, the title in [Psalm 51](Ps.51.1-Ps.51.19) connects the psalm with David’s sin and Nathan’s rebuke. The psalm speaks of sin, forgiveness, and a broken spirit, but any specifics of the situation are notoriously absent. In addition, several psalms “of David” seem to assume the existence of the Temple, which was not constructed until after David’s death (see [Ps 5:7](Ps.5.7); [122:title](Ps.122.1); [138:2](Ps.138.2)). Similarly, the title of [Psalm 30](Ps.30.1-Ps.30.12) connects David with the dedication of the Temple, and [Psalm 69](Ps.69.1-Ps.69.36) does not seem to fit with what is known of David’s life. Finally, some textual traditions vary in the mention of David in the heading (e.g., [Pss 122](Ps.122.1-Ps.122.9), [124](Ps.124.1-Ps.124.8)). It is possible, therefore, that *ledawid* should be understood in many cases as meaning “for/dedicated to/concerning David” rather than “by David.” Such psalms evoke his persona as the chief representative of the dynasty without implying that he himself was the author. Still, there are many psalms that could have been authored by David.
Literary Issues

The title *Psalms* comes from the Greek word *psalmos* (“song”; see [Luke 20:42](Luke.20.42); [24:44](Luke.24.44)), which translates the Hebrew *mizmor*, a word frequently found in the titles of individual psalms (e.g., see [Ps 3:title](Ps.3.1), translated “psalm”). The word *mizmor* is related to a verb meaning “to play a stringed instrument.” The psalms were originally accompanied by instruments and were part of the oral tradition of Israel before they were collected. The Hebrew title of the Psalter is *tehillim* (“praises”), a word that is related to *hallelujah* (“praise Yahweh”).

**Psalm Titles.** The psalm titles, or short superscriptions accompanying most of the psalms, give information such as the author, the type of psalm (e.g., song, prayer), a musical notation, the use of the psalm, a historical context, or a dedication. Much of the information is not well understood, so many scholars do not emphasize the psalm titles in the interpretation of the psalms.
In Hebrew editions, the psalm titles are typically numbered as verse 1. As a result, the verse numbers for many entire psalms differ by one from most English translations.

**Interlude (Hebrew Selah).**  This word is found throughout the book of Psalms. The meaning of the word is uncertain, though it is probably a musical or literary term. In the NLT it is consistently rendered *Interlude*.
**Groupings of the Psalms.**  The psalms can be grouped in a number of ways:
• By the names they use for God: *Yahweh* (“the LORD,” [Pss 1–41](Ps.1.1-Ps.41.13)) and *Elohim* (“God,” [Pss 42–72](Ps.42.1-Ps.72.20)).
• By genre (see below).

• By the collections of which they are already a part: e.g., the *Songs of Ascents* ([Pss 120–134](Ps.120.1-Ps.134.3)). Other collections were recognized in Jewish tradition, such as the *Egyptian Hallel* ([Pss 113–118](Ps.113.1-Ps.118.29)) and the hallelujah hymns ([Pss 146–150](Ps.146.1-Ps.150.6)).
• By thematic connections: e.g., God’s kingship ([Pss 93–100](Ps.93.1-Ps.100.5)), or the storyline from creation to the Exile ([Pss 104–106](Ps.104.1-Ps.106.48)).

**Genres of the Psalms.**  The psalm titles often designate the genre of a psalm. The most frequent genre designation in the titles is the Hebrew term *mizmor*, referring to a song originally accompanied by stringed instruments. Less frequent are the words *maskil* (meaning “psalm” or “chant”: [Pss 32](Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11); [42](Ps.42.1-Ps.42.11); [44-45](Ps.44.1-Ps.45.17); [52-55](Ps.52.1-Ps.55.23); [74](Ps.74.1-Ps.74.23); [88–89](Ps.88.1-Ps.89.52)), *miktam* (“psalm” or “chant”: [Pss 16](Ps.16.1-Ps.16.11); [56-60](Ps.56.1-Ps.60.12)), *shir* (“song”: [Pss 45](Ps.45.1-Ps.45.17); [120-135](Ps.120.1-Ps.135.21)), *shiggayon* (“psalm,” a generic or musical term: [Ps 7](Ps.7.1-Ps.7.17)), *tepillah* (“prayer”: [Pss 17](Ps.17.1-Ps.17.15); [86](Ps.86.1-Ps.86.17); [90](Ps.90.1-Ps.90.17)), *tehillah* (“psalm of praise”: [Ps 145](Ps.145.1-Ps.145.21)), *higgayon* (“meditation,” meaning unknown: [Ps 9:16](Ps.9.16)), and *todah* (“psalm of thanksgiving”: [Ps 100](Ps.100.1-Ps.100.5)).
In addition to the genre identifications that are found in the Hebrew text, the psalms may be divided into three main categories:
2. Psalms of lament (most psalms in books 1—3), which can be subdivided into individual laments and community laments

3. Hymns of praise or thanksgiving ([Pss 8](Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9), [19](Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14), [29](Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11), [65](Ps.65.1-Ps.65.13), [67](Ps.67.1-Ps.67.7), [114](Ps.114.1-Ps.114.8)), which can similarly be divided into individual and community hymns

The psalms of praise include several subgenres, including “royal” psalms about the king ([Pss 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12), [45](Ps.45.1-Ps.45.17), [72](Ps.72.1-Ps.72.20), [89](Ps.89.1-Ps.89.52), [110](Ps.110.1-Ps.110.7)); psalms ascribing kingship to the Lord ([Pss 93](Ps.93.1-Ps.93.5), [95-99](Ps.95.1-Ps.99.9)); hymns about creation ([Pss 19](Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14), [29](Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11), [104](Ps.104.1-Ps.104.35)); and hymns about Zion ([Pss 46](Ps.46.1-Ps.46.11), [48](Ps.48.1-Ps.48.14), [84](Ps.84.1-Ps.84.12), [87](Ps.87.1-Ps.87.7)).

Another way of reading the psalms is based on the movement in many psalms from instruction to a problem and from a problem to a renewal in commitment and character. The Psalter as a collection of five books is largely instructional in nature. It is “instruction” (*torah*; see [1:2](Ps.1.2)) and has the purpose of teaching God’s people how to live.
The Psalms in Israel’s Worship

The book of Psalms contains much information on music making in ancient Israel. The majority of psalms are songs of praise, thanksgiving, prayer, and repentance. Some of the psalms were used on specific occasions, such as at Passover ([Pss 113–118](Ps.113.1-Ps.118.29), or when journeying to Jerusalem for the annual festivals ([Pss 120–134](Ps.120.1-Ps.134.3). There are also historic odes that relate great national events (for example, [Ps 30](Ps.30.1-Ps.30.12), “a song for the dedication of the Temple,” and [Ps 137](Ps.137.1-Ps.137.9), which portrays the sufferings of the Jews in captivity). Such psalms played a role in the life of the community; however, the exact nature of that role is uncertain.
Meaning and Message
The psalms provide windows into the souls of the ancient saints who wrote them. Their theological reflections are not easy or simple-minded, but the psalmists’ faith, when tried, is purified.

The psalms model depth of character, wisdom, honesty, and authenticity. But the prayers in the Psalter are more than models to be imitated. They are God’s instructions for righteous living, part of his *torah* (“instruction”; see [Pss 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6); [19](Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14); [119](Ps.119.1-Ps.119.176)). God teaches who he is, what he has done, and what he expects from his people. The psalms are God-centered, instructing his people to discern error in themselves, to receive his correction, and to be like him. They also encourage God’s people to worship him vibrantly and to bear witness about him to the world.

The psalmists reflected on the transitory nature of life, on suffering, and on the many kinds of adversity that human beings experience. As the psalmists faced alienation and pain, they longed for God’s presence, provision, and protection (e.g., [Ps 23](Ps.23.1-Ps.23.6)), and for a lasting glory. Even the psalms connected with David often reveal a humble rather than a victorious David—humiliated rather than glorious. The psalmists experienced alienation and shame, and they longed for redemption, trusting in the Lord to vindicate them.

The Psalter illustrates the failures of Israel and of David’s dynasty. The best of the godly Israelites and kings were unable to bring the happiness and peace that [Psalms 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6) and [2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.11) speak of (see also [Ps 72](Ps.72.1-Ps.72.20)). The psalms are thus God’s exhortation to each person to cultivate wisdom, to trust in him, to live by grace, and to have hope in the one who can bring blessings to a needy world.

The psalms prepare God’s people for the coming of Jesus Christ as the perfect human and ideal king, the descendant of David who has absolute integrity. Jesus and the apostles understood Jesus’ life and ministry in light of the psalms (see [Matt 13:34-35](Matt.13.34-Matt.13.35); [21:16](Matt.21.16), [42](Matt.21.42); [23:39](Matt.23.39); [John 2:17](John.2.17); [15:25](John.15.25); [19:24](John.19.24), [28](John.19.28), [36](John.19.36); [Acts 2:22-35](Acts.2.22-Acts.2.35); [4:11](Acts.4.11); [13:32-38](Acts.13.32-Acts.13.38); [Rom 15:3](Rom.15.3); [1 Cor 15:25-27](1Cor.15.25-1Cor.15.27); [Eph 4:7-10](Eph.4.7-Eph.4.10); [1 Pet 2:7](1Pet.2.7)). Jesus entered the world of humans and lived out the patterns found in the psalms, including humiliation, suffering, death, vindication, and glory. He is the only human being who has completely pleased God ([Ps 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6)). He is the Messiah and King ([Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12)) who has become our means of redemption, happiness, and peace.

b.x: The first two psalms are an introduction to the entire Psalter. [Psalm 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6) introduces the Lord’s instruction in wisdom, while [Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12) introduces God’s rule over a rebellious, sinful world. Together, these psalms invite people to leave the way of folly that leads to destruction and to enter the way of God that leads to wisdom and salvation. The New Testament affirms that God will rule the nations through Jesus Christ, his appointed agent ([Heb 1:5](Heb.1.5); [Rev 12:5](Rev.12.5); [19:15](Rev.19.15)).

This wisdom psalm sets the tone for the whole Psalter. The psalmist strongly contrasts the happiness of the godly with the condemnation of the wicked; in the end, the way of wisdom will triumph. This idealization of the godly person (as in [Ps 8](Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9)) highlights the Lord’s expectations of his people and especially of the coming Messiah ([Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12)). The people of Israel did not live up to this ideal, and neither did the kings of David’s dynasty. Not even the best of them could bring in the triumph of righteousness described in [Psalms 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6), [2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12), [and 72](Ps.72.1-Ps.72.20). In the New Testament, the apostles’ use of the Psalter to describe the life and ministry of Jesus the Messiah confirms that Jesus alone fulfills the ideal of the godly person presented in the psalms. Only Jesus could please God and secure redemption, happiness, and peace. [Psalm 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6) introduces the hopeful anticipation of the final hallelujah ([Ps 150](Ps.150.1-Ps.150.6)), when the Lord will remove all evil from his creation and prosper his children.
The Lord gives true happiness to all who reject evil and delight in him.
Pss 1–8

[Psalms 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6) and [8](Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9) form an *inclusio* (set of literary bookends) that describes what God expects of the ideal person (cp. [Pss 19](Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14); [33](Ps.33.1-Ps.33.22); [104](Ps.104.1-Ps.104.35); [145](Ps.145.1-Ps.145.21)), contrasts the godly person with the wicked, and extols the godly person’s dignity. Jesus the Messiah ([Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12))—the sovereign Lord ([Heb 2:6-8](Heb.2.6-Heb.2.8); see [1 Cor 15:27](1Cor.15.27)) and perfection of humanity—embodies this ideal.

**Oh, the joys:** This Hebrew term (*’ashrey*) is used twenty-six times in Psalms. Some translations render it as “blessed,” but a different term (*barak*) is used in contexts of blessing ([5:12](Ps.5.12); [45:2](Ps.45.2); [107:38](Ps.107.38)).

The godly do not permit themselves to live under the influence of sinners. Those who do not fear the Lord are **wicked** ([36:1](Ps.36.1)); they are the enemies of those who love God, those who do right, and the poor and oppressed (see [10:2-13](Ps.10.2-Ps.10.13); [37:14](Ps.37.14)). The wicked might appear pious ([50:16](Ps.50.16)) and sometimes enjoy temporary prosperity ([37:35](Ps.37.35)), but sorrow ([32:10](Ps.32.10)) and destruction ([1:4-6](Ps.1.4-Ps.1.6)) await them when their deeds catch up with them ([9:16](Ps.9.16)).
Those who go astray ([25:8](Ps.25.8)) in rebellion against the Lord ([78:17](Ps.78.17)) are **sinners***;* they commit heinous crimes such as adultery and murder (cp. [Ps 51](Ps.51.1-Ps.51.19)).
**join in with:** This expression (literally *sit in the seat of*) depicts a life in bondage to sin (cp. [1:2](Ps.1.2); [26:3-7](Ps.26.3-Ps.26.7); [Deut 6:7](Deut.6.7)).

**Mockers** hate the Lord, scorn his wisdom, and insult anyone who attempts to correct them ([Prov 9:7-8](Prov.9.7-Prov.9.8)). They seek only the “wisdom” that justifies their actions. These brash people have little regard for the Lord, his plans, or his children (see [Pss 86:14](Ps.86.14); [119:51](Ps.119.51), [69](Ps.119.69), [78](Ps.119.78), [85](Ps.119.85), [122](Ps.119.122)). These three terms (wicked, sinners, mockers) apply to all kinds of ungodly people.
The **law** (Hebrew *torah*) **of the** **LORD** is the full revelation of God’s instructions (see study note on Deut 4:44).

**Meditating** is a process of inner reflection that can be positive ([Pss 1:2](Ps.1.2); [63:6](Ps.63.6); [77:12](Ps.77.12); [143:5](Ps.143.5)) or negative (see [2:1](Ps.2.1); [38:12](Ps.38.12)). The Lord’s word is the object of godly meditation ([119:48](Ps.119.48)).
**Day and night** includes all times, whether one is walking, standing, sitting, or sleeping (see [Deut 6:7](Deut.6.7)).
The future belongs to the godly.
Well-watered **trees** endure and bear abundant fruit (cp. [Jer 17:8](Jer.17.8)).
The coming time of judgment ([1:5](Ps.1.5)) will carry off **the wicked** and their deeds ([35:5](Ps.35.5); [83:13](Ps.83.13); [Isa 17:13](Isa.17.13); see study note on Jer 13:24).
The wicked cannot abide the scrutiny of the Lord’s **judgment***;* they are already **condemned** (see [5:5](Ps.5.5); [7:6](Ps.7.6); [101:7](Ps.101.7)).

The Lord’s care for the righteous and the demise of the wicked both demonstrate the Lord’s principle of retribution (see [Gal 6:7-10](Gal.6.7-Gal.6.10)). The brief and futile lives of the wicked will end, whereas the Lord and his saints will triumph (see [Pss 9:5](Ps.9.5), [6](Ps.9.6), [18](Ps.9.18); [10:16](Ps.10.16); [37:20](Ps.37.20); [73:27](Ps.73.27); [92:9](Ps.92.9); cp. [142:4](Ps.142.4); [Isa 57:1](Isa.57.1)).

The godly (see [Pss 5:12](Ps.5.12); [14:5](Ps.14.5)) are joyful ([1:1](Ps.1.1)) because **the** **LORD** protects and cares for them, hears them when they cry out for justice, and secures their future (see [121:3-4](Ps.121.3-Ps.121.4)).
A person’s **path** is their life and character.

This royal psalm pertains to the Lord’s appointment of a king descended from David. It celebrates the mission of all the kings in David’s line, and it introduces the hope of an ideal ruler who will accomplish the Lord’s goal of bringing all nations into submission ([2:11](Ps.2.11)) or to destruction ([2:9](Ps.2.9)). The New Testament identifies Jesus as this descendant (see [Acts 13:33](Acts.13.33); [1 Cor 15:25-27](1Cor.15.25-1Cor.15.27); [Heb 1:5](Heb.1.5); [5:5](Heb.5.5); [Rev 19:15](Rev.19.15)).
Their futile paths lead to death ([1:4](Ps.1.4), [6](Ps.1.6)), but fallen human beings unite in opposing the true God and his Messiah.

**plans:** The Hebrew verb rendered “meditate” in [1:2](Ps.1.2) here suggests an attitude of opposing the Lord in speech ([Isa 59:13](Isa.59.13)) or in thought ([Ps 38:12](Ps.38.12); [Prov 24:2](Prov.24.2)).

**The kings** hate the Lord’s established order in the world, so they desire to be independent of him (see [36:4](Ps.36.4)). They scheme about dominating the Lord’s people ([31:13](Ps.31.13); see [83:1-4](Ps.83.1-Ps.83.4)). Their goal is to subvert the Lord’s rule in the world by overthrowing **his anointed one** (or *his messiah*); the Lord chose the kings of David’s dynasty to establish his kingdom throughout the earth. The New Testament confirms that Jesus, the appointed and anointed Son of God ([Acts 4:26](Acts.4.26); [13:33](Acts.13.33); [Heb 1:5](Heb.1.5); [5:5](Heb.5.5)), fulfills the role in which these earlier kings failed.

**break their chains:** These kings believe that acknowledging the true God and his chosen ruler will result in their enslavement ([Isa 28:22](Isa.28.22); [52:2](Isa.52.2); cp. [Lam 3:7](Lam.3.7); [Rom 1:1](Rom.1.1); [1 Cor 7:22](1Cor.7.22); [Titus 1:1](Titus.1.1)).

The Lord finds the human threat insignificant. He provided a solution long before their rebellion. He will end their agitation through the appointment of a human agent, a descendant of David’s line who will rule the nations.

**rules in heaven:** The Lord’s place in the universe is so certain that he **scoffs** at humans who boast that they can rebel against his power and authority (see [37:13](Ps.37.13); [59:8](Ps.59.8)).
**my chosen king:** The Lord establishes his anointed ruler.
The Lord adopted **the king** of David’s dynasty to conquer rebellious **nations** by force (see [89:26-27](Ps.89.26-Ps.89.27)).

**Today I have become your Father:** People in the ancient Near East commonly accepted a father-son relationship between gods and kings. In Israel, the Lord adopted kings as his sons. God set David apart as his most excellent and exalted son ([89:27](Ps.89.27)). All descendants of David were the Lord’s representatives or agents. As an eternal member of the Godhead ([John 1:1](John.1.1)) and a descendant of David ([Acts 13:33](Acts.13.33); [Heb 1:5](Heb.1.5); [5:5](Heb.5.5)), Jesus is the true Son of God.

In an example of the suzerain-vassal relationship between the Lord and Israel’s king (see Deuteronomy Book Introduction, “Literary Form”), the Lord invites the king to **ask** for favors (see [Ps 21:2](Ps.21.2), [4](Ps.21.4)).
All nations will be subject to David’s descendant, the Messiah.

The Lord gives his anointed ruler the power to conquer the nations as his inheritance ([Isa 11:4](Isa.11.4); [Rev 2:27](Rev.2.27); [12:5](Rev.12.5); [19:15](Rev.19.15)), breaking their rebellion, resistance, and independence.
It pleases the Lord when his people submit to him and seek his protection. The wise accept the Lord’s rebuke and desire to repent.
**rejoice:** Rulers must welcome the Son as their true and only King.
**Submit to God’s royal son** (or *Submit to God’s royal Son,* or *kiss the son*): Kissing was an expression of submission ([Hos 13:2](Hos.13.2)).

This group of psalms moves readers from the orderly world of [Pss 1–2](Ps.1.1-Ps.2.12) to a disoriented one. The Lord’s anointed cries out while facing enemies, ferocious opposition, evil schemes, and the Lord’s apparent distance.

This psalm laments that the expectations raised by [Pss 1–2](Ps.1.1-Ps.2.12) have not been met. But even when beset by enemies, godly people need not question the Lord’s just dealings. Rather, they can confidently trust his goodness and expect God to rescue them.

The psalmist’s **many enemies** speak brashly ([4:6](Ps.4.6); [12:4](Ps.12.4); [40:15](Ps.40.15)) and question the Lord’s ability to rescue ([10:11](Ps.10.11); [22:7-8](Ps.22.7-Ps.22.8); [71:10](Ps.71.10)). Their words haunt him because it seems that the Lord will not answer his prayer.
These enemies wield great power (cp. [2:1-3](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.3)); unlike [Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12), this psalm does not resolve the crisis.
3:title

This sad episode in David’s life (see [2 Sam 15–18](2Sam.15.1-2Sam.18.33)) helps readers keep the promises of [Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12) in perspective. The Lord granted victory to his anointed king ([Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12)), but the manner and timing of this victory remained in God’s hands.
The psalmist’s eyes turn from his enemies to the Lord.
The psalmist contrasts the contention of his enemies ([3:2](Ps.3.2)) with the Lord’s provision. The Lord is a **shield** for his people; he turns their defeat and shame into victory and **glory**.

By refocusing on the Lord ([3:3-4](Ps.3.3-Ps.3.4)) in the midst of his crisis, the psalmist can rest, confident of his **safety** (see study note on 4:8). The Lord cares for his servant; he protects him and keeps his mind and heart from fear ([37:17](Ps.37.17); [54:4](Ps.54.4); [119:116](Ps.119.116); [145:14](Ps.145.14)).

The psalmist’s peaceful confidence in the Lord’s protection and care shields him from evil and gives him a new sense of reality ([23:4](Ps.23.4); [27:1](Ps.27.1), [3](Ps.27.3); [46:1](Ps.46.1); [56:4](Ps.56.4), [11](Ps.56.11); [91:5-6](Ps.91.5-Ps.91.6); [118:6](Ps.118.6)).
The psalmist does not seek revenge; instead, he waits for the Lord’s vengeance.
**Arise:** The psalmist calls upon the Lord to take action now.

This individual lament includes a prayer for rescue ([4:1](Ps.4.1)), a rebuke of the adversary ([4:2-3](Ps.4.2-Ps.4.3)), an exhortation to the godly ([4:4-5](Ps.4.4-Ps.4.5)), and an expression of confidence ([4:6-8](Ps.4.6-Ps.4.8)).
Waiting for the Lord’s **answer** allows for growth in patience and for the refinement of living faith ([38:15](Ps.38.15)).
The opponents of the godly place their hope in delusions, treachery, and idolatry.
**my reputation** (or *my glory*): The honor of the psalmist, or possibly of the Lord, is at stake.
Angry feelings are not sinful, but **letting anger control you** leads to sin (see [37:7-8](Ps.37.7-Ps.37.8); cp. [Eph 4:26-27](Eph.4.26-Eph.4.27), [31-32](Eph.4.31-Eph.4.32)).

Instead of acting on their emotions, the godly **think about** their circumstances **overnight**. They might be disturbed as they sleep, but silence opens their hearts to trust in the Lord ([Ps 4:5](Ps.4.5)).
**Offer sacrifices in the right spirit:** Redirecting emotions toward the Lord prevents a godly individual from doing too much self-reflection ([40:6-8](Ps.40.6-Ps.40.8); [51:17](Ps.51.17)).

**your face** (or *the light of your face*): The psalmist seeks God’s favor and peace ([Num 6:25-26](Num.6.25-Num.6.26)), which can transform darkness into light (see [Ps 27:1](Ps.27.1)). Confident trust in the Lord is an antidote to anger, resentment, jealousy, and materialism.
**Peace** comes from God’s blessing and protection ([4:6](Ps.4.6); see [37:11](Ps.37.11)).

This morning prayer ([5:3](Ps.5.3)) expresses unwavering confidence in the Lord’s help and protection. The psalmist asks for and awaits God’s response ([5:1-3](Ps.5.1-Ps.5.3)). He describes the schemes of the wicked in detail but does not get lost in his circumstances. The psalmist also knows that the wicked cannot coexist with God ([5:4-6](Ps.5.4-Ps.5.6), [9](Ps.5.9); see [1:5](Ps.1.5)). He keeps returning to the Lord ([5:7-8](Ps.5.7-Ps.5.8), [10](Ps.5.10); see [5:1-3](Ps.5.1-Ps.5.3)), and then he prays for the godly community ([5:10-12](Ps.5.10-Ps.5.12); see [3:8](Ps.3.8)).

The request **hear me** appears in several prayers as a call for God’s attention during a time of trouble ([39:12](Ps.39.12); [84:8](Ps.84.8); [143:1](Ps.143.1)), as does **pay attention** ([17:1](Ps.17.1); [54:2](Ps.54.2); [130:2](Ps.130.2)). The needy ask their God, “Are you listening?”
The psalmist begins and ends each day with prayer, awaiting new expressions of God’s fidelity and goodness ([143:8](Ps.143.8)).
**wait expectantly:** The psalmist does not demand God’s grace but places hope in it (see [Mic 7:7](Mic.7.7); [Hab 2:1](Hab.2.1)).
**the proud:** Mockers (see study note on 1:1), the wicked ([73:3](Ps.73.3); [75:4](Ps.75.4)), and the arrogant ([10:2](Ps.10.2)) use their mouths to twist truth and challenge the faith of the godly.
The Lord allows only the godly into his **presence** (see [1:5](Ps.1.5)). His holiness and justice do not tolerate oppression or those **who do evil**.
**you hate:** The Lord rejects proud sinners (see also [11:5](Ps.11.5)).
God promises his **unfailing love**—his covenant goodness and faithfulness—to his people (see [25:6](Ps.25.6); [69:16](Ps.69.16); [Lam 3:32](Lam.3.32)).
**your house:** The godly long to come into God’s presence with reverence and awe (see [Heb 12:28](Heb.12.28)).

God guides those who are obedient, submissive, and patient in waiting for him to **lead***,* provide, and protect them ([27:11](Ps.27.11); [43:3](Ps.43.3); [143:10](Ps.143.10)), not those who expect God simply to endorse their own decisions.
Following **the right path** of wisdom leads to the Lord ([27:11](Ps.27.11); [61:2](Ps.61.2); [139:24](Ps.139.24)).
The psalmist again describes the vile acts of the wicked, who cannot stand in God’s presence.
The psalmist prays for the justice and retribution that God promised against the wicked ([1:6](Ps.1.6))—those who have **rebelled against** the Lord.
The wicked lay **traps** to kill ([38:12](Ps.38.12)) or deceive ([140:4-5](Ps.140.4-Ps.140.5)).
A blessing rests on **all who take refuge in** God (see [18:30](Ps.18.30)).

Joy and praise make good companions. The godly **rejoice** when they see evidence of God’s rescue. They **sing joyful praises** as a new song (see [33:3](Ps.33.3)). When the Lord restores peace to this world, puts down evil, and rewards the righteous, they will have lasting **joy** ([9:2-4](Ps.9.2-Ps.9.4); [53:6](Ps.53.6); [90:14-15](Ps.90.14-Ps.90.15); [118:24](Ps.118.24)).
The children of God, who find refuge in him, **love** his **name**. To love his name is to love his very character.
The psalmist extends his concern beyond himself to all the **godly.**
A **shield***,* here an image of God’s protection, deflects spears and arrows from its bearer.
The occasion for this lament might have been sickness or a mental or spiritual depression from which the psalmist sought healing.
The psalmist asks for God’s favor and restoration at a difficult time.
**don’t rebuke me . . . or discipline me:** The psalmist does not explicitly connect God’s discipline with sin here (cp. [39:8-11](Ps.39.8-Ps.39.11)), but it might be implied.

In his longing for God’s response to his prayer, the psalmist grew physically **weak** ([6:6](Ps.6.6); see [77:3](Ps.77.3); [119:81](Ps.119.81); [142:1-3](Ps.142.1-Ps.142.3); see also [Ps 101](Ps.101.1-Ps.101.8)). Fasting might have played a part in his **agony***,* but this is not mentioned.
The experience was so painful that the psalmist might as well have been **dead***,* or perhaps he feared for his life.
**from the grave?** Hebrew *from Sheol?* In the Old Testament, Sheol is the abode of the dead. It is not necessarily associated with punishment.
The psalmist is exhausted to the depths of his being from the anguish of his spiritual distance from the Lord ([22:1](Ps.22.1); [31:9-10](Ps.31.9-Ps.31.10); [102:5](Ps.102.5)).
When **eyes** dim, the body is failing (see [13:3](Ps.13.3); [31:9](Ps.31.9); [38:10](Ps.38.10); [Matt 6:22](Matt.6.22)).
In a closing note of triumph, the psalmist reasserts his confidence in the Lord.

This psalm consists of a lament ([7:1-2](Ps.7.1-Ps.7.2)), an oath of innocence ([7:3-5](Ps.7.3-Ps.7.5)), an appeal to God’s justice ([7:6-9](Ps.7.6-Ps.7.9)), an affirmation of God’s just kingship ([7:10-16](Ps.7.10-Ps.7.16)), and a concluding hymn of praise ([7:17](Ps.7.17)).
7:title
**Cush***,* an unknown person **of the tribe of Benjamin***,* remained hostile to David.
**Persecutors** (a common term for “enemies”) intentionally seek out people in order to destroy them ([31:15](Ps.31.15); [56:1-2](Ps.56.1-Ps.56.2); [71:11](Ps.71.11); [143:3](Ps.143.3)).

**Like a lion***,* a wicked enemy relentlessly and violently pursues its prey ([10:9](Ps.10.9); [17:12](Ps.17.12); [22:13](Ps.22.13), [21](Ps.22.21); [35:17](Ps.35.17); [57:4](Ps.57.4)), but God promises victory ([91:13](Ps.91.13)).
The psalmist swears to his innocence, making himself vulnerable to scrutiny ([7:9](Ps.7.9).
The psalmist does not claim to be without sin, but he knows that he does not deserve the brutal attacks of his opponents (see [35:7](Ps.35.7)).
**into the ground . . . in the dust:** Disgrace and shame can lead to death and the grave ([143:3](Ps.143.3); see [13:3-4](Ps.13.3-Ps.13.4)).
With this appeal to God for justice in the world, the psalmist also submits to God’s examination.
God’s judgment brings **justice***,* despite the chaos created by adversaries (see [7:11](Ps.7.11)).
The judgment is against the defendants (the nations) and in favor of the **righteous** plaintiff (the psalmist; see [43:1](Ps.43.1)).

Although not **innocent** of all sin, the psalmist is a person of authentic integrity (see [15:2](Ps.15.2); [25:21](Ps.25.21); [41:12](Ps.41.12); [78:72](Ps.78.72); cp. [Job 1:1](Job.1.1), [8](Job.1.8); [9:20](Job.9.20), [22](Job.9.22)).
God examines **the mind and heart** of each person (see [11:3-4](Ps.11.3-Ps.11.4); [26:2](Ps.26.2); [139:1](Ps.139.1), [23](Ps.139.23)).

The psalmist moves from his own situation ([7:1-9](Ps.7.1-Ps.7.9)) to speak for all the godly who long for redemption ([7:10-16](Ps.7.10-Ps.7.16)). He depicts God as the righteous King who vindicates his subjects when they cry out for rescue.
The **honest** Lord cannot be bought or bribed, nor does he abuse his power ([9:4](Ps.9.4); cp. [82:1-8](Ps.82.1-Ps.82.8)).
**sword . . . bow . . . deadly weapons . . . flaming arrows:** As the Divine Warrior, **God** goes on the offensive on behalf of himself and his people.
**Evil** begins with small words or steps, and gives **birth** to increasingly worse deeds as time goes on (see [Isa 59:4-5](Isa.59.4-Isa.59.5)).
**I will thank . . . sing praise:** The laments in [Pss 3–7](Ps.3.1-Ps.7.17) usually move from lament to praise, as does the Psalter as a whole.
**Most High:** This is an ancient designation for God (see [Gen 14:19](Gen.14.19)).
God is **just** and reliable, so his order prevails in this world.

[Psalm 8](Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9) opens the second segment of Book One ([Pss 8–14](Ps.8.1-Ps.14.7)). The psalmist celebrates God’s creation and the dignity of the ideal human being (see [Ps 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6)). Instead of the world of enemies, wicked people, and distorted justice that is presented in [Pss 3–7](Ps.3.1-Ps.7.17), this psalm promotes an image of the world as God originally created it. A weary person can envision a place of dignity in God’s world.
The **LORD** (Hebrew *Yahweh*), the covenant God of Israel ([Exod 3:15](Exod.3.15)), also holds the title of **Lord** (Hebrew *’adonay*), the king of the earth.

The word translated **majestic** (sometimes translated “mighty”) can describe kings ([Ps 136:18](Ps.136.18)), heroes ([16:3](Ps.16.3)), mountains ([76:4](Ps.76.4)), or waves breaking on the seashore ([93:4](Ps.93.4)). While all are awe-inspiring and mighty, the created order pales in comparison with the Lord.
A person’s **name** embodies their reputation.
**The earth** and **the heavens** reveal the Lord’s splendor. All creation worships and praises the Lord ([66:4](Ps.66.4); [113:3](Ps.113.3); [145:21](Ps.145.21)).

**silencing:** The loud noise of the oppressors contrasts with the praise of God. In the end, the praise of God will overwhelm the sound of evil ([31:18](Ps.31.18); [63:11](Ps.63.11); [101:5](Ps.101.5); [143:12](Ps.143.12)).
Those who **oppose** God seethe with vindictive anger ([2:1-3](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.3); [44:16](Ps.44.16); cp. [149:6-7](Ps.149.6-Ps.149.7)).
In light of God’s awesome glory, it might seem that people would be insignificant to him. However, he has **crowned them with glory and honor** and placed them over all creation.

The nations around Israel worshiped heavenly objects as deities. The sun, **moon***,* and **stars** are indeed immense and glorious, but they are merely **the work of your fingers,** a reason to praise the Almighty.

**human beings** (literally *son of Adam*): The Hebrew idiom *son of man* (or *son of Adam*) means a human being. Through the influence of [Dan 7:13-14](Dan.7.13-Dan.7.14), it became a title with divine overtones in the New Testament. See [Heb 2:6-8](Heb.2.6-Heb.2.8), where this passage is quoted.

**Yet you made them only a little lower than God:** Humans bear God’s image; the Lord has endowed humans with dignity and charged them to rule ([Gen 1:26-27](Gen.1.26-Gen.1.27)). [Hebrews 2:6-8](Heb.2.6-Heb.2.8) applies these words to Jesus Christ, the ideal human who fully realized God’s purposes.

**gave them charge of everything:** The psalmist is still referring to humans in general. Paul applies these words to Jesus as the perfect man who has made the created order—even death ([1 Cor 15:25-27](1Cor.15.25-1Cor.15.27))—subject to God and his glory. The New Testament connects these themes of creation and salvation with Jesus Christ ([John 1:1-2](John.1.1-John.1.2), [14](John.1.14); [Col 1:16](Col.1.16)).

**Wild animals***,* including **birds** and **fish***,* remind readers of God’s creation of the animal world in [Gen 1](Gen.1.1-Gen.1.31). Contrary to beliefs among Israel’s neighbors in the ancient Near East, animals are not sacred.

This hymn celebrates the Lord’s kingship and victory over evil. It might also serve as a response to the laments of [Pss 3–7](Ps.3.1-Ps.7.17). Some believe that [Pss 9](Ps.9.1-Ps.9.20) and [10](Ps.10.1-Ps.10.18) should be read together as one psalm in two parts because [Ps 9](Ps.9.1-Ps.9.20) includes a title and [Ps 10](Ps.10.1-Ps.10.18) does not, and although several letters are missing or inverted, the two psalms connect as an acrostic of the Hebrew alphabet (other such alphabetic acrostics are [Pss 25](Ps.25.1-Ps.25.22), [34](Ps.34.1-Ps.34.22), [37](Ps.37.1-Ps.37.40), [111–112](Ps.111.1-Ps.112.10), [119](Ps.119.1-Ps.119.176), [145](Ps.145.1-Ps.145.21)). The ancient Greek and Latin translations treat 9 and 10 as one.
9:title

This psalm was originally **sung to the tune “Death of the Son***,***”** but that tune is no longer known. So also with the tunes mentioned in [Pss 22](Ps.22.1-Ps.22.31), [45](Ps.45.1-Ps.45.17), [56–60](Ps.56.1-Ps.60.12), [69](Ps.69.1-Ps.69.36), [75](Ps.75.1-Ps.75.10), [and 80](Ps.80.1-Ps.80.19).

The verb translated **praise** is translated “thank” in [7:17](Ps.7.17), suggesting a close connection between [Pss 7](Ps.7.1-Ps.7.17) and [9](Ps.9.1-Ps.9.20) (see [7:17](Ps.7.17); [8:1-2](Ps.8.1-Ps.8.2)). **With all my heart** expresses the psalmist’s deep devotion and commitment ([86:12](Ps.86.12); [111:1](Ps.111.1); [119:10](Ps.119.10); [138:1](Ps.138.1)).

**I will tell:** These stories educate the next generation ([78:4](Ps.78.4); [145:4](Ps.145.4)); when they are not remembered, a generation might easily depart from the Lord ([78:11](Ps.78.11), [32](Ps.78.32)).

The **marvelous things** include the Lord’s judgments on the enemies of his people ([9:4](Ps.9.4)) and his care for the oppressed ([9:9](Ps.9.9)). The wonders in creation, in redemption, and in revelation reveal his character and show his power ([89:5](Ps.89.5); [111:4](Ps.111.4); [119:18](Ps.119.18), [27](Ps.119.27)). His powerful manifestations evoke public praise ([9:1](Ps.9.1); [26:7](Ps.26.7); [75:1](Ps.75.1)).

**filled with joy . . . sing praises:** The psalmist often connects joy with praises, as one leads to the other ([5:11-12](Ps.5.11-Ps.5.12); [32:11](Ps.32.11); [67:4](Ps.67.4); [90:14](Ps.90.14); [92:4](Ps.92.4)).
The psalmist celebrates God’s judgment of the wicked, which is a testimony to the Lord’s reliable promise to establish his kingdom on earth ([1:6](Ps.1.6); [Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12)).
**retreated . . . staggered:** The Lord overpowers even powerful **enemies** (see [27:2](Ps.27.2)). Israel also experienced judgment when it resisted the Lord ([107:12](Ps.107.12)).
The **throne** represents the Lord’s royal authority.

God created the heavens and the earth with a word ([Gen 1](Gen.1.1-Gen.1.31)), and he can bring **nations** to an end with a word (see [Ps 2:5](Ps.2.5)). Evil and those who do evil will come to an absolute end ([69:28](Ps.69.28); [109:13](Ps.109.13); [Rev 21:4](Rev.21.4)).
The godly do not put their hope in corruptible human government but in God’s everlasting rule of **justice** and **fairness** (see [Pss 96–100](Ps.96.1-Ps.100.5)).

The Lord provides **shelter** in dangerous circumstances and **refuge** from powerful and oppressive people. The Psalter includes many similar images of the Lord, such as fortress ([18:2](Ps.18.2); [31:2](Ps.31.2)), rock ([18:2](Ps.18.2); [42:9](Ps.42.9)), strength ([18:1](Ps.18.1)), and strong tower ([144:2](Ps.144.2)). These images occur frequently in the royal prayers (see [9:9](Ps.9.9); [18:30](Ps.18.30)).
Even **oppressed***,* afflicted, and marginalized people ([10:17](Ps.10.17); [74:21](Ps.74.21)) can enjoy divine protection.

The **times of trouble** ([10:1](Ps.10.1); [20:1](Ps.20.1)) stand in contrast with appointed times when the Lord openly bestows his favor upon the afflicted ([69:13](Ps.69.13); [102:13](Ps.102.13); see [Ps 107:6](Ps.107.6)).

Alienation from the Lord might be part of an individual’s experience ([22:1](Ps.22.1); [42:9](Ps.42.9); [119:8](Ps.119.8)), yet the psalms affirm that the Lord will not **abandon** his people ([16:10](Ps.16.10); [37:25](Ps.37.25), [28](Ps.37.28)).

Recognition that the Lord’s judgment falls on some of the wicked ([9:3-6](Ps.9.3-Ps.9.6)) and that God promises to judge all evil ([9:7-10](Ps.9.7-Ps.9.10)) motivates praise. The psalmist calls on the godly community to join him.

The psalm writers often connect the idea that God **reigns** (or *sits,* or *is enthroned*) with a place, such as heaven ([2:4](Ps.2.4); see [47:9](Ps.47.9)), **Jerusalem***,* “between the cherubim” ([80:1](Ps.80.1); [99:1](Ps.99.1)), “on high” ([113:5](Ps.113.5)), or “at my right hand” ([110:1](Ps.110.1)). Since the Lord rules the **world***,* all people must know of **his unforgettable deeds** of salvation (see [9:1](Ps.9.1); [64:9](Ps.64.9); [66:16](Ps.66.16); [105:1](Ps.105.1)).

The Lord **avenges** and saves his servants ([18:46](Ps.18.46)) by righteously judging his enemies on earth ([58:11](Ps.58.11)). The godly do not seek revenge; they wait for the Lord to vindicate them ([94:1-2](Ps.94.1-Ps.94.2); [Deut 32:35](Deut.32.35); [Rom 12:19](Rom.12.19)).
The psalmist returns from a vision of the glorious future to the reality of facing his **enemies** ([9:3](Ps.9.3)).
The **jaws** (literally *gates)* are a vivid image of the powerful grip of **death** (see [13:3-4](Ps.13.3-Ps.13.4)).
**Jerusalem’s gates** provide an intentional contrast to the “gates” of death.

Hope requires waiting for the Lord’s rescue or justice ([25:3](Ps.25.3), [5](Ps.25.5), [21](Ps.25.21)). The godly find hope, rest, and quietness as they await the Lord (see [1:6](Ps.1.6); [27:14](Ps.27.14)).
The psalmist ends his lament with a prayer for the Lord’s intervention and divine vengeance.
**mere mortals . . . merely human:** Humans who have received authority and glory sometimes become oppressive and assume glory for themselves (see [8:4](Ps.8.4); [10:18](Ps.10.18)).

The lament of [9:13-20](Ps.9.13-Ps.9.20) continues in [Ps 10](Ps.10.1-Ps.10.18) (see study note on Pss 9–10), but the mood changes from confident assertion to anguished questioning. The psalmist prays for rescue, believing that the Lord, as a just king, takes care of the needy.
The opening questions set the mood. The Lord does not seem to hear the prayers of his people ([22:1](Ps.22.1), [19](Ps.22.19); see [2 Kgs 4:27](2Kgs.4.27); [Isa 1:15](Isa.1.15)).
Wicked and oppressive people might prosper, leaving ugly consequences. Evil can be as dramatic as the psalmist portrays it here, or it could be more subtle.

**The wicked** brazenly defy God with their acts and speech ([17:10](Ps.17.10); [31:18](Ps.31.18); [59:12](Ps.59.12); [73:8](Ps.73.8); [123:4](Ps.123.4)). Although the Lord will deal with them ([31:23](Ps.31.23)), they disturb the righteous (see [5:4-6](Ps.5.4-Ps.5.6)) prior to their condemnation and judgment.
Unlike those who have **evil desires***,* the godly wait for justice ([10:17](Ps.10.17)).
Despite their evil ways ([5:9](Ps.5.9); [28:3](Ps.28.3); [Rom 3:14](Rom.3.14)), the wicked expect a future **free of trouble** such as the righteous will enjoy.
The wicked rely on outright violence ([11:5](Ps.11.5); [37:32](Ps.37.32)) and deception ([Prov 12:6](Prov.12.6); [23:27-28](Prov.23.27-Prov.23.28)).
With confidence that the wicked will be held responsible for their deeds and that the Lord will care for the helpless, the psalmist prays intensely for rescue from evil.
Because the Lord cares for the afflicted, he will **take note** and **punish** evildoers (see [72:14](Ps.72.14); [116:15](Ps.116.15)).
The psalmist strongly invokes a curse as he prays (see “Prayers for Vengeance” Theme Note).
**Arms** represent an ability to wage war ([18:34](Ps.18.34); [44:3](Ps.44.3)).
As the true and just **king***,* God will bring the wicked to an end, as he promises ([1:6](Ps.1.6)).
The psalmist expresses his confidence in the Lord.
**Mere people** misuse their power and enslave the very people God wants them to serve (see [9:19-20](Ps.9.19-Ps.9.20); [Luke 22:25-26](Luke.22.25-Luke.22.26)).

The psalmist affirms his faith in the righteous God. Even though the world appears hopelessly chaotic, both the godly and the wicked can count on God’s justice. The godly can depend on him as a refuge and shelter.
God provides **protection** (or *refuge;* see [5:11](Ps.5.11); [9:9](Ps.9.9); [25:20](Ps.25.20)) when the foundations of justice collapse.
The **mountains** provide another place of refuge (see [121:1](Ps.121.1)).
In the inevitable battle between the evil and the godly, the wicked cannot tolerate the righteous, so they victimize them. This seems to leave the godly with nothing but questions.
The **wicked** live in the **shadows** and create gloom for the godly ([82:5](Ps.82.5); [139:11](Ps.139.11); [143:3](Ps.143.3); [Prov 4:19](Prov.4.19)).
The wicked create a world of darkness (see [82:5](Ps.82.5)).

The righteous King **rules from heaven***,* where his throne is untouched by human corruption (see [2:4](Ps.2.4)). He examines everyone and sees everything that happens on earth (see [14:2-3](Ps.14.2-Ps.14.3)).
Wicked deeds result in destruction and **violence** ([Pss 58:2](Ps.58.2); [73:6](Ps.73.6); [74:20](Ps.74.20)).
God rained **blazing coals** and **burning sulfur** on Sodom and Gomorrah ([Gen 19](Gen.19.1-Gen.19.38)) as symbols of judgment ([Pss 18:8](Ps.18.8); [120:4](Ps.120.4); [140:10](Ps.140.10)).
The godly are assured of the Lord’s favorable presence when they **see his face** (see [23:6](Ps.23.6)).
This community lament seeks the Lord’s help against the prevalence of evil. Because of the Lord’s answer, the godly can face the future knowing that God protects them.
Evil becomes so pervasive that the godly pray for rescue ([Isa 57:1](Isa.57.1); [Mic 7:2](Mic.7.2); cp. [Pss 1:6](Ps.1.6); [37:20](Ps.37.20); [58:7](Ps.58.7); [104:35](Ps.104.35)).
The words **they say** reveal the character of the wicked. They deceive and overpower the godly and arrogantly question the Lord’s purposes.
The godly can rely on the **LORD’s promises***,* but not on the lies of the wicked ([12:2-4](Ps.12.2-Ps.12.4)).
**Seven times** means totally or completely.

The godly know that the Lord cares, even though the wicked continue to oppress them. The Lord sees the corrupt and foolish people who praise evildoers (see [9:19-20](Ps.9.19-Ps.9.20); [14:2-6](Ps.14.2-Ps.14.6)).
The psalmist’s piercing cry for help becomes a confident song of hope.
**How long?** The fourfold repetition expresses agitation and deep anguish ([79:5](Ps.79.5)).

A sense of **anguish** and **sorrow** closes off any perspective of hope ([6:3](Ps.6.3)). Unless the Lord answers the psalmist’s prayers ([22:1](Ps.22.1)), death seems inescapable, torturous, and slow ([6:6](Ps.6.6); [32:3](Ps.32.3); [55:4](Ps.55.4); [61:2](Ps.61.2); [102:5](Ps.102.5); [116:3](Ps.116.3)). The psalmist hardly knows how to pray; he longs for God’s redemption ([25:17-18](Ps.25.17-Ps.25.18); [31:10](Ps.31.10); [38:8](Ps.38.8); [39:2](Ps.39.2)).
Only the Lord can bring enlightenment and relief. The psalmist longs for the Lord’s vindication so that his foes will not rejoice.
The psalmist no longer hears the ridicule of his foes. Instead, because of his trust in the Lord, he is full of joy.

This wisdom psalm contains some characteristics of lament and prophetic speech. The ideals of [Ps 8](Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9) have run aground on the reality of foolish human attitudes and sinful actions. With the exception of vv [5-6](Ps.5.1-Ps.6.10), this psalm parallels [Ps 53](Ps.53.1-Ps.53.6).
Paul uses phrases from the Greek translation of this passage in his description of the depravity of all people ([Rom 3:10-12](Rom.3.10-Rom.3.12)).

Also known as **fools***,* the wicked speak to themselves, think, scheme ([10:4](Ps.10.4), [6](Ps.10.6), [11](Ps.10.11)), and make claims; however, because they do not heed God’s revelation, they possess no understanding ([14:1](Ps.14.1); [39:8](Ps.39.8); [53:1](Ps.53.1); [74:18](Ps.74.18), [22](Ps.74.22)).

From **heaven** ([33:13](Ps.33.13); [80:14](Ps.80.14); [102:19](Ps.102.19)), the Lord sees the wicked, who stand out as vile sinners ([11:3-5](Ps.11.3-Ps.11.5)). The **entire human race** lacks wisdom and fails to live up to the glory originally given to them ([10:4-11](Ps.10.4-Ps.10.11); see [Rom 1–3](Rom.1.1-Rom.3.31)).
The evil live at the expense of others ([27:2](Ps.27.2); [44:11](Ps.44.11); [53:4](Ps.53.4); see [Isa 5:8](Isa.5.8)) and have no reverence or knowledge of God ([Ps 79:6](Ps.79.6)).
Though the wicked perish ([1:5-6](Ps.1.5-Ps.1.6)), **God is with** the godly.
The psalmist prays for the renewal of God’s relationship with his people.
**Jacob** is a synonym for **Israel** (see [Gen 35:9-10](Gen.35.9-Gen.35.10)).

The psalms in this section affirm integrity and purity ([17:15](Ps.17.15); [18:20-26](Ps.18.20-Ps.18.26); [19:13-14](Ps.19.13-Ps.19.14)). They refer to people as dwelling in God’s presence ([16:9-11](Ps.16.9-Ps.16.11); [17:15](Ps.17.15)) and as not being shaken ([15:5](Ps.15.5); [16:8](Ps.16.8)).

In this wisdom poem, the psalmist contrasts the lifestyle of the godly with the actions of fools ([Ps 14](Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7)). The questions in this psalm invite readers to examine themselves and to look away from problems with the wicked. The question of who dwells in God’s presence leads into a description of godly character qualities (cp. [24:3-6](Ps.24.3-Ps.24.6); [Isa 33:14-16](Isa.33.14-Isa.33.16)).
Only the godly may reside in the Lord’s **presence** ([5:4](Ps.5.4)). As his guests, they experience his hospitality and protection.

**sanctuary** (or *tent*): In David’s time, God’s sanctuary was a tent (the Tabernacle; see [1 Sam 21:6](1Sam.21.6); [2 Sam 6:17](2Sam.6.17); [7:6](2Sam.7.6); [12:20](2Sam.12.20); [1 Chr 6:32](1Chr.6.32)).
The godly speak truthfully and act faithfully in their relationships. Unlike the wicked, they are open and transparent ([12:2-4](Ps.12.2-Ps.12.4)).
The Lord prohibited Israel from **charging interest** to people in need ([Exod 22:25-27](Exod.22.25-Exod.22.27)).

The assurance of God’s presence keeps the godly from destruction ([Pss 16:8](Ps.16.8); [46:5](Ps.46.5); [125:1](Ps.125.1)). Their circumstances might shake them temporarily, but they ultimately **stand firm** ([30:6](Ps.30.6); [94:18](Ps.94.18); [112:6](Ps.112.6)).

In this psalm of confidence, the poet moves quickly from a short petition ([16:1](Ps.16.1)), to expressions of passionate commitment to God and his people ([16:2-6](Ps.16.2-Ps.16.6)), to a conclusion of confident praise ([16:7-11](Ps.16.7-Ps.16.11)).
The psalmist feels **safe** because the Lord alone offers security ([16:5-6](Ps.16.5-Ps.16.6)), guidance ([16:7-8](Ps.16.7-Ps.16.8)), and the joy of his presence ([16:9-11](Ps.16.9-Ps.16.11)).
**I said to the** **LORD:** The various writers of the psalms pray, lament, and praise the Lord throughout the Psalter, and the Lord answers them (see [12:5-6](Ps.12.5-Ps.12.6)).
The psalmist dissociates himself from ungodly worship, rituals, and words (see [15:3-5](Ps.15.3-Ps.15.5)).
The **cup of blessing** represents God’s provision for all the psalmist’s needs ([23:5](Ps.23.5); see [116:13](Ps.116.13); cp. [75:8](Ps.75.8); [Isa 51:17](Isa.51.17)).
The **land** is God’s gift for his people ([Deut 18:8](Deut.18.8)).

The psalmist so deeply depends on the Lord for strength and joy that he senses that God is **right beside** him ([16:11](Ps.16.11); see [73:23](Ps.73.23); [109:31](Ps.109.31); [110:1](Ps.110.1), [5](Ps.110.5); [121:5](Ps.121.5)).
Peter quoted [16:8-11](Ps.16.8-Ps.16.11) in his sermon on the day of Pentecost ([Acts 2:25-28](Acts.2.25-Acts.2.28)).

Knowing that not even death can separate him from the Lord strengthens the psalmist’s confidence. He fears a separation (see [13:3-4](Ps.13.3-Ps.13.4)), but he remains confident of seeing the Lord (see [11:7](Ps.11.7)).
The psalmist expresses his confidence that life continues beyond death. The apostles applied this text to the resurrection of Jesus ([Acts 2:25-33](Acts.2.25-Acts.2.33); [13:35](Acts.13.35)).
The psalmist pleads for God’s protection and vindication, affirms his own integrity, and prays that the Lord will prevail against his fierce enemies.

**comes from honest lips:** Deception characterizes the wicked. The godly reject such deceit as a failure of character and pray for rescue from such people ([5:6](Ps.5.6); [43:1](Ps.43.1); [120:2](Ps.120.2)). They love honesty, truth, and integrity ([15:2-3](Ps.15.2-Ps.15.3); [24:4](Ps.24.4); [101:7](Ps.101.7)).
The psalmist declares his innocence ([17:1](Ps.17.1)) and commits himself to integrity by being open to God’s examination.

Though he is not perfect, the psalmist commits himself to the Lord. He does not want to **sin** through deception, flattery, or gossip (see [10:7](Ps.10.7); [15:2-3](Ps.15.2-Ps.15.3); [17:1](Ps.17.1)).
This prayer for God’s care returns to the petition begun in [17:1-2](Ps.17.1-Ps.17.2) for redemption from evil.
**as you would guard your own eyes** (literally *as the pupil of your eye*): This metaphor expresses God’s care and affection for the psalmist (see [Deut 32:10](Deut.32.10)).
The **shadow of** God’s **wings** is a place of his protection from enemies and adversity ([Pss 36:7](Ps.36.7); [57:1](Ps.57.1); [61:4](Ps.61.4); [63:7](Ps.63.7); [91:4](Ps.91.4)).

The psalmist confidently prays for the Lord’s victory, knowing that God possesses more power than the evildoers. The psalmist finds his joy in the Lord’s inheritance ([16:5](Ps.16.5)), whereas the wicked search for joy in this world.
**see you face to face:** The psalmist does not allow temporary concerns raised by adversaries to stand in the way of his experiencing a real and lasting relationship with the Lord.

This royal drama of divine rescue (also found with minor variations in [2 Sam 22:1-51](2Sam.22.1-2Sam.22.51)) encourages readers who are following the laments and requests for rescue in [Pss 16](Ps.16.1-Ps.16.11) and [17](Ps.17.1-Ps.17.15). The psalmist describes the dramatic nature of God’s rescue in three different ways ([18:7-15](Ps.18.7-Ps.18.15), [16-19](Ps.18.16-Ps.18.19), [30-36](Ps.18.30-Ps.18.36)). The psalm also extends hope that a future Son of David will be totally victorious over evil ([18:43-50](Ps.18.43-Ps.18.50); cp. [Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12)).
18:title
David was a faithful **servant of the** **LORD***,* charged with the responsibility of establishing God’s kingdom on earth (see [78:70](Ps.78.70); [132:10](Ps.132.10); [144:10](Ps.144.10)).
The Lord **rescued** David **from all his enemies** when he enabled David to conquer them (see [2 Sam 8:1-14](2Sam.8.1-2Sam.8.14)).

A **shield** is an image of protection, salvation, and victory ([7:10](Ps.7.10); [18:2](Ps.18.2), [30](Ps.18.30), [35](Ps.18.35); [84:11](Ps.84.11); [91:4](Ps.91.4); [115:9](Ps.115.9), [10](Ps.115.10), [11](Ps.115.11); [119:114](Ps.119.114); [144:2](Ps.144.2)). It evokes a response of trust, waiting, and godly confidence.
God deserves praise for his greatness and faithfulness ([48:1](Ps.48.1); [96:4](Ps.96.4); [145:3](Ps.145.3)).

God dwells in **his sanctuary***,* the heavenly temple ([102:19](Ps.102.19); see [14:2-3](Ps.14.2-Ps.14.3)). He knows everything, sees everyone, and will vindicate the godly (see [11:3-7](Ps.11.3-Ps.11.7)).

The psalmist depicts the Lord’s descent from heaven to earth with phenomena such as earthquakes, flames, smoke, darkness, and rain. Creation shudders at God’s marvelous coming as the Divine Warrior (see [97:2-5](Ps.97.2-Ps.97.5)) and Judge (see [50:1-6](Ps.50.1-Ps.50.6)).
**his nostrils . . . his mouth:** The psalmist likens God to an angry person or a fierce creature (see [Job 41:12-22](Job.41.12-Job.41.22)).
The terrifying images of **smoke***,* **flames***,* and **glowing coals** express God’s wrath against sin.
The Lord’s sovereignty extends over all of nature (see [104:2-4](Ps.104.2-Ps.104.4); [148:5-6](Ps.148.5-Ps.148.6)).
**a mighty angelic being** (Hebrew *a cherub*): See study notes on 1 Chr 28:18; 2 Chr 3:10-13.
Because God loves and **delights in** the psalmist (see [18:1](Ps.18.1)), he will save him ([37:23](Ps.37.23); [41:11](Ps.41.11); [91:14-16](Ps.91.14-Ps.91.16)).

The psalmist affirms that loyalty is rewarded. He puts his trust in the Lord (see [16:1](Ps.16.1)) and commits himself to living with integrity (see [Pss 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6), [15](Ps.15.1-Ps.15.5), [24](Ps.24.1-Ps.24.10); see also [19:12-14](Ps.19.12-Ps.19.14)).
**kept the ways of the** **LORD:** The psalmist faithfully obeys God’s instructions (see [25:8-10](Ps.25.8-Ps.25.10)).

**not turned . . . to follow evil:** The psalmist rejects the way of folly (see [Pss 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6) and [14](Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7)) and chooses the way of wisdom (see [Pss 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6) and [15](Ps.15.1-Ps.15.5)).
The **faithful** God remains true to his character. He loves faithfulness, blamelessness, and purity, and he hates the perverse (see [1:6](Ps.1.6)).
The **pure** have clean hands (see [18:20-24](Ps.18.20-Ps.18.24)).
**to the crooked you show yourself shrewd:** The Lord knows each person’s character, and he justly responds to them in kind.
**light a lamp:** The Lord renews the psalmist’s life, helping him overcome the **darkness** of adversity (see [Pss 112:4](Ps.112.4); [119:105](Ps.119.105)).
**scale any wall:** God helps his servants fight their battles.
The psalmist experiences God’s rescue and provision of victory.
**perfect:** God’s character has integrity (see [18:26](Ps.18.26)).
God **promises** to protect his people, and he does so.

Seeking God’s **protection** entails trust and faith. Regardless of his feelings or external circumstances, the psalmist makes a deep commitment to the Lord. He experiences joy ([5:11](Ps.5.11); [64:10](Ps.64.10)) as he awaits the Lord’s rescue ([57:1](Ps.57.1)).
The psalmist’s victories come from the Lord. He completely depends on God.
A **wide path** represents freedom and safety (see [4:8](Ps.4.8); [119:35](Ps.119.35)).
With help from the Divine Warrior, the psalmist experienced victory over his enemies.
Placing a **foot** on the **necks** of the enemy represents total victory (see [Josh 10:23-26](Josh.10.23-Josh.10.26)).

With God’s victorious help, the psalmist achieved military and political success, thus fulfilling the history of David’s dynasty ([Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12)). The previous laments find some resolution in this psalm.
The psalmist again reflects on the Lord’s victories. God’s marvelous rescue and the king’s victory are cause for celebration.
God vindicates his servant and so fulfills his mission ([Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12); see [47:3](Ps.47.3); [144:2](Ps.144.2)).
The psalmist’s vision of **praise . . . among the nations** motivated Paul in his mission to the Gentiles ([Rom 15:9](Rom.15.9)).
God appointed David, his **anointed** ruler, to bring order into God’s world (see [Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12)). Both **David** and **his descendants** received this responsibility.

God’s wisdom is manifest in heaven ([19:1-4](Ps.19.1-Ps.19.4)), in nature ([19:4-6](Ps.19.4-Ps.19.6)), in his instruction ([19:7-11](Ps.19.7-Ps.19.11)), and in the life of the psalmist ([19:12-14](Ps.19.12-Ps.19.14)). Like [Ps 8](Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9), this hymn uses creation to motivate reflection—it is a peaceful oasis after the drama of the lament and victory psalms. The psalm begins with creation as a source of wisdom, then moves to God’s word as the perfect source of wisdom, and ends with the human need for redemption.

The created order is an arena of God’s wisdom, and the heavens are the place of God’s dwelling ([2:4](Ps.2.4); see [8:1](Ps.8.1); [57:5](Ps.57.5); [89:6](Ps.89.6); [115:3](Ps.115.3)). From heaven, God observes humanity ([11:4](Ps.11.4); [14:2](Ps.14.2); [33:13](Ps.33.13); [53:2](Ps.53.2); [80:14](Ps.80.14); [102:19](Ps.102.19)) and comes to the rescue of his servants ([18:6-8](Ps.18.6-Ps.18.8), [13](Ps.18.13); [20:6](Ps.20.6); [57:3](Ps.57.3); [76:8](Ps.76.8); [144:5](Ps.144.5)). The heavens remain unaffected by human failures and rebellions (see [2:1-4](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.4)). They display God’s qualities of fidelity, righteousness ([36:5](Ps.36.5); [50:6](Ps.50.6); [57:10](Ps.57.10); [85:11](Ps.85.11); [89:2](Ps.89.2), [5](Ps.89.5); [97:6](Ps.97.6); [108:4](Ps.108.4)), and wisdom ([136:5](Ps.136.5); see [119:89-90](Ps.119.89-Ps.119.90)). The heavens reveal the Lord’s glory (see [19:1](Ps.19.1)) and give evidence of his presence and handiwork.
The **glory of God** refers to the splendor or manifest presence of the Creator ([113:4](Ps.113.4)).
**God** (Hebrew *’el*): *El* is an ancient designation for God that signifies his creative power.

God’s wisdom does not need to be spoken. Through creation, it is seen, felt, and experienced. Paul applied this text to condemn Israel for its lack of receptivity to Jesus Christ ([Rom 10:18](Rom.10.18)).
The **sun** is part of God’s creation, but it is not a deity, as people of other nations in the ancient Near East commonly believed.

God’s **instructions** to humans reveal his character and wisdom. God’s instruction is precious and pleasant ([119:103](Ps.119.103)). It nourishes the person ([Prov 16:24](Prov.16.24); [24:14](Prov.24.14)) and is of more value than objects of human worth ([Ps 81:13-16](Ps.81.13-Ps.81.16)).
The psalmist knows his faults, so he prays to remain faithful and commits himself to the Lord.
An individual who commits **deliberate sins** does so with an insolent ([86:14](Ps.86.14)) or arrogant ([119:21](Ps.119.21), [69](Ps.119.69)) attitude.
The **great sin** is rebellion (see [32:1](Ps.32.1)).
**words of my mouth . . . meditation of my heart:** The psalmist desires to please God in everything he says and thinks (see [Luke 6:45](Luke.6.45); [Rom 12:1-2](Rom.12.1-Rom.12.2)).

This sequence of psalms expresses the experience of moving from confidence and commitment ([Pss 20–21](Ps.20.1-Ps.21.13)), through anguish and abandonment ([Ps 22](Ps.22.1-Ps.22.31)), and finally to comfort, insight, and hope ([Pss 23–24](Ps.23.1-Ps.24.10)).
This royal prayer for God’s victory ([20:1-5](Ps.20.1-Ps.20.5)) leads to confidence in God’s rescue ([20:6-8](Ps.20.6-Ps.20.8)) and a communal request for God’s response ([20:9](Ps.20.9)).
The community prays for the king’s protection and victory.

The title **God of Jacob** affectionately expresses God’s ancient relationship with his people (see [46:7](Ps.46.7), [11](Ps.46.11); [75:9](Ps.75.9); [76:6](Ps.76.6); [81:1](Ps.81.1), [4](Ps.81.4); [84:8](Ps.84.8); [94:7](Ps.94.7); [114:7](Ps.114.7); [146:5](Ps.146.5)).
**keep you safe from all harm:** See [59:1-2](Ps.59.1-Ps.59.2).
**Gifts** and **burnt offerings** express submission to the Lord (cp. [40:6](Ps.40.6)).
**make all your plans succeed . . . answer all your prayers:** These requests could be those stated in [21:3-6](Ps.21.3-Ps.21.6) (cp. [27:4](Ps.27.4)).
Troops carried a **victory banner** to battle, under which they gathered and roused one another to action (see [Isa 11:10](Isa.11.10), [12](Isa.11.12)).
An individual member of the community ([20:1-5](Ps.20.1-Ps.20.5)) responds with a word of assurance and confidence in God’s help.
God chose **his anointed king** to be ruler (see [2:7](Ps.2.7)).
God’s people thank him for giving victory to the king.
The king has experienced **his heart’s desire**—God’s protection and blessing (see [20:5](Ps.20.5); see also [2:8](Ps.2.8)).
The king returned victorious from battle and received honor from the people. His greatest honor came from God, who gave him blessings, life, and his presence.
**success and prosperity:** See [Prov 10:6](Prov.10.6).
God’s **eternal blessings** also bring fullness of life in the present (see [Ps 133](Ps.133.1-Ps.133.3)).
The king enjoyed victory not because of his strength or intrinsic goodness but because God honored his faith.
As long as even a single enemy opposed the king’s authority, God’s kingdom was not fully present. This prayer requests victory over all evil in the world.

The **flaming furnace** and **fire** portray the severity of God’s judgment on the wicked. In the Old Testament, this image often refers to hell ([11:6](Ps.11.6); [18:8](Ps.18.8); [50:3](Ps.50.3); [68:2](Ps.68.2); [78:21](Ps.78.21); [79:5](Ps.79.5); [80:16](Ps.80.16); [89:46](Ps.89.46); [97:3](Ps.97.3); [104:4](Ps.104.4); [140:10](Ps.140.10); see [Isa 66:24](Isa.66.24)).

**children . . . descendants:** Evil will end when God destroys all opposition to himself ([109:13](Ps.109.13); cp. [18:50](Ps.18.50); [22:30-31](Ps.22.30-Ps.22.31); [25:13](Ps.25.13); [102:28](Ps.102.28)).
**Rise up** (or *be exalted,* as in [57:5](Ps.57.5), [11](Ps.57.11); [108:5](Ps.108.5)) expresses communal praise and joy in God’s greatness and **power**.

All previous laments pale in comparison with this outcry against the enemy and God’s abandonment. The psalm contains two main sections: the lament ([22:1-21](Ps.22.1-Ps.22.21)) and praise for redemption ([22:22-31](Ps.22.22-Ps.22.31)), which leads naturally to [Ps 23](Ps.23.1-Ps.23.6). The apostles saw in this psalm an expression of the sufferings of Jesus Christ, who ultimately fulfilled the purpose of David’s humiliation, rejection by people, and divine abandonment ([Matt 27:35](Matt.27.35), [39](Matt.27.39), [43](Matt.27.43), [46](Matt.27.46); [Mark 15:34](Mark.15.34); [John 19:23-24](John.19.23-John.19.24), [28](John.19.28); [Heb 2:12](Heb.2.12)).
The psalmist alternates between reflections on his present dire circumstances and memories of the Lord’s past faithfulness; he ends with a prayer for rescue.
A deep sense of alienation from God overwhelms the psalmist (see [10:1](Ps.10.1)).
God, the **holy** King, is set apart from all his creation, but he chooses to reveal himself to Israel.
God greatly desires that his people offer **praises** to him.
Both the Lord and people reject the psalmist. He vividly describes his anguish ([22:1-2](Ps.22.1-Ps.22.2)); he lives like a lowly animal.

Everyone **mocks** the psalmist’s confidence in the Lord (see [3:2](Ps.3.2); [Matt 27:43](Matt.27.43)), which shames him ([Pss 44:13-14](Ps.44.13-Ps.44.14); [74:10](Ps.74.10); [89:50](Ps.89.50); [109:25](Ps.109.25)).
The psalmist reflects on his past relationship with God (see [22:3-5](Ps.22.3-Ps.22.5)). The Lord has been his very life.
The Lord took care of the psalmist before he could do anything for himself (see [71:6](Ps.71.6); [139:13](Ps.139.13)).
The psalmist returns to expressing his anguish and suffering (see [22:1-2](Ps.22.1-Ps.22.2), [6-8](Ps.22.6-Ps.22.8)). His trouble comes from human beings who act like beasts.
**Bashan***,* a region known for its herds and vegetation, produced strong **bulls** ([68:30](Ps.68.30)).
The psalmist’s sense of being **poured out like water** expresses a meaningless, transitory existence that leaves him depleted.
Facing adversity is as horrible as dying of thirst (see [137:6](Ps.137.6)).
Jesus may have had this verse in mind when he said, “I am thirsty” ([John 19:28](John.19.28)).
The wild **pack of dogs** represents fierce and unscrupulous people.
**I can count all my bones:** The psalmist’s enemies have utterly shamed him by taking his garments. Jesus also suffered this disgrace (see [Matt 27:35](Matt.27.35)).
**stare at me and gloat:** Enemies make the psalmist the object of their scorn (see [Pss 35:24](Ps.35.24), [26](Ps.35.26); [38:16](Ps.38.16); [55:3](Ps.55.3); cp. [59:10](Ps.59.10)).

**throw dice:** Literally *cast lots.* The casting of lots was sometimes a way for godly people to find God’s direction ([Lev 16:8](Lev.16.8); [Num 27:21](Num.27.21); [Acts 1:24-26](Acts.1.24-Acts.1.26)). Here, the lots are thrown simply as a game of chance. The soldiers threw dice for Jesus’ clothing after the crucifixion ([Matt 27:35](Matt.27.35); [Mark 15:24](Mark.15.24); [Luke 23:34](Luke.23.34); [John 19:24](John.19.24)).
The psalmist faces his troubles by praying for God’s rescue. Only the Lord has the strength to ward off **dogs**, **lions**, and **oxen**.
The **sword** makes evident the lethal intent of the enemy.
The psalmist praises the Lord and calls for the godly to join him. He tells of God’s goodness to the needy, including himself.
**I will proclaim your name:** The writer to the Hebrews ascribes these words to Jesus ([Heb 2:12](Heb.2.12)).
**my brothers and sisters:** Literally *my brothers.* In the New Testament quotation, the Greek translation picks up the broader meaning as “my brothers and sisters.”
The godly respond with awe (see [22:25](Ps.22.25)).
Unlike his response to the wicked (see [21:8-12](Ps.21.8-Ps.21.12)), God cares about the needy and hears their prayers ([51:17](Ps.51.17); [69:33](Ps.69.33); [102:17](Ps.102.17)).
The psalmist vows to praise the Lord, the great King of the earth ([22:27-28](Ps.22.27-Ps.22.28)) who cares for the needy. God alone deserves praise.
The **great assembly** might include all nations ([22:27](Ps.22.27); [26:12](Ps.26.12); [35:18](Ps.35.18)).

**families of the nations:** All clans and tribes of humanity (see [Gen 12:3](Gen.12.3); [Rev 5:9-10](Rev.5.9-Rev.5.10)) will live in submission to the Lord ([Ps 96:1-3](Ps.96.1-Ps.96.3); see [Pss 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12), [72](Ps.72.1-Ps.72.20); [Isa 2:2-4](Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4); [1 Cor 15:25-27](1Cor.15.25-1Cor.15.27)).
The universal kingdom belongs to God alone ([Obad 1:21](Obad.1.21)).
The Lord invites all people, **rich** and poor ([22:26](Ps.22.26)), to the banquet as long as they **worship** him.

**Future generations** will join those from the past who praised the Lord ([22:3-5](Ps.22.3-Ps.22.5)). The descendants of the godly will receive blessings ([22:30-31](Ps.22.30-Ps.22.31)), unlike the offspring of the wicked ([21:10](Ps.21.10)).

The Lord’s **acts** of redemption ([40:9](Ps.40.9); [50:6](Ps.50.6); [71:15](Ps.71.15), [16](Ps.71.16), [24](Ps.71.24); [97:6](Ps.97.6)) demonstrate that he is **righteous** (see [4:1](Ps.4.1)). His righteousness provides the character required for rule, judicial decisions, and relationships. This virtue leads to harmony and order (see [50:6](Ps.50.6)).

This psalm of trust and confidence in the Lord has been a favorite of God’s people for generations. It expresses assurance of God’s presence in the midst of adversity. It evokes images of the Good Shepherd ([23:1-3](Ps.23.1-Ps.23.3); see [Ezek 34:12](Ezek.34.12); [John 10:11](John.10.11)) and of the messianic banquet ([Ps 23:5-6](Ps.23.5-Ps.23.6); see [Isa 25:6](Isa.25.6); [Rev 19:9](Rev.19.9)).
People in the ancient Near East commonly viewed their rulers as shepherds.

The Lord promises to take care of his children ([34:9-10](Ps.34.9-Ps.34.10); [Isa 51:14](Isa.51.14)). He demonstrated this ability to Israel in the wilderness ([Deut 2:7](Deut.2.7)) and in the Promised Land ([Deut 8:9](Deut.8.9)).
Sheep **rest** after they have eaten their fill ([Zeph 3:13](Zeph.3.13); see [Isa 11:7](Isa.11.7); cp. [Isa 13:20](Isa.13.20); [27:10](Isa.27.10)).
The Lord **leads** the sheep for their own benefit (see [Ps 5:8](Ps.5.8)).
Sheep only drink from still water, so the shepherd seeks out **peaceful streams** for his flock.
Cp. [19:7](Ps.19.7); the Lord’s word **renews my strength.**

The Lord **guides** by rescuing his people from evil ([23:4-5](Ps.23.4-Ps.23.5); see [31:3](Ps.31.3)), bringing them back to himself ([5:8](Ps.5.8); [61:2](Ps.61.2)), caring ([48:14](Ps.48.14); [139:10](Ps.139.10)), ruling ([67:4](Ps.67.4)), counseling ([73:24](Ps.73.24)), protecting ([78:53](Ps.78.53); [107:30](Ps.107.30); [143:11](Ps.143.11)), and instructing them in wisdom ([27:11](Ps.27.11); see [Prov 4:11](Prov.4.11)).

The Lord’s **name** guarantees the relationship; he guards his reputation against any accusation of his abandoning his people or allowing them to sin (see [Pss 25:11](Ps.25.11); [31:3](Ps.31.3); [106:8](Ps.106.8); [143:11](Ps.143.11)).
The shepherd used his **rod** and **staff** to fend off danger.
A **feast** demonstrates the Lord’s care and mercy toward his people (see [22:26](Ps.22.26), [29](Ps.22.29)). Although **enemies** can watch, they cannot trouble the guests.
The ritual of **anointing** the **head with oil** showed guests **honor** ([92:9-11](Ps.92.9-Ps.92.11)), hospitality, and refreshment ([104:15](Ps.104.15); [133:2](Ps.133.2)).

The Lord expresses his **unfailing love** through the **goodness** of his presence and other benefits that he alone provides ([69:16](Ps.69.16); [86:17](Ps.86.17); [109:21](Ps.109.21); see [18:6](Ps.18.6); [61:4](Ps.61.4)). He actively bestows care that is greater than the temporary trials imposed by enemies ([7:1](Ps.7.1)).
The shepherd of [Ps 23](Ps.23.1-Ps.23.6), who is also the King of the whole world, takes possession of Zion.
The kingdom belongs to the Creator, the Great King (cp. [22:27](Ps.22.27)).

The Lord created and now rules the **earth** and **everything in it** (see [1 Cor 10:25-26](1Cor.10.25-1Cor.10.26)). He sees **all its people** ([Ps 33:14](Ps.33.14)), regardless of their status ([49:1-2](Ps.49.1-Ps.49.2)).
God created everything in an orderly and stable manner (see [89:11](Ps.89.11); [102:25](Ps.102.25); [104:5](Ps.104.5)).
The citizens of the King’s realm include all who seek him. The Lord invites them to enter his presence.
These questions invite readers to look away from their problems with the wicked and to examine themselves (see [15:1](Ps.15.1)).
