God’s **holy place** is the holy **mountain**, a reference both to Jerusalem and to heaven.
Those with pure **hands** have not shed blood or injured relationships between people (see [9:12](Ps.9.12); [15:2-5](Ps.15.2-Ps.15.5)).
Those with pure **hearts** commit themselves fully to the Lord, as evidenced in strength of character, transparency, and selflessness ([51:10](Ps.51.10); [73:1](Ps.73.1); see [Matt 5:8](Matt.5.8)).

**The** **LORD of Heaven’s Armies** reigns from his home, the Temple in Jerusalem ([84:3-5](Ps.84.3-Ps.84.5)). He excludes sin and sinners ([24:3-6](Ps.24.3-Ps.24.6)) but protects all who dwell in Zion.

This individual lament includes instruction in wisdom and a community lament; it begins and ends with an affirmation of trust in the Lord ([25:1-3](Ps.25.1-Ps.25.3), [15-22](Ps.25.15-Ps.25.22)). The psalmist prays for guidance ([25:4-7](Ps.25.4-Ps.25.7)) and encourages the godly to practice a lifestyle of wisdom ([25:12-14](Ps.25.12-Ps.25.14)). In addition to the enemies who trouble him, the psalmist confesses his sins ([25:7](Ps.25.7), [11](Ps.25.11), [18](Ps.25.18)) as part of his anguish. Trust develops with understanding God’s character: He is compassionate, faithful, and good ([25:8-10](Ps.25.8-Ps.25.10)).
The psalmist expresses confidence that the godly will be vindicated and his enemies will not succeed (see [25:15-22](Ps.25.15-Ps.25.22)).
The psalmist commits himself to the Lord instead of to idols (see [24:3-4](Ps.24.3-Ps.24.4)).
Enemies would **rejoice** by singing a victory song.

In this prayer for guidance, compassion, and forgiveness, the psalmist turns to the Lord for instruction in wisdom. He confesses his past failures and acknowledges that his hope lies with his merciful Savior.
The **right path***,* the path of wisdom (see [5:8](Ps.5.8)), means being open to instruction that leads to life ([27:11](Ps.27.11); [43:3](Ps.43.3); [73:24](Ps.73.24); [119:12](Ps.119.12)).
Biblical **hope** does not mean wishing for an event to turn out favorably. Hope trusts the Lord’s will and gives the courage to face disappointments ([33:22](Ps.33.22); [130:5](Ps.130.5)).
The Lord keeps his people close to himself.

The psalmist again asks forgiveness for his **many sins** ([25:7](Ps.25.7); [32:1-5](Ps.32.1-Ps.32.5)). The sins of Israel’s kings demonstrated the weaknesses inherent in David’s dynasty and the reasons for its failure in Old Testament Israel (see [Ps 89](Ps.89.1-Ps.89.52)).
Those who fear the Lord will receive further instruction and experience God’s presence ([25:14](Ps.25.14)) and blessing ([25:13](Ps.25.13)).
**prosperity:** See [23:6](Ps.23.6).

**inherit the land:** Unlike the wicked, who will perish ([1:6](Ps.1.6)), the godly have a secure future. In the end, God will bless them, and their blessings will endure (see [37:9](Ps.37.9), [11](Ps.37.11), [22](Ps.37.22), [29](Ps.37.29), [34](Ps.37.34); [Isa 57:13](Isa.57.13); [Matt 5:5](Matt.5.5)).
The psalmist expresses confidence in the Lord, commits to a life of integrity, and prays for rescue.

The psalmist can find no relief (see [4:1](Ps.4.1); [13:1-2](Ps.13.1-Ps.13.2)) as his **problems go from bad to worse**. He associates his anguish with sin, but he does not elaborate on the nature of his sin (see [25:7](Ps.25.7), [11](Ps.25.11)).
Knowing that the Lord hates violent people (see [11:5](Ps.11.5)), the psalmist pleads with God to deal with these **enemies**.
Just as it opened, the psalm closes with a commitment of trust and **hope** (see [9:18](Ps.9.18); [25:5](Ps.25.5)).
In this individual lament, the psalmist prays for redemption on the basis of his own innocence and the Lord’s justice.
The psalmist opens himself to divine examination of his life, especially in the areas of his character and devotion.
For God’s **truth** to become part of one’s character requires a habitual commitment.
Because of his devotion to the Lord ([26:1-3](Ps.26.1-Ps.26.3)), the psalmist dissociates himself from evil people (see [1:1](Ps.1.1)).
The psalmist demonstrates his loyalty to the Lord through pious rituals, praise, and acknowledgment of the Lord’s presence in the Temple.
Ritual purity required the worshiper to **wash** their **hands***,* symbolic of separation from evil and evildoers (see [73:13](Ps.73.13)).
The **altar** symbolizes God’s presence ([43:4](Ps.43.4)).
The **sanctuary** symbolized the manifest **presence** of the Lord (see [18:6](Ps.18.6)).
**Don’t let me suffer:** The end of the godly cannot be the same as that of the wicked.
The psalmist’s footing on **solid ground** represents salvation (cp. [143:10](Ps.143.10)).
**publicly:** Or *in the great assembly* at the Temple ([26:6-8](Ps.26.6-Ps.26.8); [22:25](Ps.22.25)).

This psalm mixes two genres—a psalm of confidence ([27:1-6](Ps.27.1-Ps.27.6)) and an individual lament ([27:7-14](Ps.27.7-Ps.27.14))—held together by the theme of longing for the Lord’s presence. The psalmist focuses on the Lord; his circumstances are secondary. The strength of the psalmist’s faith is expressed in his openness to the Lord’s instruction, timing, and priorities.

The psalmist acknowledges the Lord at the center of his life ([27:1](Ps.27.1)). Because of God’s presence, he engages his adversaries with confidence. They cannot intimidate him or penetrate his inner security.
The psalmist’s enemies seek to **devour** him by living at his expense (see study note on 14:4).
**remain confident:** See [25:2](Ps.25.2); [26:1](Ps.26.1).

Searching for and enjoying the Lord’s presence provides the psalmist’s foundation for confidence and security. He lives in the assurance of God’s protection and looks forward to offering sacrifices of thanksgiving and praise (see [18:6](Ps.18.6)).
**sanctuary** (or *tabernacle*): This early shrine was the Israelites’ place of worship before the Temple was constructed.
**hold my head high:** A sign of victory.
The granting of the request of [27:4](Ps.27.4) prompts **sacrifices with shouts of joy**.
The psalmist requests the Lord’s mercy, presence, and instruction. God is the psalmist’s greatest good; enemies and other circumstances are peripheral.

Unlike the wicked ([10:4](Ps.10.4)), who only want a temporary advantage ([78:34-36](Ps.78.34-Ps.78.36)), the godly search for the Lord as a thirsty person searches for water in the desert ([63:1](Ps.63.1); [105:4](Ps.105.4); [119:2](Ps.119.2), [10](Ps.119.10); [Matt 6:33](Matt.6.33)). They act wisely ([Ps 34:10](Ps.34.10), [14](Ps.34.14)) while waiting for the Lord to resolve their crisis ([34:4](Ps.34.4); [69:6](Ps.69.6); [77:2](Ps.77.2); [119:58](Ps.119.58)).

The psalmist expresses confidence and hope in the Lord’s presence. To live in faith means to **wait patiently** in recognition of the Lord’s goodness. Such a life is not always pleasant for the godly ([42:2-3](Ps.42.2-Ps.42.3); [43:5](Ps.43.5)), but their future is secure ([37:9](Ps.37.9); [130:7](Ps.130.7); see [9:18](Ps.9.18)).
In this individual lament, the psalmist pleads for justice and mercy. He expresses confidence in the Lord’s strength and faithfulness, and he intercedes for the Lord’s people.
The psalmist urges the Lord to listen; his urgency flows out of the tension between his deep relationship with the Lord and the adversity he faces.
**if you are silent:** The psalmist appeals to the Lord to take action ([35:22](Ps.35.22); [50:3](Ps.50.3); [83:1](Ps.83.1); [109:1](Ps.109.1)).
It was common to **lift** up one’s **hands** in a gesture of devoted prayer ([63:4](Ps.63.4); [134:2](Ps.134.2)).
The psalmist curses his enemies, asking God for retribution and vindication.
The wicked do not acknowledge the difference between the sacred and the common, so they have no respect for the Lord’s creation, redemption, or revelation.
The psalmist anticipates rescue because of his confidence in the Lord’s justice.
**my strength and shield:** The Lord protects the psalmist (see [59:9](Ps.59.9), [17](Ps.59.17)).
The poem closes with intercession for the Lord’s people.
**Bless Israel, your special possession:** See [29:11](Ps.29.11); [133:3](Ps.133.3).
This nature hymn in praise of the Creator declares that the Lord holds all power over nature. God uses the same unsurpassed strength to care for his people.
The psalmist issues a call to **honor** the Lord for his power (cp. [96:7-8](Ps.96.7-Ps.96.8)).

**you heavenly beings:** Angels or deities who, some believed, held special powers. The psalmist did not believe in other deities but called on people who thought they were real to look to the Lord as the only God.

The word translated **voice** (Hebrew *qol*) can also mean “noise” ([1 Kgs 1:45](1Kgs.1.45)) or “thunder” ([Joel 3:16](Joel.3.16)). The Lord’s voice is awe-inspiring, and it dominates whatever rumblings people might attribute to other deities.
The **cedars of Lebanon** were known for their size and quality (see [Isa 2:13](Isa.2.13)).
**Lebanon’s mountains** and **Hermon** are high mountains to the north of Israel.
The Lord can cause even immense **mountains** to shake at his command (see [114:4](Ps.114.4)).
The **wilderness of Kadesh** was located south of Judah. God’s voice can be heard throughout the land, from the north ([29:6](Ps.29.6)) to the south.
The image of powerful **floodwaters** connects with the Genesis flood ([Gen 6:17](Gen.6.17)). The Lord **reigns as king** over the whole created order; no one contests his kingdom.
The ruler of nature **blesses** his people **with peace** (see [28:8-9](Ps.28.8-Ps.28.9); [37:11](Ps.37.11); [133:3](Ps.133.3)).

This individual thanksgiving psalm opens in praise to the Lord for his salvation ([30:1-3](Ps.30.1-Ps.30.3)), then contrasts God’s favor with his anger ([30:4-7](Ps.30.4-Ps.30.7)), and ends with a transformation from mourning to dancing ([30:8-12](Ps.30.8-Ps.30.12)).
The psalmist praises God for his triumph over adversity, which he likens to salvation from the grave.
30:title
Perhaps **David** wrote this psalm in advance for **the dedication of the Temple***,* making his own experience representative of the nation’s.

**I will exalt you** is a call to lift up the Lord’s name in praise and thanksgiving ([34:3](Ps.34.3); [81:1](Ps.81.1); [99:5](Ps.99.5), [9](Ps.99.9); [107:32](Ps.107.32); [118:28](Ps.118.28); [145:1](Ps.145.1); see [Exod 15:1](Exod.15.1); [Isa 25:1](Isa.25.1)).
**you rescued me:** God pulled the psalmist from death ([Ps 30:3](Ps.30.3)).
In his justice and care, God **refused to let** the psalmist’s **enemies triumph** (see [26:9](Ps.26.9); [27:12](Ps.27.12); [28:3](Ps.28.3); [31:8](Ps.31.8)).
The godly should celebrate the Lord’s acts of rescue with song and **praise** ([33:21](Ps.33.21); [97:12](Ps.97.12); [103:1](Ps.103.1); [105:3](Ps.105.3); [145:21](Ps.145.21)).
**Nothing can stop me now!** The psalmist confesses his presumptuous attitude (cp. [32:3-4](Ps.32.3-Ps.32.4)).
**I was shattered:** The absence of God’s favor destroys the security of the proud (cp. [104:27-30](Ps.104.27-Ps.104.30)).

The psalmist faced death (also in [30:1-3](Ps.30.1-Ps.30.3))—perhaps literally, perhaps figuratively. But when he turned to the Lord, the Lord rescued him and turned his **mourning into joyful dancing**. Only God’s favor can permanently and powerfully overcome human failure and the depths of despair.

The psalmist encourages the godly to find refuge in the Lord and wait for his salvation. Despite having had a death-like experience, he testifies to the Lord’s faithfulness. This psalm foreshadows the suffering of Jesus ([Luke 23:46](Luke.23.46)).
The Lord offers refuge to anyone who comes to him for protection. The psalmist trusts in and submits to the Lord. See also [71:1-3](Ps.71.1-Ps.71.3).
The psalmist issues an urgent call for the Lord to pay attention to his desperate situation ([71:2](Ps.71.2); [88:2](Ps.88.2); [102:2](Ps.102.2)).
**I entrust my spirit into your hand:** Whether he lives or dies, the psalmist will trust his Lord. Jesus uttered these words on the cross just before he died ([Luke 23:46](Luke.23.46)).
Trust in the Lord requires confidence that he has our best interests at heart.
A **safe place** literally means a broad place, in contrast to a “narrow” or constricted place of distress (see [18:19](Ps.18.19)).
In this prayer for mercy, the psalmist wedges a description of the intensity of suffering and the pain of rejection between two affirmations of trust ([31:6](Ps.31.6), [14](Ps.31.14)).
**wasting away from within:** This is a powerful description of how despair takes a toll on our physical well-being.
Hope does not confide in frail and changeable human beings but only in the Lord. The sufferer entrusts himself to God while waiting for the Lord’s justice.
**My future is in your hands:** To relinquish control of timing is one way to express submission.
The psalmist, who did not deserve to be **disgraced***,* invokes the principle of retribution (see study note on 1:6; see also “Prayers for Vengeance” Theme Note).
The psalmist thanks the Lord for answering his prayer ([31:1-18](Ps.31.1-Ps.31.18)) and rescuing him.
Since the godly are under the Lord’s protection and shelter, evil has no power over them.
**Praise the** **LORD:** The psalmist expresses his joy at the experience of God’s goodness and love. Throughout his ordeal, the Lord has cared for him.

Out of his own pain and renewed awareness of the Lord’s goodness, the psalmist turns to others who suffer. He holds out the promise of God’s loving care for those who persevere in hoping for the Lord.

This wisdom psalm of confession and thanksgiving encourages and exhorts the godly to learn from the psalmist’s experience of sin, denial, confession, and forgiveness. This psalm was one of the seven psalms of penitence used in the early church (also [Pss 6](Ps.6.1-Ps.6.10), [38](Ps.38.1-Ps.38.22), [51](Ps.51.1-Ps.51.19), [102](Ps.102.1-Ps.102.28), [130](Ps.130.1-Ps.130.8), [143](Ps.143.1-Ps.143.12)).

The Lord’s forgiveness restores people to fellowship with him, clears them of **guilt***,* and gives them great **joy**. Paul quoted this text when explaining justification by faith alone ([Rom 4:4-8](Rom.4.4-Rom.4.8)).

The psalmist acknowledges his own sin (see [19:12-13](Ps.19.12-Ps.19.13); [25:7](Ps.25.7), [11](Ps.25.11), [15-22](Ps.25.15-Ps.25.22)) and his resistance to confessing sin. The Lord pressed him hard until he confessed his guilt.
The psalmist attributes his suffering directly to the Lord’s **hand of discipline** (cp. [38:2](Ps.38.2); [39:10](Ps.39.10)).

God has forgiven the **guilt** and **rebellion** of [32:1](Ps.32.1). The Lord’s nature is to reconcile and forgive ([78:38](Ps.78.38); [85:2](Ps.85.2); [130:4](Ps.130.4)), but he requires confession and repentance.
The **godly** will learn from the psalmist’s experience to pray for forgiveness before it is too late.
The Lord promises to be his people’s **hiding place** ([31:20](Ps.31.20)). Instead of being overwhelmed by terror ([31:13](Ps.31.13)), the psalmist is surrounded by **songs of victory**.
God interrupts the psalmist’s teaching with a message that invites the godly to receive the Lord’s wisdom (see [5:8](Ps.5.8); [23:3](Ps.23.3); [25:4-6](Ps.25.4-Ps.25.6)).
The **senseless** person is not wise. Rejecting the Lord’s counsel ruins life and makes one like an animal (see [Isa 1:3](Isa.1.3); [Jas 3:3](Jas.3.3)).
Difficulties common to all of life will ensnare the wicked, whereas the Lord promises to protect the godly with his care.

This hymn of creation (see also [Pss 8](Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9), [19](Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14), [104](Ps.104.1-Ps.104.35), [145](Ps.145.1-Ps.145.21)) might be a continuation of [Ps 32](Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11). It exhorts readers to praise God ([33:1-3](Ps.33.1-Ps.33.3)), to recognize the power of his word in creation ([33:4-7](Ps.33.4-Ps.33.7)), and to fear the Creator ([33:8-11](Ps.33.8-Ps.33.11)). It offers hope to forgiven sinners ([Ps 32](Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11)) that they can live a new life in the fear of the Lord and under divine protection.
The psalmist exhorts **the godly** to praise the Lord **with melodies***,* with **a new song***,* and with **skillfully**-played music.
God’s **word** displays his character and his power.
The nations surrounding Israel thought that the **sea** had divine power, but it is under God’s control, within **boundaries** that he set (see [104:8-10](Ps.104.8-Ps.104.10)).

**Fear** of the Lord begins with awe for God and for his powerful word. His word created everything and continues to order and sustain creation. He **frustrates** the plans of people who oppose his will.
The power of the Lord extends to all the nations (see 2; [96:1-3](Ps.96.1-Ps.96.3)).
The **plans** and **schemes** of the mighty will not prevail, except by God’s will (see [Isa 8:9-10](Isa.8.9-Isa.8.10)).
God’s word still orders creation and will do so **forever**.
God’s **intentions** are marvelous ([40:5](Ps.40.5); [92:5](Ps.92.5)).
People who fear God are **chosen as his inheritance** (see [33:13-19](Ps.33.13-Ps.33.19)); this excludes rebellious people ([78:62](Ps.78.62)).
From the heavens, the Lord searches out and cares for anyone who fears him (see [14:2-3](Ps.14.2-Ps.14.3)).
**army . . . great strength . . . warhorse:** Even military might is under God’s control (see [33:10-11](Ps.33.10-Ps.33.11); [Eccl 9:11](Eccl.9.11)).
God **watches over** all who live by his counsel ([32:8](Ps.32.8)). He protects, rescues, and remains close to them ([34:15-22](Ps.34.15-Ps.34.22)).
The godly respond to this magnificent vision of God’s power in creation and in the affairs of the world with an affirmation of trust, commitment, joy, and hope as they pray and wait for God’s rescue.
Using a play on words, the psalmist contrasts his people’s sure **hope** (Hebrew *yakhal*) in the Lord with the supposed strength ([33:17](Ps.33.17); Hebrew *khayil*) of the horses of the wicked.

This wisdom psalm includes a thanksgiving hymn ([34:1-7](Ps.34.1-Ps.34.7)) that celebrates the Lord’s care for and protection of godly sufferers. It also includes an invitation to wisdom ([34:8-14](Ps.34.8-Ps.34.14)) and an exposition of wisdom concerning the Lord’s care for the needy and the suffering of the wicked ([34:15-22](Ps.34.15-Ps.34.22)).
The psalmist exhorts the **helpless** to join him in praise.
34:title
**Abimelech** is another name for Achish (see [1 Sam 21:10-15](1Sam.21.10-1Sam.21.15)). The body of the psalm makes no explicit connection to this event.
The psalmist narrates his experiences of answered prayer.

The **angel of the** **LORD** represented the Lord’s presence during the wilderness journey. He protected Israel from the forces of Egypt ([Exod 14:19-20](Exod.14.19-Exod.14.20)), and he will guard all the godly ([Ps 91:11](Ps.91.11)).
The godly encourage everyone to seek wisdom, to fear the Lord, and to place themselves under the protection of the Lord’s angel.
Fear of the Lord includes reverence and respect, and it motivates a life of wisdom (see [Prov 1:7](Prov.1.7); [9:10](Prov.9.10)).
Wisdom contains three components: fearing the Lord ([34:11](Ps.34.11)), doing good ([34:14](Ps.34.14)), and rejecting evil ([34:13](Ps.34.13)).
Anyone who listens, even **children***,* can become wise followers of God.
Peter quotes this passage in his instructions for peaceful living ([1 Pet 3:10-12](1Pet.3.10-1Pet.3.12)).
Godly people control their words; **speaking evil** and **telling lies** are foolish (see [10:7](Ps.10.7); cp. [17:1](Ps.17.1)).
The way of **peace** leads to harmony and order, whereas **evil** destroys them (see [37:11](Ps.37.11)).

The Lord distinguishes between wise and foolish people; he shows his concern for the wise by rescuing them from trouble ([34:15](Ps.34.15), [17-20](Ps.34.17-Ps.34.20)), but he destroys the foolish ([34:16](Ps.34.16), [21](Ps.34.21)).

Those who are **brokenhearted** possess a spirit of deep contrition and dependence on the Lord. God accepts this spirit as a proper sacrifice ([51:17](Ps.51.17)). The wicked hate the brokenhearted ([109:16](Ps.109.16)), but the Lord heals them ([147:3](Ps.147.3); see [Isa 57:15](Isa.57.15); [61:1](Isa.61.1)).
The godly might suffer, but the Lord will reward them in the end. Similarly, the wicked might prosper for a time, but ultimately they will perish ([1:6](Ps.1.6); [34:15-16](Ps.34.15-Ps.34.16)).
**Bones** represent a person’s entire being (see [6:2](Ps.6.2)).
**not one of them is broken:** John applied this statement to Jesus at the crucifixion ([John 19:36](John.19.36)).
In this lament, the Lord’s troubled servant calls for God to see his circumstances and vindicate him.
The psalmist longs for the Lord’s salvation. The language seems vindictive, but it arises from a desire for justice and for the Lord to care for the needy and oppressed.

A **path** that is **dark and slippery** suggests instability and untimely doom under the Lord’s judgment (see [69:23](Ps.69.23); [73:18](Ps.73.18); [82:5](Ps.82.5); [107:10](Ps.107.10); [143:3](Ps.143.3)).
The **angel of the** **LORD** is an agent of judgment as well as salvation.
Nothing in the universe can **compare** with the Lord (see [86:8](Ps.86.8); [89:6](Ps.89.6), [8](Ps.89.8); [Isa 40:18](Isa.40.18), [25](Isa.40.25)).
The psalmist presents the Lord with the reasons for his suffering. Evil has many faces. He is tired and worn out, and he knows that only the Lord can help him.
**Malicious witnesses** want nothing but violence (see [11:4-6](Ps.11.4-Ps.11.6); [54:3](Ps.54.3)).
The psalmist’s attackers **snarl** to express their bitter envy.

In this prayer for vindication, the psalmist’s crisis looms so large that a resolution must be found in the Lord. The psalmist has taken the high road, believing that vengeance belongs to the Lord. God’s patience hardens the hearts of the wicked and gives them reasons to justify their evil lifestyle.
John applied this claim of innocence (see also [69:4](Ps.69.4)) to Jesus ([John 15:25](John.15.25)).
**Aha! . . . Look:** Both words translate the same expression of glee (Hebrew *he’akh*).
The psalmist calls on the Lord to judge the wicked and to rescue the godly and bring them joy.

This lament contrasts the world of folly devised by the wicked with the world of wisdom created and sustained by the Lord. The wicked care only about themselves, whereas the Lord cares for all of creation. He will intervene to bring about justice in his world. The righteous will enjoy his protection, but the wicked will perish.
Fools despise what is wise and good as they pursue evil.
**no fear of God:** Paul includes this phrase in his description of the depravity of all people ([Rom 3:18](Rom.3.18)).
As the source of wisdom, the Lord is reliable and incomparable. His faithful care extends to all parts of the created order.
God’s all-encompassing goodness surpasses that of the created order. God graciously meets his people’s practical needs.
All creatures live by God’s grace ([1 Tim 4:10](1Tim.4.10)).
God invites **all humanity** to the banquet in his **house** (cp. [Prov 9:1-6](Prov.9.1-Prov.9.6)).
**Light** represents salvation and celebration ([18:25-29](Ps.18.25-Ps.18.29); [27:1](Ps.27.1); cp. [35:6](Ps.35.6)).
Since God’s wisdom extends to all of creation, it protects the godly.
The psalmist remains confident that the disorder caused by the wicked ([36:1-4](Ps.36.1-Ps.36.4)) will end when they meet their demise.

This psalm elaborates on the problems posed in [Ps 36](Ps.36.1-Ps.36.12): How should the godly respond to the reality of evil? When will the Lord bring justice? Why does he permit the wicked to destroy his created order? [Psalm 37](Ps.37.1-Ps.37.40) offers clear responses that reduce the tensions of life ([37:1-9](Ps.37.1-Ps.37.9), [34](Ps.37.34)) and promise that the meek will have a future ([37:10-11](Ps.37.10-Ps.37.11), [39-40](Ps.37.39-Ps.37.40)). The alternating contrast between the godly and the wicked emphasizes the futility of folly ([37:12-24](Ps.37.12-Ps.37.24), [27-33](Ps.37.27-Ps.37.33)). The personal observations of the psalmist add a human touch ([37:25-26](Ps.37.25-Ps.37.26), [35-38](Ps.37.35-Ps.37.38)). He encourages viewing the inheritance of the land from a long-range perspective: The earth belongs to the Lord, who will give it to those he blesses—the lowly and godly who trust in him, put their hope in him, and follow him (see [37:9](Ps.37.9), [11](Ps.37.11), [22](Ps.37.22), [29](Ps.37.29), [34](Ps.37.34); see also [Isa 57:13](Isa.57.13); [Matt 5:5](Matt.5.5)).

The wise respond to evil by trusting in the Lord. Trust includes five dimensions: (1) renouncing irritability and envy ([37:1-2](Ps.37.1-Ps.37.2)); (2) delighting in the Lord ([37:3-4](Ps.37.3-Ps.37.4)); (3) submitting to the Lord ([37:5-6](Ps.37.5-Ps.37.6)); (4) practicing patience in hope ([37:7](Ps.37.7)); and (5) avoiding anger ([37:8-9](Ps.37.8-Ps.37.9)).
**envy:** The jealous desire to have what others enjoy leads to further sin ([73:3](Ps.73.3); [Prov 3:31](Prov.3.31); [Jas 1:14-15](Jas.1.14-Jas.1.15); [4:1-2](Jas.4.1-Jas.4.2)).
The antidote to irritability and envy ([37:1](Ps.37.1)) is trust in the Lord.
To **do good** means cultivating a devotion to wisdom (see [34:14](Ps.34.14); [Prov 3:5-7](Prov.3.5-Prov.3.7)).
To **take delight in the** **LORD** means aligning with the Lord’s way in order to enjoy him.
**Justice** occurs when the Lord’s will triumphs and the godly experience his rescue ([Isa 45:8](Isa.45.8); [51:5-6](Isa.51.5-Isa.51.6); [58:8](Isa.58.8), [10-11](Isa.58.10-Isa.58.11)).
**Be still:** We should let the Lord be God rather than taking matters into our own hands.
Irritability and anger quickly corrode character.
The wicked will not **possess the land***;* those who **trust in the** **LORD** will. The Lord promises an inheritance because he is committed to caring for his people.

The Lord is the author of **peace** ([85:10](Ps.85.10))—he brings peace to a chaotic world ([29:11](Ps.29.11); [37:11](Ps.37.11); [85:8](Ps.85.8); [147:14](Ps.147.14)). His wisdom guides **the lowly** into the way of peace ([119:165](Ps.119.165); [Matt 5:5](Matt.5.5)).
**The wicked** seek to destroy the Lord’s order, but he defeats them.
The wicked **snarl** to express their bitter envy. They plot to bring an end to the godly, but the Lord derides them because they cannot succeed ([2:4](Ps.2.4)).
The weapons of the wicked will turn against them (cp. [7:12-13](Ps.7.12-Ps.7.13)).
Being wise with modest means is **better** than having prosperity and power and being wicked ([Prov 15:16](Prov.15.16); [16:8](Prov.16.8), [19](Prov.16.19); [17:1](Prov.17.1); [28:6](Prov.28.6)).
The Lord cares for the blameless in this life and for eternity, but the wicked will perish.
**Smoke** depicts the temporary nature of life ([68:2](Ps.68.2); [102:3](Ps.102.3)).
To **borrow and never repay** is a behavior of a crooked lifestyle.
**Generous givers** freely share what they freely receive from the Lord (see [111:5](Ps.111.5); [112:5](Ps.112.5)).
The rectitude and strength of a godly person’s life comes from the Lord (see [Prov 4:12](Prov.4.12); [14:15](Prov.14.15); [16:9](Prov.16.9); [20:24](Prov.20.24)).
The Lord does not abandon his children or their descendants.

The **godly** are wise; they do good and reject evil. The Lord cares for them, protecting them and ensuring that they receive their rightful portion of **the land** as their inheritance. The **wicked** might try to **ambush** the **godly***,* but they will not succeed.
**The godly** base their **counsel** on the Lord’s wisdom.
**They have made God’s law their own:** The godly internalize God’s wisdom and instructions (see [119:11](Ps.119.11); [Jer 24:7](Jer.24.7); [31:31-34](Jer.31.31-Jer.31.34)).
The **wicked** might appear to be **flourishing like a tree** (cp. [52:8](Ps.52.8); [92:12-13](Ps.92.12-Ps.92.13)), but they eventually die and are forgotten ([37:2](Ps.37.2)).
The Lord provides strength for his people.
This psalm is a lament and prayer for healing. The psalmist’s suffering is associated with his unconfessed sin. He confesses his sin and entrusts his case to the Lord.
These verses form a prelude to the psalmist’s confession ([38:18](Ps.38.18)) and describe his woeful condition.
The psalmist’s **sins** had triggered the Lord’s **anger** and **rage***,* resulting in the **arrows** and **blows** of **discipline** and **rebuke***;* as a result, his **whole body is sick**.
38:title
**asking God to remember him:** The meaning of this phrase is uncertain (also in [70:title](Ps.70.1)).

Sin can lead to sickness and even death ([1 Cor 11:30](1Cor.11.30)). Whether the psalmist actually felt physically ill or his sickness was a metaphor for emotional turmoil, he knew that it came from God and threatened his life (see [Pss 32:3](Ps.32.3); [39:10](Ps.39.10)).
The psalmist’s **burden** results from sin (see [40:12](Ps.40.12); [41:4](Ps.41.4); cp. [Gen 4:13](Gen.4.13)).
The severity of God’s punishment brings anguish that affects every part of the psalmist’s being.
The psalmist longs for a restored relationship with God, but he feels alienated. He finds himself lost and alone as his friends disappear.
The psalmist suffers quietly before his opponents (see [Isa 53:7](Isa.53.7)).
The Lord alone will resolve the conflict ([9:18](Ps.9.18); [27:14](Ps.27.14); [37:9](Ps.37.9), [34](Ps.37.34)).
No longer able to endure his suffering and teetering **on the verge of collapse** (cp. [15:5](Ps.15.5)), the psalmist confesses his sin (see [32:5](Ps.32.5)).
That the psalmist’s enemies hate him **without reason** compounds his pain.

Asking the Lord to act quickly in times of great need is common in the Psalter ([22:19](Ps.22.19); [31:2](Ps.31.2); [40:13](Ps.40.13); [69:17](Ps.69.17); [70:1](Ps.70.1); [71:12](Ps.71.12); [79:8](Ps.79.8); [102:2](Ps.102.2); [141:1](Ps.141.1); [143:7](Ps.143.7)). However, wisdom and experience teach that God’s people must often wait for him to act ([27:14](Ps.27.14); [37:7](Ps.37.7); [Isa 8:17](Isa.8.17); [40:31](Isa.40.31)).
This prayer for rescue reflects the psalmist’s discouragement, which comes from having a limited perspective on his situation.
Suffering in **silence** only intensifies the psalmist’s anguish, pain, and inner **turmoil**.
39:title
**Jeduthun** was a levitical singer appointed by David along with Asaph ([1 Chr 9:16](1Chr.9.16); [16:38](1Chr.16.38); [25:1](1Chr.25.1)).

Because of his suffering and sin, the psalmist concludes that life is meaningless and fleeting (see [Job 7:7-10](Job.7.7-Job.7.10); [Isa 40:6-8](Isa.40.6-Isa.40.8)). He had expected a wicked life to have those qualities (see [Pss 37:2](Ps.37.2), [20](Ps.37.20); [103:15-16](Ps.103.15-Ps.103.16)), but now whether a person is godly or not seems to be irrelevant.

**how fleeting my life is:** This perspective comes out of suffering (see [78:39](Ps.78.39); [89:47-48](Ps.89.47-Ps.89.48); [90:3-10](Ps.90.3-Ps.90.10)). The human **lifetime** is but a **moment** to God ([90:4](Ps.90.4)), as temporary as a **breath** (see [39:11](Ps.39.11); [144:4](Ps.144.4)).
The idea that **rebellion** brings on suffering is a common thread in [Pss 32](Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11), [38–41](Ps.38.1-Ps.41.13).
The psalmist links suffering with God’s **discipline**, assuming that it is **punishment** for his sin.
The Lord uses **discipline** to correct his children ([38:1](Ps.38.1), [3](Ps.38.3), [7](Ps.38.7); [40:12](Ps.40.12); see [Prov 3:11-12](Prov.3.11-Prov.3.12); [Heb 12:5-6](Heb.12.5-Heb.12.6)).
A **guest** (or *foreigner*) had no rights of land ownership (see [Lev 25:23](Lev.25.23)). The patriarchs had lived as guests in Canaan ([Ps 105:23](Ps.105.23)).

Unlike the psalmist’s earlier request that God stay close to him ([38:21-22](Ps.38.21-Ps.38.22)), his present desire for God to **leave** him **alone** echoes Job’s disposition ([Job 7:17-19](Job.7.17-Job.7.19)).

This psalm includes a thanksgiving song ([40:1-10](Ps.40.1-Ps.40.10)) followed by a lament ([40:11-17](Ps.40.11-Ps.40.17)). The thanksgiving song includes the reason for the thanksgiving ([40:1-5](Ps.40.1-Ps.40.5)), an affirmation of commitment ([40:6-8](Ps.40.6-Ps.40.8)), and a public testimony of God’s character ([40:7-10](Ps.40.7-Ps.40.10)). The lament concerns the psalmist’s troubles because of his sins ([40:11-12](Ps.40.11-Ps.40.12)) and is followed by two prayers for vindication ([40:13-15](Ps.40.13-Ps.40.15), [17](Ps.40.17)).
The psalmist thanks the Lord for his rescue and testifies that God can be trusted.
The Lord delights in the attitude and character of the person making an offering more than in the offering itself.

**Now that you have made me listen, I finally understand:** Greek text reads *You have given me a body.* In [Heb 10:5-7](Heb.10.5-Heb.10.7), the writer quotes from the Greek version of [Ps 40:6-8](Ps.40.6-Ps.40.8). He casts the words as something Jesus said as he left heaven and came into the world.
**As is written about me in the Scriptures:** Moses had recorded God’s requirements for Israel’s kings in [Deut 17:14-15](Deut.17.14-Deut.17.15).
The psalmist prays that the Lord will be true to his character when answering this plea for mercy.
The psalmist is troubled by both his adversities and his own **sins** and prays for rescue.
This passage is repeated almost verbatim as [Ps 70](Ps.70.1-Ps.70.5).

In this wisdom psalm, the psalmist prays for healing ([41:4](Ps.41.4), [10](Ps.41.10)), laments his distress ([41:5-9](Ps.41.5-Ps.41.9)), and expresses confidence in the Lord’s blessing ([41:1-3](Ps.41.1-Ps.41.3), [11-12](Ps.41.11-Ps.41.12)).

The **poor** who suffer hardship have special protection under God’s law ([Lev 14:21](Lev.14.21); [19:10](Lev.19.10)); they receive God’s justice and godly rule ([Pss 72:13](Ps.72.13); [82:3-4](Ps.82.3-Ps.82.4)). The word translated *poor* is often a synonym for the godly ([113:7](Ps.113.7); see [Zeph 3:12](Zeph.3.12)).
**when they are sick:** This illness might be physical or spiritual (see [6:2](Ps.6.2); [Ps 38](Ps.38.1-Ps.38.22)).

The psalmist applies the blessing to himself ([41:12](Ps.41.12)). Apparently he has taken care of the poor ([41:1](Ps.41.1)), but he has sinned against the Lord in other ways. Out of his pain, he cries for healing while confessing his sin. The Lord alone can grant the restoration that brings true joy ([30:2](Ps.30.2); [107:20-21](Ps.107.20-Ps.107.21)).
The psalmist’s enemies disguise themselves as friends, while his friends openly become his enemies.
**How soon will he die?** The psalmist’s opponents regard his suffering as a divine judgment (cp. [1:6](Ps.1.6)).

**the one who shared my food:** Eating together was a sign of unity ([Acts 2:42](Acts.2.42)). Refusing to eat with someone indicated hostility ([1 Cor 5:11](1Cor.5.11)). Jesus experienced the same kind of betrayal ([John 13:1](John.13.1), [18](John.13.18)).
The psalmist knows that the Lord has forgiven him and will bless him.
This doxology closes Book One ([Pss 1–41](Ps.1.1-Ps.41.13)). Cp. [106:48](Ps.106.48).

These psalms, like [Pss 9](Ps.9.1-Ps.9.20) and [10](Ps.10.1-Ps.10.18), form a unit comprising a lament with a bittersweet refrain of hope ([42:5](Ps.42.5), [11](Ps.42.11); [43:5](Ps.43.5)). In many Hebrew manuscripts these two psalms are combined as one. The historical context is uncertain; these psalms might be the voice of God’s people in exile, confessing their loyalty to God as he punishes them for their prevailing apostasy. The psalmist longs for fellowship with God such as he enjoyed in Jerusalem ([42:4](Ps.42.4)); his memories only make him more discouraged. As the psalmist cries out to God, he recalls God’s love and faithfulness ([42:8](Ps.42.8)), which moves him to plead for vindication ([43:1-4](Ps.43.1-Ps.43.4)).
The psalmist’s longing for God comes from being geographically distant from the Temple as he remembers the past.

The verb translated **longs** is found only here and in [Joel 1:20](Joel.1.20) (“cry out”); in both cases it refers to extreme **thirst** in a waterless desert (see [Pss 63:1](Ps.63.1); [143:6](Ps.143.6); see also [84:2](Ps.84.2)).
42:title

**The descendants of Korah** were members of a Levitical choir appointed by David to serve as Temple singers (see [1 Chr 6:22-38](1Chr.6.22-1Chr.6.38); [9:19-34](1Chr.9.19-1Chr.9.34); [2 Chr 20:19](2Chr.20.19)). Their ancestor Korah was the apostate who had rebelled against Moses and whom the earth swallowed up ([Exod 6:24](Exod.6.24); [Num 16](Num.16.1-Num.16.50)).
The wicked try to hold God to their timetable and deny his power to intervene.
The psalmist recalls **leading a great procession** as a member of the Levitical choir, possibly during the high holy days.
The psalmist encourages himself with questions and answers.
The psalmist feels depressed, but it does not incapacitate him. He remembers that the living God is his **Savior**. This verse is repeated in [42:11](Ps.42.11) and [43:5](Ps.43.5).
**Mount Hermon** is a high mountain range northeast of Israel. The **source of the Jordan** is by Dan at the foot of Mount Hermon.
**Mount Mizar** might be a peak in the Mount Hermon range.
The **raging seas***,* **waves***,* and **surging tides** conjure images of God’s wrath (see [88:7](Ps.88.7)).
The psalmist sees rays of hope. A life oriented to God includes **songs** of joy and **praying** for justice and vindication ([42:9-10](Ps.42.9-Ps.42.10); [43:1-4](Ps.43.1-Ps.43.4)).
The psalmist brings his many doubts, discouragements, and questions directly to God.
The psalmist turns to the Lord for rescue from his troubles, for guidance, for restoration, and for vindication.
The Temple on the **mountain** in Jerusalem symbolized God’s **holy** presence among his people ([Pss 15:1](Ps.15.1); [43:3](Ps.43.3); [99:5](Ps.99.5), [9](Ps.99.9); [132:7](Ps.132.7)).
This verse is repeated in [42:5](Ps.42.5), [11](Ps.42.11).

This national lament after defeat in battle continues the tone of the previous two psalms, including reflecting on an unspecified moment in Israel’s history and calling on God for salvation. The people recite God’s past acts of rescue ([44:1-3](Ps.44.1-Ps.44.3)), acknowledge God’s power to save ([44:4-8](Ps.44.4-Ps.44.8)), describe their humiliation in exile ([44:9-16](Ps.44.9-Ps.44.16)), claim their innocence and lament the injustice of their current situation ([44:17-22](Ps.44.17-Ps.44.22)), and cry for vindication ([44:23-26](Ps.44.23-Ps.44.26)).

**we have heard . . . of all you did:** The story of redemption encompasses the story of God’s favor and power in his past acts of rescue (see [78:1-4](Ps.78.1-Ps.78.4); see also [Pss 105–106](Ps.105.1-Ps.106.48)).
God **drove out the pagan nations** during the conquests recorded in Joshua.

Though the Israelites used **swords** and other weapons ([44:6](Ps.44.6)), they would have lost their battles without the **light** of the Lord’s favor (see [18:25-29](Ps.18.25-Ps.18.29); [27:1](Ps.27.1); [89:15](Ps.89.15)).
God’s people feel confident about his mighty acts; he was with them in the past, and he is their king in the present.
The people have experienced defeat ([44:9-12](Ps.44.9-Ps.44.12)), so they understand suffering and disgrace ([44:13-16](Ps.44.13-Ps.44.16)).
**scattered us among the nations:** This probably refers to the Exile (see [51:18-19](Ps.51.18-Ps.51.19); [89:38-51](Ps.89.38-Ps.89.51); [106:40-47](Ps.106.40-Ps.106.47); [137](Ps.137.1-Ps.137.9)).
Paul quotes this verse as a parenthetical aside in his list of things that cannot separate us from Christ’s love ([Rom 8:36](Rom.8.36)).
In the end, God’s people can turn to the Lord and trust him for rescue. Their petition for God to remedy their situation is as strong as their lament about God’s rejection.
**Wake up:** Biblical authors often call for God’s attention in a crisis ([35:23](Ps.35.23); [44:23](Ps.44.23); [73:20](Ps.73.20); [80:2](Ps.80.2); [Mark 4:38](Mark.4.38)).

This psalm celebrates a royal wedding; it might have been sung on many occasions and not just at one wedding. As God’s representative, the king carried the responsibility of dispensing justice and maintaining order in God’s world (see [Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12)).
45:title
The **tune “Lilies”** is no longer known (see also [Ps 69](Ps.69.1-Ps.69.36)).

This general description of the king’s symbolic status anticipates his permanent legacy ([45:16](Ps.45.16)). That the Lord has **blessed** him and charged him to bear God’s attributes is symbolized by his **handsome** appearance and **gracious words**.
The psalmist expounds on the royal splendor the king showed when fighting his enemies.
Glory and majesty belong to the Lord ([96:6](Ps.96.6); [111:3](Ps.111.3)).
As God’s agent of **truth, humility, and justice** (see [72:1-2](Ps.72.1-Ps.72.2), [4](Ps.72.4), [7](Ps.72.7)), the king can carry out **awe-inspiring deeds** ([65:5](Ps.65.5); [96:4](Ps.96.4)).
The king is like a god among humans; he is anointed by God, he has received a mighty throne, and he dispenses justice as he rules forever.
The writer to the Hebrews applies [45:6-7](Ps.45.6-Ps.45.7) to Jesus as he argues that the Son is greater than the angels ([Heb 1:8-9](Heb.1.8-Heb.1.9)).
**Justice** characterizes God’s **rule***,* as it should characterize the king’s administration.
Fine spices mixed with oil create distinctive perfumes.
The king’s **palaces** were wood paneled with ivory inlays (cp. [6:4](Ps.6.4); [Amos 3:15](Amos.3.15)).
Marriages often sealed diplomatic connections between kings; the **women** became part of the harem (see [1 Kgs 11:1-3](1Kgs.11.1-1Kgs.11.3)).

The bride is a representative of the king. Powerful people and nations try to gain her favor in order to get close to the king. This is a great honor, and she is encouraged to give herself fully to her new position.
**The princess of Tyre:** Israel traded with Tyre, a powerful city-state. The noblest woman of the city bears a wedding gift to her counterpart, the new queen, who represents an honored kingdom.

This psalm of Zion celebrates God’s special presence in Jerusalem (see also [Pss 48](Ps.48.1-Ps.48.14), [76](Ps.76.1-Ps.76.12), [87](Ps.87.1-Ps.87.7), [122](Ps.122.1-Ps.122.9)), inviting confidence in the Lord because the citizens of Zion enjoy his protection.
Even when faced with natural disasters, the citizens of Zion express no fear.
46:title
**sung by soprano voices:** Hebrew *according to alamoth* (“maidens”; see also study note on 1 Chr 15:20). In worship, a choir or a group of instrumentalists performed this hymn.

The strong city where **God dwells** protects its inhabitants. They enjoy the **river** flowing inside the city. This river contrasts with the turbulent waters (the powers of the nations) outside the city.

Like the streams flowing through Eden, this **river** brings the water of life, restoration, and healing ([36:8-9](Ps.36.8-Ps.36.9); see [Gen 2:10](Gen.2.10); [Ezek 47](Ezek.47.1-Ezek.47.23); [Rev 22:2](Rev.22.2)).
**From the very break of day:** In the ancient Near East, enemies attacked cities during the day; even during the most dangerous times, the Lord **will protect** the place where his name dwells.

People and **nations** live **in chaos***,* characterized by opportunism ([83:2](Ps.83.2)), busyness ([39:6](Ps.39.6)), and noise. These people shake, totter, and **crumble***,* unlike the city of God (cp. [15:5](Ps.15.5)). In contrast, when the godly feel disturbed, they cry out for God’s help ([42:5](Ps.42.5), [11](Ps.42.11); [43:5](Ps.43.5); [55:17](Ps.55.17)).
This refrain reminds readers of the identity of the God of Zion.
**among us:** Hebrew *‘immanu,* part of the name Immanuel, “God with us” ([Isa 7:14](Isa.7.14); [8:8](Isa.8.8); [Matt 1:23](Matt.1.23)).
This invitation to trust in the Lord offers a perspective on God’s interactions with human powers.

Israel saw the Lord’s **glorious works** in the wilderness ([107:24](Ps.107.24); [111:2](Ps.111.2)), but the wicked, who have no concern for them ([28:5](Ps.28.5)), are left desolate ([73:19](Ps.73.19)).
A message directly from the Lord confirms the authenticity of the psalmist’s vision (see also [12:5-6](Ps.12.5-Ps.12.6); [32:8](Ps.32.8)).
**know that I am God:** The Lord will do what he promises ([Isa 45:3](Isa.45.3); [49:23](Isa.49.23); [60:16](Isa.60.16)).

God will be exalted ([Ps 47](Ps.47.1-Ps.47.9); [Isa 6:1](Isa.6.1)); he will judge the nations and rescue his people (see [Pss 57:11](Ps.57.11); [89:13](Ps.89.13); [108:5-6](Ps.108.5-Ps.108.6); [118:16](Ps.118.16)).

This psalm celebrates God’s kingship over all the earth; it tells of God’s victory in dealing with Israel and the nations. Both Israel ([47:3-4](Ps.47.3-Ps.47.4)) and the nations ([47:9](Ps.47.9)) participate in God’s kingdom.
As the sovereign king over the nations, God requires praise.
People **clap** their **hands** in praise and recognition of marvelous deeds ([47:3-4](Ps.47.3-Ps.47.4); see [98:8](Ps.98.8); [Isa 55:12](Isa.55.12); cp. [Nah 3:19](Nah.3.19)).
The Lord made Israel victorious, especially under David (see [18:40-50](Ps.18.40-Ps.18.50)). God’s mighty deeds of redemption manifest his love for Israel.
**Jacob’s descendants:** Jacob was the father of all Israelites ([Gen 32:28](Gen.32.28)); the name Jacob often represents the nation of Israel.
God **loves** and commits himself to Jacob (see [Pss 78:68](Ps.78.68); [127:2](Ps.127.2); see [Rom 11:28](Rom.11.28)).
The psalmist portrays the Lord as returning to heaven, having accomplished his victories. For a portrayal of his descent, see [18:9-16](Ps.18.9-Ps.18.16).
**trumpets:** Or *rams’ horns* (see [81:3](Ps.81.3)). At times, rams’ horns were sounded in celebration ([98:5-6](Ps.98.5-Ps.98.6); [2 Kgs 11:14](2Kgs.11.14); [1 Chr 15:28](1Chr.15.28)).
People from **all the earth** (see [96:1-3](Ps.96.1-Ps.96.3)) will worship God.

This song of Zion (see also [Pss 46](Ps.46.1-Ps.46.11), [76](Ps.76.1-Ps.76.12), [87](Ps.87.1-Ps.87.7), [122](Ps.122.1-Ps.122.9)) explicitly views Jerusalem (Zion) as the city of the Great King where the godly find protection ([48:1-3](Ps.48.1-Ps.48.3)). God rules from Zion in faithfulness, righteousness, and justice, and he inspires his subjects with confidence and joy ([48:9-11](Ps.48.9-Ps.48.11)). They commit themselves to seeing the glory of Zion for themselves so that they can tell the next generation about it ([48:8](Ps.48.8), [12-14](Ps.48.12-Ps.48.14)).
God dwells in Zion to protect it from all enemies (see [46:5](Ps.46.5)).

The **ships of Tarshish***,* built for long voyages, represent human accomplishment (see also [2 Chr 9:21](2Chr.9.21); [Isa 2:16](Isa.2.16)). Their destruction might be the event mentioned in [1 Kgs 22:48](1Kgs.22.48).
The psalmist joyfully celebrates the Lord’s presence in the midst of the community, reflecting on the faithfulness, righteousness, and justice of God’s rule.
**towers . . . fortified walls . . . citadels:** These structures provide a visual tour of Zion’s strength.

In this wisdom psalm, a wise teacher warns against enemies, whom he portrays as living a rich lifestyle and caring only for themselves ([49:5-9](Ps.49.5-Ps.49.9)). They cannot keep anyone alive, least of all themselves, even in their memories ([49:10-12](Ps.49.10-Ps.49.12)). Like fattened animals, they are led to slaughter ([49:14-20](Ps.49.14-Ps.49.20)).
The wisdom teacher invites everyone to the hall of wisdom; he promises to instruct with a proverb and a riddle.
Anyone who will **listen** can gain wisdom ([Prov 1:5](Prov.1.5), [8](Prov.1.8), [33](Prov.1.33)).
The teacher used both **proverbs** and **riddles** for instruction in wisdom (see [Prov 1:5-6](Prov.1.5-Prov.1.6)).
If enemies who live for material rewards cannot sustain themselves, how can they give life to others?
The teacher brings wisdom through irony. Everyone dies, and even those with **estates** named after them will be forgotten.
The teachers of false wisdom cannot rescue themselves from death. Only God has that power.
The **wicked** might have rich, luxurious lives, but they forget that they cannot avoid death.
God appears as judge to remind the godly and the ungodly in turn that outward performance of sacrificial rituals and recitation of the law are worthless without thankfulness, repentance, and justice.
The whole universe must pay attention when **God approaches** to bring justice into the world.

The Lord is coming to bring righteousness. This hope encourages his **faithful people***,* but those who have been unfaithful will not experience blessing when **the heavens above and earth below** testify against them (cp. [Deut 30:19](Deut.30.19); [31:28](Deut.31.28); [32:1](Deut.32.1); [Isa 1:2](Isa.1.2)). The Lord comes to restore order to the world ([Pss 5:8](Ps.5.8); [22:31](Ps.22.31); [33:5](Ps.33.5); [40:9](Ps.40.9); [50:6](Ps.50.6); [71:16](Ps.71.16); [97:6](Ps.97.6)).
The psalmist delivers a message against those who regard the sacrificial rituals as more important than having a proper heart attitude.
Unlike pagan gods, God does **not need** food; instead, he wants his people to serve him with a right heart ([50:14-15](Ps.50.14-Ps.50.15)).
**I own the cattle on a thousand hills:** God has no needs; he possesses everything.
**Thankfulness** means looking beyond self-interest to express gratitude for God’s blessings (see [51:15-17](Ps.51.15-Ps.51.17); [54:6](Ps.54.6)).
True **sacrifice** requires offering one’s self to the glory of God ([50:23](Ps.50.23); [Rom 12:1-2](Rom.12.1-Rom.12.2)).
God’s response to his people’s cry is to **rescue** them.
This message is against the wicked, who only pretend to listen to God.
**my discipline . . . my words:** The wicked may observe rituals, but they reject more important matters such as justice, mercy, and faithfulness (cp. [Matt 23:23-24](Matt.23.23-Matt.23.24)).
Because he is patient, God **remained silent**.
The wicked will experience God’s justice, while the godly will see God’s everlasting salvation.
God **will tear** the wicked **apart** like a lion tearing its prey ([Isa 5:29](Isa.5.29); [31:4](Isa.31.4); [Ezek 19:3](Ezek.19.3); cp. [Pss 7:2](Ps.7.2); [22:13](Ps.22.13)).

These psalms of David share a common thread in their reflection on the experience of evil. In [Ps 51](Ps.51.1-Ps.51.19), the psalmist confesses the evil he has done and asks God’s forgiveness. [Psalms 52–64](Ps.52.1-Ps.64.10) lament specific evils that David experienced. A song of praise ([Ps 65](Ps.65.1-Ps.65.13)) brings David’s laments to an end.

This moving prayer for restoration asks for God’s favor, mercy, forgiveness, and cleansing. Out of a broken spirit, the psalmist confesses and accepts responsibility for his sin ([51:3-6](Ps.51.3-Ps.51.6)), then petitions God to remove his guilt and renew him inwardly ([51:7-12](Ps.51.7-Ps.51.12)). The psalmist then recommits himself to a lifestyle of wisdom and joy in the service of God and others ([51:13-17](Ps.51.13-Ps.51.17)).
The repentant offender has nothing to offer God. He needs God’s favor, mercy, forgiveness, and blessing before he can experience renewal and restoration.
51:title
**regarding the time Nathan . . . Bathsheba:** See [2 Sam 11:1-27](2Sam.11.1-2Sam.11.27). The text of the psalm contains no explicit reference to this event.

A prayer for God’s **mercy** and kindness is part of the genre of lament. Sometimes the plea comes from the psalmist’s acknowledgment of his weakness and sin, as here (see also [6:2](Ps.6.2); [9:13](Ps.9.13); [25:16](Ps.25.16); [31:9](Ps.31.9); [41:4](Ps.41.4), [10](Ps.41.10)). At other times, it arises from the psalmist’s commitment to the Lord (see [26:11](Ps.26.11); [27:7](Ps.27.7); [119:29](Ps.119.29), [58](Ps.119.58), [132](Ps.119.132)). In each case, God’s mercy brings an inner renewal.
**Wash me . . . Purify me:** The psalmist prays for cleansing and release from the **guilt** of his sin ([51:7](Ps.51.7); see [26:6](Ps.26.6); [Isa 1:16](Isa.1.16), [18](Isa.1.18); [4:4](Isa.4.4)).
The psalmist accepts the consequences of his sin against God. He knows that there is nothing good in him unless God renews his life.

**Against . . . you alone:** This is hyperbole—the psalmist knows he also **sinned** against human beings ([2 Sam 11:2-4](2Sam.11.2-2Sam.11.4), [15-17](2Sam.11.15-2Sam.11.17)), but his offense against God is more important. He expects God to rebuke him and will accept whatever verdict God renders (see [Rom 3:4](Rom.3.4)).
**I was born a sinner:** The psalmist is not making excuses but is acknowledging the depth of his sinfulness. From the time we are **conceived***,* we all share in the human condition of sinfulness.

**Purify me from my sins** (literally *Purify me with the hyssop branch*; see [Exod 12:22](Exod.12.22); [Lev 14:4](Lev.14.4); [John 19:29](John.19.29); [Heb 9:19](Heb.9.19)): The psalmist depends on God to purify and renew him (see [Isa 1:18](Isa.1.18)).
Regaining **joy** is a gracious gift from God.
**you have broken me:** The psalmist’s whole being feels broken ([6:2](Ps.6.2); cp. [34:20](Ps.34.20)).
God’s Spirit renews and recreates the human spirit.
**A loyal spirit** yields the inner qualities of constancy and perseverance.
**your Holy Spirit:** Only the power of the Holy Spirit can change the human will to make it “loyal” ([51:10](Ps.51.10)) and “willing to obey” ([51:12](Ps.51.12)).
As he learns from his sin and its consequences, the psalmist wants to **teach** others.
**shedding blood:** This idiom includes any injustice, not just homicide ([9:12](Ps.9.12); [58:10](Ps.58.10); see [2 Sam 11:14-26](2Sam.11.14-2Sam.11.26); cp. [Isa 1:15-17](Isa.1.15-Isa.1.17)).

**rebuild the walls of Jerusalem:** These verses were probably added as a prayer for national restoration after the Exile (see [Pss 42–43](Ps.42.1-Ps.43.5)); the entire community in exile identified with the spirit of the psalm.

**Sacrifices offered in the right spirit** come from a heart that is right with God and with others (see [15:2-5](Ps.15.2-Ps.15.5); [24:3-6](Ps.24.3-Ps.24.6); [50:14](Ps.50.14); [Matt 5:23-24](Matt.5.23-Matt.5.24)).

Wicked people use words to destroy relationships and communities. They foolishly think that they can be heroes by their words ([52:1-4](Ps.52.1-Ps.52.4)), but their fate suddenly overtakes them ([52:5-7](Ps.52.5-Ps.52.7)). In contrast, the godly renew their commitment to the Lord ([52:8-9](Ps.52.8-Ps.52.9)) and find their future secure in him.

Liars foolishly deceive themselves by thinking that they can be heroes by their words. They believe themselves innocent of any charges of evildoing, though they love evil and cause destruction. Those who speak curses, sarcasm, bitterness, arrogant boasting, and deceptions ([31:18](Ps.31.18); [34:13](Ps.34.13); [59:7](Ps.59.7), [12](Ps.59.12); [120:2-3](Ps.120.2-Ps.120.3); [140:3](Ps.140.3), [9](Ps.140.9)) bring about chaos, alienation, and destruction ([Jas 3:5](Jas.3.5)). Their sharp words cut like swords and daggers ([Pss 55:21](Ps.55.21); [57:4](Ps.57.4); [64:3](Ps.64.3)), the fangs of a snake ([140:3](Ps.140.3)), or a **razor.**
52:title
This psalm refers to an incident in [1 Sam 21:1-10](1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.10); [22:9-10](1Sam.22.9-1Sam.22.10). The accuser, **Doeg the Edomite***,* is a paradigm of evil.
Deceptive speech changes one’s character.
God’s judgment on the wicked will come suddenly and forcibly. The godly rejoice in God’s justice, not in the misfortunes of the wicked.
God **will strike** the wicked **down** like a pagan altar, idol, or unclean vessel ([Exod 34:13](Exod.34.13); [Lev 11:35](Lev.11.35); [2 Kgs 10:27](2Kgs.10.27)).
In Hebrew, the verbs here translated **see** and **be amazed** sound almost alike.
The psalmist commits himself to a life of trust in the Lord.

An **olive tree** lives a long time when cared for ([1:3](Ps.1.3); [128:3](Ps.128.3)). The psalmist desires to be close to the Lord, his Savior and the source of his blessing ([18:6](Ps.18.6); [23:6](Ps.23.6)).
This psalm parallels [Ps 14](Ps.14.1-Ps.14.7), differing only in verse 5.
Paul uses the Greek translation of this passage in his description of the depravity of all people ([Rom 3:10-12](Rom.3.10-Rom.3.12)).

**scatter the bones:** Israel’s **enemies** would suffer shameful defeat and lack the peaceful rest of a decent burial (cp. [141:7](Ps.141.7); [2 Kgs 9:10](2Kgs.9.10); [Jer 8:1-2](Jer.8.1-Jer.8.2); [Ezek 6:5](Ezek.6.5)).

In this individual lament, occasioned by violent and godless people ([54:3](Ps.54.3)), the psalmist turns to God in prayer and maintains his focus on God’s help ([54:4](Ps.54.4)). He prays for God to save him from evil and to judge his enemies ([54:5](Ps.54.5), [7](Ps.54.7)).
54:title
This psalm refers to the account of [1 Sam 23:19-20](1Sam.23.19-1Sam.23.20), when the **Ziphites** were bent on violence.
The **strangers** were alienated from the covenant community (see [109:11](Ps.109.11); [Prov 5:10](Prov.5.10)).
Proud and **violent people** hold no regard for God or for other people (see [Pss 35:11](Ps.35.11), [25](Ps.35.25); [86:14](Ps.86.14); [Prov 11:16](Prov.11.16)).
In anticipation of God’s response, the mood of the psalm changes from gloom to thanksgiving.
A **voluntary offering** is a sacrifice of praise. Sacrifices of praise are the kind of offering God most desires (see [Ps 50:14-15](Ps.50.14-Ps.50.15), [23](Ps.50.23)).

The psalmist is faced with adversaries whose leader is a former friend ([55:12-14](Ps.55.12-Ps.55.14)), and he is overwhelmed with anguish. He turns to the Lord in prayer and commits himself to the Lord for redress ([55:22-23](Ps.55.22-Ps.55.23)). Jesus experienced similar suffering when his friend (Judas) betrayed him. He also experienced the answer to the psalmist’s prayer: (1) by taking the place of the wicked and receiving their judgment ([Isa 53:7-9](Isa.53.7-Isa.53.9)), and (2) by committing himself to the Father, who rescued ([Luke 23:46](Luke.23.46)) and rewarded him ([Isa 53:10-12](Isa.53.10-Isa.53.12)).
The occasion for this prayer is an attack by an enemy.
In the experience of deep anguish, the psalmist confesses that his adversity has become unbearable and he seeks an escape.
The psalmist’s enemy was once a **friend**; memories of that close relationship bring him pain (see [31:11](Ps.31.11)).
God is good and faithful, but the psalmist’s enemies and so-called friend are deceitful and wicked.
The psalmist commits all his cares **to the** **LORD**.
To **die young** means that one fails to experience God’s full blessing (cp. [Prov 3:2](Prov.3.2), [16](Prov.3.16)).
This individual lament moves from petition to confidence two times ([56:1-4](Ps.56.1-Ps.56.4), [5-13](Ps.56.5-Ps.56.13)).
56:title
David was **seized** by **Philistines** concerned about his loyalties and brought before King Achish ([1 Sam 21:10-15](1Sam.21.10-1Sam.21.15)).
**mere mortals:** Or *mere flesh,* in contrast to the immortal and infinitely more powerful God (see [Isa 2:22](Isa.2.22)).
The psalmist specifies his charge against his attackers as he prays for their evil to cease.
The psalmist makes a play on the Hebrew words translated **sorrows** (Hebrew *nod*) and **bottle** (Hebrew *no’d*).

**mere mortals** (Hebrew *’adam*)**:** The psalm also uses two other words for man: *’enosh* (“people,” [56:1](Ps.56.1)) and *basar* (“mere mortals,” [56:4](Ps.56.4)). All express the ideas of mortality and finitude.
The **light** of God’s goodness and salvation will replace the darkness of **death** (see [18:25-29](Ps.18.25-Ps.18.29); [27:1](Ps.27.1)).

The psalmist’s cry for mercy and protection quickly turns into an affirmation of trust and confidence in the Lord ([57:1-4](Ps.57.1-Ps.57.4)). When the wicked fall into their own traps ([57:6](Ps.57.6)), the psalmist will praise the Lord ([57:7-10](Ps.57.7-Ps.57.10)).
57:title
**David . . . fled from Saul and went into the cave:** See [1 Sam 22:1](1Sam.22.1) or [Ps 24:1-8](Ps.24.1-Ps.24.8).
**shadow of your wings:** As a bird protects its young, God protects the one who trusts in him (see [17:8](Ps.17.8)).

**God Most High** (Hebrew *Elohim-Elyon*) is a generic title for God, who is more powerful than all real or imagined supernatural beings (see [91:1](Ps.91.1); [97:9](Ps.97.9); [Gen 14:18-22](Gen.14.18-Gen.14.22)).
**who will fulfill his purpose:** Or *who will end my \[trouble\],* or *who deals kindly with me*.

These verses are a prayer for rescue from powerful enemies. The metaphor of **fierce lions** describes human enemies; the psalmist feels unable to escape them without God’s intervention (see also [35:11-21](Ps.35.11-Ps.35.21); [124:6](Ps.124.6)).
This verse is repeated in [57:11](Ps.57.11) and [108:5](Ps.108.5).
God’s **glory**—his manifest presence that excludes all evil ([8:1](Ps.8.1); [19:1-4](Ps.19.1-Ps.19.4); [24:7](Ps.24.7))—will fill the whole created order ([Isa 6:3](Isa.6.3)).
This section is repeated with a few modifications in [108:1-5](Ps.108.1-Ps.108.5).
The psalmist is **confident** that God will end the night of evil (cp. [56:13](Ps.56.13)).
God’s glory extends to the whole universe, as will praise for his **unfailing love** and **faithfulness**.

The administration of justice is a mark of good government. God expects nothing less from his people. The psalmist condemns Israel’s leaders for abusing their power, and he calls on the Lord to rain down his curses upon the wicked. The demonstration of divine justice will reassure the godly that God is just.
The administrators of justice were furthering their own interests rather than those of the needy. The absence of justice gradually resulted in a violent society.

**rulers** (or *gods*): This designation was used for high officials and administrators of **justice** ([82:1](Ps.82.1), [6](Ps.82.6)). Elsewhere, it might refer to angelic creatures ([89:7](Ps.89.7)) or to the gods of the nations ([82:1](Ps.82.1); [Dan 11:36](Dan.11.36)).

All human beings are **born sinners** (see [51:5](Ps.51.5)); however, whereas the **wicked** indulge their sinful nature, the godly fight against it ([Rom 7:19-23](Rom.7.19-Rom.7.23); [Jas 4:1-10](Jas.4.1-Jas.4.10)).
**Venom** here means poisonous speech (see [140:3](Ps.140.3)).
The psalmist calls on God to **break** the destructive power of the wicked.
When moving over dry ground, **snails** dry up.
God’s judgment will come suddenly. The certainty of vindication brings joy to the godly.
Vindication is the reward of **those who live for God**.
The psalmist laments the power of enemies who conspire with other nations.
**Protect me** (or *place me on* *high*): When surrounded by evil, the godly pray for God to set them apart for himself and protect them.
59:title
**the time Saul sent soldiers to watch David’s house:** See [1 Sam 19:11-18](1Sam.19.11-1Sam.19.18).
The psalmist asks God to show the treacherous, deceptive, and **wicked traitors** no mercy (see [25:2](Ps.25.2)).
The wicked threaten like **vicious dogs***,* but the Lord responds with scorn.
The psalmist prays that the wicked will be forced to endure the same agonizing pain they have caused.
The wicked will go **unsatisfied***,* but the psalmist will praise the Lord’s **power** and **unfailing love**.
The psalmist laments a national defeat and cries out to God for rescue.
When God’s people experience his discipline, they affirm their loyalty and await God’s answer.
60:title
**useful for teaching:** This psalm was taught to young people as part of their education.
**regarding the time:** See [2 Sam 8:13-14](2Sam.8.13-2Sam.8.14).
**Aram-naharaim** and **Aram-zobah** refer to the Arameans of northwest Mesopotamia and Syria (see study note on Gen 24:10).
The **tune “Lily of the Testimony”** is unknown today.

**wine** (Hebrew *yayin*) **that sent us reeling:** *Yayin,* the generic Hebrew term meaning “wine,” is often associated with drunkenness ([2 Sam 13:28](2Sam.13.28); [Isa 5:11](Isa.5.11); [28:7-8](Isa.28.7-Isa.28.8); cp. [Ps 104:15](Ps.104.15); [Deut 14:26](Deut.14.26); [Isa 55:1](Isa.55.1)); it symbolized God’s judgment of the wicked ([Ps 75:8](Ps.75.8); [Jer 51:7](Jer.51.7)).
God **raised a banner** over his people to serve as **a rallying point** and as a source of pride and confidence.
The **fear** of God that leads to wisdom ([111:10](Ps.111.10)) is not weakness; it provides the perspective and strength required to do what is right.
This section is repeated verbatim in [108:6-13](Ps.108.6-Ps.108.13).
The psalmist prays for rescue based on the special relationship between God and his people.
The Lord responds with a message of promise. He shares his land with his people as spoils of war.
**Shechem** and **Succoth** represent Israel’s heartland.

Destroying a defeated invader’s capital (**the fortified city**) would help to ensure that they would not attack again. The capital of **Edom** was Bozrah, located to the southeast of Israel. Only God could grant **victory.**
In these royal prayers, the psalmist longs for God’s presence. All three psalms concern themselves with the king’s security.
The lamenting psalmist petitions God to protect him and lead him into his presence ([61:4-5](Ps.61.4-Ps.61.5)). He prays for God to extend and protect the king’s rule and makes vows to praise God.
**the ends of the earth:** This expression has the connotation of a cry that comes from a place far away from God.
The psalmist’s **heart is overwhelmed** with deep anguish.

The poet longs for God’s presence and seeks entrance into God’s home on earth for divine protection and care. To be received into God’s **sanctuary** (literally *tent*) is the greatest good (see [15:1](Ps.15.1); [23:6](Ps.23.6); [24:3-6](Ps.24.3-Ps.24.6)). The Hebrew word translated *sanctuary* recalls the Tabernacle and the tent that David built for the Ark ([1 Chr 15:1](1Chr.15.1)). See also study note on John 1:14.
The **shelter of your wings** symbolizes God’s protection and care (see [Pss 9:9](Ps.9.9); [17:8](Ps.17.8)).

**you have heard my vows:** The psalmist’s vows might also be a part of ceremonial sacrifices ([66:13-15](Ps.66.13-Ps.66.15); [76:11](Ps.76.11); [116:14](Ps.116.14), [18](Ps.116.18)). He praises and thanks God for his rescue.

The **inheritance** refers to the promise of the land (see [Ps 60](Ps.60.1-Ps.60.12)), the sacredness of the Temple, the joy of God’s presence ([119:111](Ps.119.111)), or any similar reward ([16:6](Ps.16.6); [37:9](Ps.37.9), [11](Ps.37.11), [18](Ps.37.18), [22](Ps.37.22), [29](Ps.37.29), [34](Ps.37.34); [127:3](Ps.127.3)).

This psalm expresses confidence in the king and offers prayer for him. The king rests in God despite his difficulties. Although his deceptive and powerful adversaries push hard against him, he remains undaunted. He encourages himself and his people to trust in God and to see their human adversaries from God’s perspective, where they appear frail, fleeting, and deceptive ([62:9](Ps.62.9)).
62:title
The enemies desire to topple the king with lies and cunning.
**My high position** refers to the royal throne.
The psalmist encourages himself and others to place their hope in God.
Unlike God, humans are transient beings. Even when they thrive, their prosperity is fleeting.
**not what they appear to be:** People often try to look stronger and better than they are.
The crime of **extortion** means using intimidation and threats to make others give up what is theirs, while **stealing** is taking what belongs to others.
Strength and **unfailing love** remain in balance only in God. He cares for his people by ridding the world of evildoers (see [1:6](Ps.1.6)).

The king longs for God’s presence so vividly that he eats, drinks, and sees God’s goodness. Though worn out and harassed by the wicked, the king sees God, and this animates him with praise. God becomes his life ([63:3](Ps.63.3)), while the wicked perish ([63:9](Ps.63.9)).
Together, **soul** and **whole body** refer to a person’s entire being.
**parched and weary land:** When David was living in the desert, he also found himself in a spiritual wasteland, separated from God’s people and the sanctuary.
The psalmist remembers that he had found God to be present in his **sanctuary** (see [18:6](Ps.18.6); [61:4](Ps.61.4); [62:5](Ps.62.5), [11-12](Ps.62.11-Ps.62.12)).
**better than life itself:** The highest quality of life is found in relationship with God (see [4:7](Ps.4.7); [63:5](Ps.63.5); [Prov 16:8](Prov.16.8)).

The psalmist reflects and meditates on God’s presence **through the night**. In the absence of light, God is the light. The quietness of the night and the longing for dawn provide time to focus on the true significance of life with the Lord.
**Meditating** on God requires focused awareness, concentration, thought, and reflection (see [1:2](Ps.1.2)).
The wicked were **plotting to destroy** the psalmist’s life through deception and lies, but they would meet their end.
The **depths of the earth** refers to the place of the dead.

Wild **jackals** are associated with desolation and abandonment ([Isa 13:20-22](Isa.13.20-Isa.13.22); [34:10-15](Isa.34.10-Isa.34.15); [Jer 9:11](Jer.9.11); [49:33](Jer.49.33); [51:37](Jer.51.37); [Lam 5:18](Lam.5.18); [Mal 1:3](Mal.1.3)). The wicked will not receive honor in death; their bodies will be left to scavenging animals ([Eccl 6:3](Eccl.6.3); [Jer 22:18-19](Jer.22.18-Jer.22.19); [36:29-30](Jer.36.29-Jer.36.30)).

This lament decries the destructive plots and arrogant attitude of the wicked ([64:1-6](Ps.64.1-Ps.64.6)). The psalmist turns to God in prayer and takes heart in God’s justice because whatever the wicked do will be undone by the righteous judge. The godly will rejoice and grow in wisdom as they reflect on God’s mighty acts.
These verses form a prayer for rescue from bold and powerful liars.
**their tongues . . . bitter words:** Liars use their speech to kill. This description might also refer to practicing magic.
The enemies create a **perfect plan** to harm the innocent without getting caught.
Human beings will sink to unthinkable depths with evil words, acts, or plans ([83:3](Ps.83.3); see [Jer 17:9](Jer.17.9)).
What God does is righteous. God undoes what is wicked and pays the wicked back with what they planned for others.
This psalm recounts the reasons why all people should praise and revere God for his almighty power and merciful care for his universe.
Praise is the appropriate response to God’s majestic deeds in redemption ([65:3-5](Ps.65.3-Ps.65.5)) and in nature ([65:5-13](Ps.65.5-Ps.65.13)).
God alone deserves **praise** and is worthy to have **vows** made to him.
**All of us** means all humans.
**you forgive:** God graciously removes the guilt of sin (see [32:5](Ps.32.5)).
**those you choose to bring near:** This includes people from Israel and from other nations.
Only those whom God sees as blameless **live in** his **holy courts** ([Pss 15](Ps.15.1-Ps.15.5) and [24](Ps.24.1-Ps.24.10)).
At the **Temple***,* God’s earthly palace, all nations can gather to experience God’s holy presence. No structure can separate humans from God (see [Rev 21:22](Rev.21.22)).
God brought order to **the mountains***,* the **raging oceans***,* and the **pounding waves** (see [Pss 95:4-5](Ps.95.4-Ps.95.5); [104:6-9](Ps.104.6-Ps.104.9)).
The psalmist compares the chaotic forces of nature with the rebellion of the **nations** (see [2:1-12](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12); [33:6-11](Ps.33.6-Ps.33.11); [46:6](Ps.46.6)).
All over the world ([Job 38:13](Job.38.13); see [Ps 50:1-3](Ps.50.1-Ps.50.3)), people should **stand in awe of** the Lord.
The created order provides clear evidence of God’s power ([65:6-8](Ps.65.6-Ps.65.8)). He shows his love by maintaining nature. Everything praises the Lord as all the parts fit together harmoniously.

The **river of God** and all rivers demonstrate God’s victorious power and goodness through the order in nature and the regularity of the harvests (see [1:3](Ps.1.3); [36:8](Ps.36.8); [46:4](Ps.46.4); [Ezek 47:6-12](Ezek.47.6-Ezek.47.12); [Zech 14:8](Zech.14.8); [Rev 22:1](Rev.22.1)).
This anonymous psalm includes two hymns ([66:1-12](Ps.66.1-Ps.66.12), [13-20](Ps.66.13-Ps.66.20)) that praise God for his redemption.
The psalmist exhorts nature to join in a mighty chorus to praise God’s glory, name, and power.
The **glory of his name** represents the perfection of God’s character.

The story of the Exodus and God’s victory over the sea evokes responses of astonishment ([66:5](Ps.66.5)) and worship ([66:6](Ps.66.6)). God works **miracles . . . for people** in order to redeem them for himself.
God’s **power** brings redemption. The same word occurs in [65:6](Ps.65.6) for God’s power in creation (see also [80:2](Ps.80.2)).
The orderly lives of the redeemed reflect the order of God’s world. The Lord protects them from evil and purifies them.
God guides his people into wisdom and away from folly ([17:5](Ps.17.5); [37:31](Ps.37.31); [121:3](Ps.121.3)).
**You have tested us, O God:** As the silversmith heats **silver** to remove the dross, God’s discipline removes sin from his people (see [12:6](Ps.12.6)).
God decrees and permits the many trying circumstances his people experience.
**Then you put a leader over us:** Or *You made people ride over our heads.* This expression possibly refers to a foreign ruler who kept the Israelites in submission.
Vows often included sacrifices of thanksgiving, including **burnt offerings** (see [20:3](Ps.20.3); [40:6](Ps.40.6); [50:8](Ps.50.8); [51:19](Ps.51.19)).
The private testimony in the conclusion of the psalm parallels the public praise of its opening ([66:1-4](Ps.66.1-Ps.66.4)).
Confession leads to restoration (see [32:5](Ps.32.5)).

In this anonymous prayer for God’s blessing, the psalmist addresses the knowledge and worship of God among the nations (cp. [64:9](Ps.64.9); [65:8](Ps.65.8)). The prayer requests that God’s name be kept holy and that his kingdom come (cp. [Matt 6:9-13](Matt.6.9-Matt.6.13)).
This prayer is based on the priestly blessing found in [Num 6:24-26](Num.6.24-Num.6.26). God’s goodness to Israel affects his reputation among the nations (see [Ps 96:1-3](Ps.96.1-Ps.96.3)).
God’s international reputation leads to his praise among the **nations** (see [138:4](Ps.138.4)), whose turmoil and rebelliousness will cease when they join Israel in praise of God.
One God rules over all, and the nations will give thanks for God’s just rule (see [67:4](Ps.67.4)).
God brings the ultimate **justice** that human beings desire ([96:10](Ps.96.10); [98:9](Ps.98.9)).
Bountiful **harvests** are evidence of God’s blessing ([Gen 26:12](Gen.26.12); [Isa 30:23](Isa.30.23)).
**all over the world:** See [Pss 2:8](Ps.2.8); [96:1-3](Ps.96.1-Ps.96.3).
All **will fear him***,* joining with Israel to acknowledge the God of Israel.

This prayer for God’s victorious rule traces God’s march from Sinai to Zion ([68:7](Ps.68.7), [16-18](Ps.68.16-Ps.68.18), [24](Ps.68.24)). He rescued the nation of Israel from Egypt, guided it through the wilderness, brought it into the Promised Land, and established his kingdom. He is a caring and victorious God, whose nature is unchanging. Therefore, the godly hope and rejoice in the prospect of God’s universal dominion.

These verses form a prayer for God to **rise up** and **scatter** his **enemies***,* as he did when Israel entered the Promised Land (cp. [Num 10:35-36](Num.10.35-Num.10.36); [Josh 6–12](Josh.6.1-Josh.12.24)).
Both **smoke** and **wax** represent a transitory existence ([22:12-18](Ps.22.12-Ps.22.18); [37:20](Ps.37.20); [102:3](Ps.102.3)).
The lot of **the godly** contrasts with that of the wicked (see [1:6](Ps.1.6)).
The psalmist praises God’s powerful and compassionate reign.

**him who rides the clouds:** This is an ancient description of Baal, a Canaanite deity. The psalmist applies it to **the** **LORD** as the true “Rider of the Clouds” (see [68:33](Ps.68.33); [104:3](Ps.104.3)). God wields power over the clouds and the rain.
God, the **Father** of all marginalized and needy people, shows them compassion and protects their rights (see [10:14](Ps.10.14), [18](Ps.10.18); [69:33](Ps.69.33); [82:3](Ps.82.3)).
Like his **dwelling***,* the Lord **is holy**. The supreme example of the holy God coming down to rescue humanity is Jesus Christ.
God released Israel from slavery in Egypt ([Exod 20:2](Exod.20.2); see [Ps 69:33](Ps.69.33)), and he still **sets the prisoners free**.
The **sun-scorched** desert represents alienation from God and separation from blessing.
The **earth trembled** as in an earthquake (see [Exod 19:18](Exod.19.18)).
**the heavens poured down rain:** Wells in the desert and rain showers in Canaan supplied an abundance of water.
**a great army** (or *a host of women*) **brings:** The Hebrew suggests women singers caroling **the good news** of victory (see [68:25](Ps.68.25); [Exod 15:20](Exod.15.20)).
The seminomadic pastoral people **who lived among the sheepfolds** were surprised to receive **silver** and **gold** carvings from the battle.
**The Almighty** (Hebrew *Shaddai*) is an ancient designation for God (see [91:1](Ps.91.1); [Gen 17:1](Gen.17.1)).
The identification of **Mount Zalmon** is uncertain; it was possibly a mountain in Bashan (see [Ps 68:15](Ps.68.15)).

**Bashan** is a plateau northeast of Jerusalem and east of the Sea of Galilee that was known for its woods and pastureland (see [22:12](Ps.22.12); [Isa 2:13](Isa.2.13)). The **mountains** might have included Mount Hermon to the north of the plateau or Mount Zalmon, which might be Jebel ed-Druze on the east.

**Why do you look with envy?** Bashan is physically much more impressive than the mountains around Jerusalem, but it was not the home of the Lord. Only Mount Zion enjoyed the privilege of providing God’s dwelling place.
**Chariots***,* the ultimate weapon of the armed forces in the psalmist’s day, are an image of the Lord’s power to grant victory ([20:7](Ps.20.7); [44:3](Ps.44.3)).
**When you ascended to the heights:** The Most High established his reign victoriously in Zion.
**a crowd of captives . . . gifts:** This is an image of a victorious ruler leading the victory march after battle. Paul applied this image to Jesus Christ ([Eph 4:8-13](Eph.4.8-Eph.4.13)).
The Divine Warrior cares for his people like a shepherd; the people praise him.
Like a caring father or a shepherd, God **carries** his people **in his arms** (see [55:22](Ps.55.22); [68:5-6](Ps.68.5-Ps.68.6)).
**God will smash the heads of his enemies:** Cp. [Gen 3:15](Gen.3.15).
God will deal with all **enemies***,* whether from high places (represented by **Bashan**) or low (**the depths of the sea**).
A great company joins together in the pilgrimage to Zion.
The people pray for God’s success and for victory over the enemy nations ([68:1-3](Ps.68.1-Ps.68.3)).
The conquered **kings** will bring gifts to the Lord.
Hostile and rebellious people delight in warfare and insurrection (see [2:1-3](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.3)).
The psalmist calls for the people to praise God, who is victorious over his enemies.
The term **kingdoms of the earth** includes all nations and power structures.
When the Lord demonstrates his **power***,* **majesty***,* and **strength** against the nations, he strengthens his people (see [96:4-6](Ps.96.4-Ps.96.6)).

These last four psalms of Book Two contrast with the psalms describing God’s mighty acts in creation and in redemption, capped by God’s march to Zion ([Pss 65–68](Ps.65.1-Ps.68.35)). [Psalms 69–71](Ps.69.1-Ps.71.24) portray the king’s anguish, and [Ps 72](Ps.72.1-Ps.72.20) responds with a prayer for God to bless the king.
In this individual lament, the poet expresses his vulnerability, humiliation, and overwhelming pain, asking God to vindicate him for the sake of the righteous.
The psalmist sees himself as almost drowning but still surviving chaotic forces and alienation from God (see [42:7](Ps.42.7); [69:14](Ps.69.14), [15](Ps.69.15); [Isa 8:8](Isa.8.8)).
69:title

**to the tune “Lilies”:** [Psalm 45](Ps.45.1-Ps.45.17) also notes this tune, but [Ps 45](Ps.45.1-Ps.45.17) celebrates the glory of kingship, whereas [Ps 69](Ps.69.1-Ps.69.36) is the cry of a tired king who feels abandoned by the Lord.
John applied this lament to Jesus ([John 15:25](John.15.25)).
The psalmist confesses his **sins** and prays that God’s response to him will encourage others in similar conditions to place their hope in the Lord.
Mistreated and abandoned by family, friends, and community, the psalmist turns to the Lord for comfort, relief ([69:13-18](Ps.69.13-Ps.69.18)), and redress ([69:22-28](Ps.69.22-Ps.69.28)).
