Though the psalmist concerns himself with God and all that is holy, **insults** have been his earthly reward. This verse was later applied to Jesus’ anger at the Temple’s money changers ([John 2:17](John.2.17)) and to his undeserved suffering ([Rom 15:3](Rom.15.3)).
When the psalmist denies himself normal comforts to seek God in prayer, the wicked ridicule him.
The psalmist’s only recourse is to pray for rescue and relief from his enemies.
Alone and misunderstood, the psalmist confesses that he cannot bear his doubts. His heart has been broken by his problems.
**sour wine for my thirst:** This description applies to Jesus’ suffering ([Matt 27:34](Matt.27.34), [48](Matt.27.48); [Luke 23:36](Luke.23.36); [John 19:28-29](John.19.28-John.19.29)).
The psalmist wants God to transfer his suffering ([69:3](Ps.69.3)) to his enemies. Paul applied these words to the unbelieving Jews of his day ([Rom 11:9-10](Rom.11.9-Rom.11.10)).
Peter quoted this verse after the death of Judas Iscariot ([Acts 1:20](Acts.1.20)).
The psalmist prays that his pain will turn to praise.

The psalmist prays for Zion, offering a new petition from a new circumstance. He applies the prayer ([69:1-33](Ps.69.1-Ps.69.33)) to the desperate condition of Judah (see [51:18-19](Ps.51.18-Ps.51.19)).
God’s people **will inherit the land** because the wicked will perish (see [37:8-9](Ps.37.8-Ps.37.9)).
This psalm, nearly identical to [40:13-17](Ps.40.13-Ps.40.17), contains an urgency ([70:1](Ps.70.1), [5](Ps.70.5)) that fits with the surrounding psalms (cp. [69:17](Ps.69.17); [71:12](Ps.71.12)).
70:title
**asking God to remember him:** The meaning of this phrase is unknown (also found in [38:title](Ps.38.1)).

This untitled lament by an aging believer is more of a confession of confidence and hope than the cry of someone abandoned by God. The psalmist experienced God’s power and protection in his youth ([71:5-8](Ps.71.5-Ps.71.8)) and now prays for rescue from the adversaries who stalk him in his old age ([71:9-13](Ps.71.9-Ps.71.13)). Even in the midst of his peril, he continues to tell of God’s past faithfulness and looks forward with hope to a time when he can testify to the next generation that God is faithful and righteous.
The poet has learned to acknowledge God as the reliable rock who will do what is right toward him and his oppressors. See also [31:1-3](Ps.31.1-Ps.31.3).
The psalmist has **trusted** God throughout his life (see [22:9](Ps.22.9)).

The aging believer turns to the Lord for hope. As questions from his adversaries get under his skin and his own strength fails, he asks God to answer his prayers. He does not seek answers to prayer for himself but so that he can tell the story to the next generation.
The poet prays for continued fellowship with God (see [9:10](Ps.9.10); [51:11](Ps.51.11)). In his weakness, he needs the Lord’s strength even more (see [143:7](Ps.143.7)).
In their **plotting***,* the psalmist’s enemies take counsel and scheme together ([2:2](Ps.2.2); [21:11](Ps.21.11); [31:13](Ps.31.13); [35:4](Ps.35.4); [63:9-10](Ps.63.9-Ps.63.10)).
The psalmist contrasts his own goodness with his enemies’ evil; he centers his life in the Lord, even during hard times (see [9:17-18](Ps.9.17-Ps.9.18); [27:13-14](Ps.27.13-Ps.27.14)).
God’s righteous character provides encouragement and strength in the midst of suffering. The wounded psalmist confesses faith in God’s ability to transform his misery and weakness into abundant life.
**lift me up from the depths:** The psalmist hopes for the renewal of an abundant earthly **life**. This later became grounds for belief in the resurrection of the dead.

Being assured of God’s **comfort** also assures the poet of God’s presence, care, and goodness ([23:4](Ps.23.4), [6](Ps.23.6); [86:17](Ps.86.17)). God’s comfort enhances the psalmist’s sense of being alive (see [119:50](Ps.119.50)).
As he awaits God’s rescue, the psalmist prepares himself to declare with instruments and voice that God is faithful and righteous.

This royal psalm closes Book Two, with [72:18-20](Ps.72.18-Ps.72.20) functioning as an epilogue to all of Book Two. The psalmist reflects on the prospects of David’s royal line and on Zion (see [Pss 46](Ps.46.1-Ps.46.11), [48](Ps.48.1-Ps.48.14)). He prays that Israel’s kings will be good and prosperous, extending the Lord’s blessing on his people throughout the whole earth. The surpassing righteousness and dominion sought in this prayer foreshadow the coming of Jesus, the Son of David.
The blessings of justice create a balance in nature, resulting in harmony, prosperity, and fertility.
**love of justice . . . righteousness:** Kings in the ancient Near East were expected to represent justice; the standard for Israel’s kings was much higher because the Lord was their model.
The administration of justice transforms the earth into fruitfulness, abundance, harmony, and goodness (see [Isa 32:16-17](Isa.32.16-Isa.32.17)).
A just ruler will **defend the poor** against injustice, **rescue** them from violence, and bring **their oppressors** to account for their wrongdoing.

**May they fear you:** In Hebrew, this clause seems to be a response to the enforcement of justice. The Greek version reads *May they endure,* which makes this a prayer for longevity ([21:4](Ps.21.4); [72:15](Ps.72.15), [17](Ps.72.17)).
The administration of justice is **refreshing like spring rain***,* enabling the **godly** to **flourish** (see [Isa 45:8](Isa.45.8)) like flowers.
**until the moon is no more:** This phrase means forever (see [Ps 89:36-37](Ps.89.36-Ps.89.37)).

The anointed king will rule over the whole world. Even hostile nations will submit to him. In the ancient Near East, bearing gifts to the king acknowledged his success and his reputation (see [1 Kgs 10](1Kgs.10.1-1Kgs.10.29)).
**from sea to sea:** This phrase represents the whole world.

Solomon’s kingdom extended **from the Euphrates River** in the east to the Philistine territory in the west ([1 Kgs 4:21](1Kgs.4.21); see [Pss 80:8-11](Ps.80.8-Ps.80.11); [89:19-25](Ps.89.19-Ps.89.25)), where the Mediterranean Sea appeared to be at **the ends of the earth** (see [2:8](Ps.2.8)). Everyone **will bow before** this king, including the **desert nomads** ([72:9](Ps.72.9)), **his enemies***,* and all the kings of the world (see [Mic 7:17](Mic.7.17)).

**The western kings of Tarshish** came from a major colony in the western basin of the Mediterranean. **The eastern kings of Sheba** came from an area in southern Arabia, home of the queen of Sheba ([1 Kgs 10](1Kgs.10.1-1Kgs.10.29)).
**Seba** was probably located somewhere south of Egypt, perhaps on the western shore of the Red Sea across from Sheba.
The **gifts** offered to the king represented a tribute and a token of submission.

**All kings** and **all nations** must submit to the messianic king. The hope expressed in [2:10-11](Ps.2.10-Ps.2.11) will be realized (see [96:1-3](Ps.96.1-Ps.96.3); [1 Cor 15:25](1Cor.15.25)) when other leaders and peoples **bow before** and **serve** this king.
The anointed king will rescue the needy. He is not only the judge but also a father to the poor ([10:14](Ps.10.14), [17](Ps.10.17); [68:5](Ps.68.5)).
To **rescue the poor** means to bring an end to the rule of their oppressors.
Like a father, the king **feels pity** for those in need (see [Mal 3:17](Mal.3.17)).
The just kingdom will be long-lasting and universal. The summary combines the themes of abundance of crops, longevity, tribute of the nations, and the prayer of the nations.
The **people** will **bless him***,* fulfilling God’s promise to Abraham ([Gen 12:3](Gen.12.3); see [Ps 133:3](Ps.133.3)).
**the trees of Lebanon:** Lebanon was renowned for its lumber (see study note on 2 Chr 2:8).
This doxology concludes Book Two of the Psalter.

This parenthetical note ends Book Two, which consists mostly of **prayers of David**. Books Three to Five were probably compiled after Book Two; they include additional psalms of David ([Pss 86](Ps.86.1-Ps.86.17), [101](Ps.101.1-Ps.101.8), [103](Ps.103.1-Ps.103.22), [108–110](Ps.108.1-Ps.110.7), [122](Ps.122.1-Ps.122.9), [124](Ps.124.1-Ps.124.8), [131](Ps.131.1-Ps.131.3), [133](Ps.133.1-Ps.133.3), [138–145](Ps.138.1-Ps.145.21)).

The apparent prosperity of the wicked ([Ps 73](Ps.73.1-Ps.73.28)) and God’s apparent rejection of his people ([Ps 74](Ps.74.1-Ps.74.23)) raise questions about his justice. God is sovereign over the whole world, and he determines the time for judgment ([Ps 75](Ps.75.1-Ps.75.10)).

This wisdom psalm examines the injustice of the prosperity of the wicked. The psalmist affirms that God is good to the godly but his own experience differs ([73:2-12](Ps.73.2-Ps.73.12)). Nearly overcome by his doubts ([73:13-16](Ps.73.13-Ps.73.16)), the psalmist meets the Lord in the sanctuary and gains a perspective that stretches beyond his life and renews his confidence in God ([73:17-26](Ps.73.17-Ps.73.26)). His disturbing doubts stir a greater passion for truth. He knows that he can trust God and that God will rescue him ([73:27-28](Ps.73.27-Ps.73.28)).
73:title

**Asaph** was a Levitical singer appointed by David ([1 Chr 6:39](1Chr.6.39)); his descendants were singers and instrumentalists ([1 Chr 15:16-17](1Chr.15.16-1Chr.15.17)). Many of the psalms of Asaph ([Pss 50](Ps.50.1-Ps.50.23), [73–83](Ps.73.1-Ps.83.18)) were probably written by Asaph’s descendants at a later time in Israel’s history (e.g., [Ps 74](Ps.74.1-Ps.74.23)).

People **whose hearts are pure** are renewed by God’s Spirit ([51:10](Ps.51.10)), commit themselves to lives of godliness, keep away from anything that is sinful, and enjoy God’s presence (see [24:3-4](Ps.24.3-Ps.24.4)).
The poet sees the prosperity of the wicked as unfair (see [72:7](Ps.72.7)) and resents it.

The psalmist’s **feet were slipping** from the way of wisdom and godliness (see [17:5](Ps.17.5); [37:31](Ps.37.31)), but God kept him from falling off the trail entirely ([38:16](Ps.38.16); [66:9](Ps.66.9); [94:18](Ps.94.18); [121:3](Ps.121.3)).
**when I saw them prosper:** Cp. [72:3](Ps.72.3), [7](Ps.72.7).
The psalmist presents a caricature of the bliss of the wicked (cp. [Ps 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6)).
The proud adorn themselves with **pride** and **cruelty** rather than wisdom ([Prov 1:9](Prov.1.9)).
The proud **boast**, claiming that they own everything and are not subject to anyone (see [2:1-3](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.3)).
Recognizing the ramifications of his discouragement and doubt, the psalmist turns to the Lord and receives special insight.
These rhetorical questions expect a discouraging “yes” for an answer. The psalmist wonders if godliness has become a meaningless ritual (see [Mal 3:14-15](Mal.3.14-Mal.3.15)).
**My heart** refers to his whole being.
The psalmist’s **pain** comes from discipline and rebuke ([Ps 39:11](Ps.39.11); [Prov 1:23](Prov.1.23), [25](Prov.1.25); [12:1](Prov.12.1)).

If the psalmist had verbalized his suspicions about the futility of godly living, he would have discouraged God’s people and given God’s enemies an opportunity to blaspheme (cp. [John 13:20](John.13.20)). Instead, the psalmist internalizes the problem and reflects on it.
At this time, God’s **sanctuary** was the Temple in Jerusalem. There, in God’s presence, the psalmist receives special insight (cp. [18:6](Ps.18.6)).

God deals with the **wicked** over the long term. He waits patiently and gives them time to repent ([Ezek 33:11](Ezek.33.11); [2 Pet 3:9](2Pet.3.9)); those who do not repent will get what they deserve.
The psalmist’s feelings about the prosperity of the wicked had given him a **bitter** spirit.
The Lord leads the godly through their troubles and changes their misery into splendor.
Nothing **in heaven** or **on earth** is better than being near God.
The psalmist laments the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem (586 BC) with vivid imagery, questions, fresh memories, and a direct appeal for the Lord to act ([74:19-23](Ps.74.19-Ps.74.23)).
In the aftermath of Jerusalem’s fall, it seemed that God had forgotten his special covenant relationship with his people.
God **rejected** his people because their sin aroused his anger ([106:34-46](Ps.106.34-Ps.106.46)).
Like a tender shepherd, God cares for his people, **the sheep of** his **pasture** ([Pss 23](Ps.23.1-Ps.23.6); [100:3](Ps.100.3)).
The Lord **chose** and **redeemed** Israel from Egypt in the Exodus (cp. [Exod 15:13](Exod.15.13)).
**your own special possession:** This is another expression for “your people” ([Pss 28:9](Ps.28.9); [78:62](Ps.78.62); [94:14](Ps.94.14); [106:40](Ps.106.40)).
Like a guide, the psalmist points out to the Lord what took place during the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC.
**my king from ages past:** The psalmist acknowledges God’s power and his historical bond with Israel ([5:2](Ps.5.2); [44:4](Ps.44.4); [84:3](Ps.84.3)).

**Leviathan:** See [104:26](Ps.104.26); [Job 3:8](Job.3.8); [41:1](Job.41.1), [12](Job.41.12), [22](Job.41.22), [31](Job.41.31); [Isa 27:1](Isa.27.1). Here, the creature’s multiple **heads** suggest a mythical monster.

**springs and streams to gush forth:** God provided water in the desert for his people (see [68:8-9](Ps.68.8-Ps.68.9); [Exod 17:6](Exod.17.6)); he **dried up** the Red Sea ([Exod 14:21](Exod.14.21)) and the Jordan River ([Josh 3:17](Josh.3.17)).
The poet urges God to act.

This hymn of thanksgiving includes two direct messages from God that provide assurance of his justice ([75:2-3](Ps.75.2-Ps.75.3), [10](Ps.75.10)). The Lord rebukes arrogant people who defy him, promising to forcibly humble them ([75:4-8](Ps.75.4-Ps.75.8)). Together, the community and the psalmist respond with thanksgiving for God’s character ([75:1](Ps.75.1), [9](Ps.75.9)).
The Lord will bring justice in his own time.
**The wicked** arrogantly defy **the heavens**—the dwelling place of God. Through their **boasting** they insist that they are wiser than God.
No creature has the right to rebel against its Creator.
The Lord alone is the Judge, with the power to exalt and humble (see [1 Sam 2:7](1Sam.2.7); [Luke 1:52](Luke.1.52)).

This psalm appears to celebrate a victory. The victory might have been recent, such as over the Assyrians (see note on [76:title](Ps.76.1); see also [Isa 37](Isa.37.1-Isa.37.38)); or the psalm might be recalling God’s great acts of rescue in the past.
God’s victory over Zion’s enemies foreshadows his worldwide victory over all his enemies.
76:title
**to be accompanied by stringed instruments:** The Greek version reads *for the Assyrian.*
God brings an end to the attacks of his enemies (see [46:9](Ps.46.9)).
The psalmist praises God for his achievement and for his **glorious** majesty.
The victorious king’s splendor, glory, and majesty are greater than anything in the created order ([8:1](Ps.8.1); [29:4](Ps.29.4); [111:3](Ps.111.3)).
The needy await their victorious God, while the wicked stand in fear of him.
The word translated **feared** (Hebrew *nora’*) is a wordplay on the word translated “glorious” in [76:4](Ps.76.4) (Hebrew *na’or*).

The psalmist laments that God has turned away from him, even though he feels innocent. He reflects on his situation ([77:3](Ps.77.3), [6](Ps.77.6), [12](Ps.77.12)) and finds hope (see [25:5](Ps.25.5)) in remembering God’s past deeds ([77:11](Ps.77.11)).
**I think of God:** God’s people inevitably face difficult times, but recalling his mighty acts at the beginning of their relationship assures them of God’s commitment.
Feeling **overwhelmed***,* the psalmist is unable to deal with the crisis ([142:3](Ps.142.3); [143:4](Ps.143.4)).
As the psalmist meditates at night, he feels so disturbed that he cannot sleep or speak. He has pleasant memories of the past, but he cannot look beyond the present moment into the future.
The psalmist questions his status before God.
Feeling **rejected** (see [43:2](Ps.43.2)), the psalmist asks if the situation is permanent.
The memories of God’s mighty works in the past fill the psalmist’s mind.

The psalmist fears that God’s **hand** of protection ([44:3](Ps.44.3); [77:15](Ps.77.15); [Exod 6:6](Exod.6.6)) and favor ([Pss 16:7-8](Ps.16.7-Ps.16.8); [110:1](Ps.110.1)) is now **against** him for no apparent reason.
This central section of the poem reflects on God as the holy and powerful redeemer.
**the Red Sea:** The Canaanites attributed divine power to the sea, but God is the one who made the sea and uses it for his own purposes.
This wisdom psalm exhorts the people to learn wisdom and faithfully pass it on.
The prologue is an invitation to learn wisdom.
The psalmist recites Israel’s story ([78:5-72](Ps.78.5-Ps.78.72)) **in a parable** in order to teach wisdom and insight.
Jesus quoted this verse to explain why he taught in parables ([Matt 13:35](Matt.13.35)).
This story of what God has done should be told from generation to generation (see [Deut 6:20-25](Deut.6.20-Deut.6.25); [Prov 4:1-4](Prov.4.1-Prov.4.4)).
The telling of the story should motivate God’s people to obey what he **commanded** ([Deut 6:4-9](Deut.6.4-Deut.6.9)).

God holds **each generation** responsible for its own response, which should be to maintain faith and **hope** (see [9:18](Ps.9.18); [27:14](Ps.27.14)) and avoid being **stubborn, rebellious, and unfaithful** (see [Deut 9:6-7](Deut.9.6-Deut.9.7); [10:16](Deut.10.16); [30:6](Deut.30.6); [31:27](Deut.31.27)).

**Ephraim***,* the second son of Joseph, received a special blessing from Jacob ([Gen 48:15-20](Gen.48.15-Gen.48.20); [49:22-26](Gen.49.22-Gen.49.26); [Deut 33:13-17](Deut.33.13-Deut.33.17)). The land that his descendants received included fertile valleys and strategic roads ([Judg 8:2](Judg.8.2)). However, the people of Ephraim did not live in obedience to God’s gracious covenant.
The focus shifts from Ephraim ([78:9-11](Ps.78.9-Ps.78.11)) to Israel as a whole as the psalmist reflects on God’s power in Egypt (see [81:4-7](Ps.81.4-Ps.81.7)) and in the wilderness.
**The miracles** are the ten plagues against Egypt that God performed during Israel’s captivity ([Exod 7–12](Exod.7.1-Exod.12.51)).
God **divided the sea** when Israel crossed through the Red Sea (see [Exod 14–15](Exod.14.1-Exod.15.27)).
God used a **cloud** and a **pillar of fire** to guide and protect Israel in the wilderness ([Exod 13:21-22](Exod.13.21-Exod.13.22)).
Israel rebelled in the wilderness despite God’s abundant provision.
Abundance comes through **the doors of heaven** ([Gen 8:2](Gen.8.2); [2 Kgs 7:2](2Kgs.7.2); [Mal 3:10](Mal.3.10)).
Israel ate **manna** for forty years in the wilderness ([Exod 16:31-36](Exod.16.31-Exod.16.36); [John 6:31](John.6.31)).
God powerfully satisfied the people’s desires, but they did not respond with gratitude or faith. Therefore, God exercised his justice.
Israel’s rebellion resulted in God’s judgment, but even their short-lived and insincere repentance motivated God to exercise forbearance.
An entire generation died in the wilderness ([Num 14:22-23](Num.14.22-Num.14.23), [28-35](Num.14.28-Num.14.35)).
Israel’s continued existence, in spite of the people’s rebellion and unbelief ([78:7-8](Ps.78.7-Ps.78.8)), was due to God’s compassion.
**They repented:** This demonstration of zeal was not sincere.
The Israelites **remembered** the right doctrine ([9:9](Ps.9.9); [91:1](Ps.91.1)), but they did not allow God to change their **hearts** ([Lev 26:41](Lev.26.41)).
The Israelites **rebelled** even though the Lord had rescued them from powerful plagues.

Israel’s rebellion desecrated the Promised Land. The people built **shrines** to false gods and worshiped **idols** ([78:58](Ps.78.58)) during the period of the judges (e.g., [Judg 2:11](Judg.2.11); [3:7](Judg.3.7), [17-18](Judg.3.17-Judg.3.18)).
God **abandoned his dwelling at Shiloh** because of the people’s idol worship ([1 Sam 4:11](1Sam.4.11); [Jer 7:12](Jer.7.12)).
**The tribe of Ephraim** was not completely **rejected***,* but God favored Judah ([78:68](Ps.78.68)).
In the choice of **Mount Zion** instead of Shiloh as God’s **sanctuary** on earth, God moved from the north to the south (see [Ps 69](Ps.69.1-Ps.69.36)).

The God who had turned against his **own people** ([78:62](Ps.78.62)) chose **David***,* a shepherd ([Gen 46:34](Gen.46.34); [1 Sam 16:10-11](1Sam.16.10-1Sam.16.11)), to become their **shepherd** ([Ps 78:52](Ps.78.52); cp. [23:1](Ps.23.1)).

This lament describes the occasion of Jerusalem’s fall in 586 BC. The early history of Israel’s rebellions described in [Ps 78](Ps.78.1-Ps.78.72) provoked God’s wrath, resulting in the desolation of Zion described here as the defilement of the Temple and the disgraced bodies that littered the landscape. The psalmist then prays for forgiveness and rescue ([79:8-9](Ps.79.8-Ps.79.9)), as well as for God to pay back the nation’s enemies ([79:12-13](Ps.79.12-Ps.79.13)). Other psalms lamenting the Exile include [Pss 42–44](Ps.42.1-Ps.44.26), [102](Ps.102.1-Ps.102.28), [107](Ps.107.1-Ps.107.43), [126](Ps.126.1-Ps.126.6), [137](Ps.137.1-Ps.137.9).
The poet laments the desecration of the Temple and the success of the enemy.
**your special possession:** This phrase might refer to the **land**, the **Temple** (see [61:5](Ps.61.5)), or the people (see [79:2](Ps.79.2); [78:71](Ps.78.71)).

The intensity of God’s judgment surprises the people; they cry out in despair for compassion, forgiveness, and relief. Verses [6-7](Ps.6.1-Ps.7.17) are repeated almost verbatim in [Jer 10:25](Jer.10.25).
The repentant among God’s people ask him to vent his anger not on them but on their wicked and unrepentant enemies.

The people’s accumulation of past **sins** contributed to the Exile ([2 Kgs 17:7-23](2Kgs.17.7-2Kgs.17.23); [24:3-4](2Kgs.24.3-2Kgs.24.4)); however, the people perished because of their own sins ([Jer 31:30](Jer.31.30); [Ezek 18:20](Ezek.18.20)).
The people ask God to rescue them. Although Israel’s sins caused the tragedy, the **pagan nations** must also be held responsible for the bloodshed.
The Exile resulted in national suffering and in individual searching for the Lord.
The expression **seven times** signifies something complete.
Israel’s **neighbors** included Edom, Moab, and Ammon (see [Ps 137:7](Ps.137.7); [2 Kgs 24:2](2Kgs.24.2); [Obad 1](Obad.1.1-Obad.1.21)).

This psalm of lament might originate with the remnant of the northern kingdom after its fall in 722 BC. The people call on God as their Shepherd and as the God of Heaven’s Armies in the hope that he will return to them and restore them. They remember the Exodus and their special relationship with the Lord and conclude with an expression of renewed commitment to him ([80:18](Ps.80.18)).
The psalmist urgently calls upon the Lord to act.
**radiant glory . . . power:** These expressions ([145:11](Ps.145.11)) refer to God’s manifest presence.
80:title
**The tune “Lilies of the Covenant”** is unknown today.
This verse is repeated (with an increasing crescendo) in [80:7](Ps.80.7), [19](Ps.80.19).
The people cry out for rescue from the shame of their recent defeat. The enemy’s victory is less devastating, however, than the knowledge that they themselves are objects of God’s wrath.
Israel has a glorious past, beginning with its redemption from Egypt.

Israel had been a prosperous **grapevine** ([Gen 1:28](Gen.1.28); [Gal 5:22-23](Gal.5.22-Gal.5.23)) that God **transplanted** into the land of Canaan at the time of the conquest. However, the people forgot the source of their prosperity and chose to do evil ([Isa 5:1-7](Isa.5.1-Isa.5.7); [Hos 10:1](Hos.10.1)).
Solomon’s kingdom had extended **west to the Mediterranean Sea** and **east to the Euphrates River** (see [72:8-9](Ps.72.8-Ps.72.9); [89:25](Ps.89.25); [1 Kgs 4:21](1Kgs.4.21)).
**broken down our walls:** God no longer defended Israel ([Isa 5:5](Isa.5.5)).
The surrounding nations were ceremonially unclean, like a **wild boar** or vicious **wild animals**.
Israel was the **son** that God had brought out of Egypt (see [Hos 11:1](Hos.11.1)) and **planted** in the Holy Land.
The community prays for God to change their desperate situation and restore them. They are still the Lord’s chosen people.
The **son of your choice** was probably the northern kingdom of Israel, although it might allude to the king of David’s dynasty ([110:1](Ps.110.1)).
This warning message invites Israel to worship only the Lord and to enjoy the fullness of his blessing.
As a prelude to the message of warning, the psalmist invites Israel to contemplate their God in song and dance.

An Israelite **tambourine** was a hand drum—a round frame covered with a skin, used as a percussion instrument during festivities, often to accompany dancing ([68:25](Ps.68.25); [149:3](Ps.149.3); [150:4](Ps.150.4)).

The **sweet lyre** and **the harp***,* both stringed instruments, are the instruments most frequently mentioned in the psalms (e.g., [33:2](Ps.33.2); [57:8](Ps.57.8); [71:22](Ps.71.22); [150:3](Ps.150.3)).
The **ram’s horn** mustered armies and announced special holy days ([47:5](Ps.47.5); [98:6](Ps.98.6)).
**new moon:** The first day of the lunar month marked **a festival**.
The festival, a time to celebrate and listen to the Lord, took place at God’s appointed time.
**for Israel:** Literally *for Joseph.* The tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh (the sons of Joseph) are used here to refer to the entire nation of Israel.
The Lord heard Israel’s cry in Egypt and rescued them from oppressive slavery.
God pleads with his people to remember the covenant and the Ten Commandments.
God emphasizes that he and no one else **rescued** Israel.
The nation should **open** its **mouth wide** to take in God’s word (cp. [Deut 8:3](Deut.8.3); [Ezek 3:1](Ezek.3.1)).
The Lord helps Israel to understand that their failure was not because of his weakness.
God wants to give his children his goodness, but only if they **listen** ([Isa 1:18-19](Isa.1.18-Isa.1.19); [28:12](Isa.28.12); [48:18-19](Isa.48.18-Isa.48.19); see [Deut 6:3](Deut.6.3)).
God promises to **subdue** the **enemies** ([Deut 9:3](Deut.9.3)) of those who walk the **paths** of obedience and loyalty. He will also richly feed his people ([Isa 1:19](Isa.1.19)).
God condemns those who mistreat the helpless.
**God presides** and stands ready to render **judgment** (see [Isa 3:13](Isa.3.13)).
**heaven’s court:** See [Job 1:6](Job.1.6).
Since justice marks God’s reign ([89:4](Ps.89.4)), he opposes **favoring the wicked**. So the psalmist is perplexed and cries out to God for justice ([82:3-4](Ps.82.3-Ps.82.4), [8](Ps.82.8)).
The unjust **oppressors** cannot bring or restore order. **They wander about in darkness***,* unmoved by circumstances even when the whole world order falls apart around them (cp. [11:3](Ps.11.3)).
The **gods** (see study notes on 29:1-2; 58:1), **like mere mortals***,* cannot escape the judgment common to human rulers. Jesus quoted from this passage in [John 10:34](John.10.34).
The **nations belong to** God; he will take over the realms formerly ruled by local deities and give them to his people, just as he did with the Promised Land.

This community lament asks God for rescue and victory. The terse poetry suggests difficult times. A powerful coalition desires to destroy Israel ([83:1-4](Ps.83.1-Ps.83.4)) and allies itself against God ([83:5-8](Ps.83.5-Ps.83.8)). Recalling the fate of others who came against Israel ([83:9-12](Ps.83.9-Ps.83.12)), the psalmist prays that the same will happen to these enemies ([83:13-16](Ps.83.13-Ps.83.16)) so that God will receive honor among them ([83:17-18](Ps.83.17-Ps.83.18)). It is unclear whether this psalm arose out of a specific historical instance of opposition by these nations, or if it is a poetic collage of nations representing Israel’s enemies.
The enemy has successfully intimidated God’s people, so the poet prays that the Lord will hear and act.
**signed a treaty:** The **allies** agreed to fight against God and his people. The nations that are named in the alliance were situated around Israel and Judah.
The **Edomites***,* descendants of Esau, were located to the southeast of Judah (see [Gen 25:30](Gen.25.30); [32:3](Gen.32.3); [36:1-8](Gen.36.1-Gen.36.8)).
**Ishmaelites** were desert-dwelling descendants of Hagar.
**Moabites** and **Ammonites** descended from Lot; both were located to the east of Israel and Judah.
The **Hagrites** were possibly located north of the Ammonites ([1 Chr 5:10](1Chr.5.10)).
The **Gebalites** probably came from Gebal/Byblos on the coast of Lebanon.
The **Amalekites** were located south of Israel in the Negev.
**Philistia** was southwest of Judah, by the Mediterranean Sea.
**Tyre** was a port city on the Mediterranean, northwest of Israel.
**Assyria** was northeast of Israel and north of the Persian Gulf.
The **descendants of Lot** were the Moabites and the Ammonites ([83:6-7](Ps.83.6-Ps.83.7)).
The psalmist prays that God will miraculously destroy the new coalition as he did three other enemies; doing so would bring him glory.

The **Midianites***,* ruled by **Zebah** and **Zalmunna** and led by **Oreb and Zeeb***,* were Israel’s enemy in the days of Gideon ([Judg 7:1–8:5](Judg.7.1-Judg.8.5)). Barak’s coalition defeated **Sisera and Jabin** ([Judg 4](Judg.4.1-Judg.4.24)).
The coalition’s motivation for wiping out Israel was to acquire the land (see [Jer 3:19](Jer.3.19)).
**tumbleweed . . . chaff:** This dry plant material easily blows away (see [Isa 17:13](Isa.17.13)).
**fire . . . fierce storm . . . tempest:** These are images of God’s manifestation in judgment (see [Isa 29:6](Isa.29.6)).

The psalmist expresses his deep spiritual longing for God’s presence. He faints with longing as he reflects on the Temple and on pilgrims making the journey to Jerusalem ([84:1-7](Ps.84.1-Ps.84.7)). He prays for himself and for the community ([84:8-9](Ps.84.8-Ps.84.9)). The conclusion of the psalm ([84:10-12](Ps.84.10-Ps.84.12)) clarifies that the Temple represents God—the psalmist truly longs for God’s presence. He knows that God’s goodness is greater than life and that only God can give his people favor and honor ([84:10-11](Ps.84.10-Ps.84.11)).
The psalmist is far from the Temple. He turns toward it in hopeful reflection.
The poet envies the birds that have nesting places in and around the Temple.
The priests and Temple personnel lived in the Temple.

The pilgrimage to Jerusalem reenacted the Exodus, when God marvelously provided for his people (see [78:15-16](Ps.78.15-Ps.78.16); [105:41](Ps.105.41)). The psalmist imagines the pains of travel turning to the joy of arrival.
Travelers needed **strength** to meet the challenges of **pilgrimage** by foot along unpaved paths, in all kinds of weather and with the possibility of assaults.
The **Valley of Weeping** probably refers to the anguish that lonely pilgrims endured (see [23:4](Ps.23.4)), rather than to an actual location.

**refreshing springs . . . autumn rains:** Even when pilgrims feel totally exhausted, the prospect of drawing near to the Lord renews their spirits (cp. [Isa 35:6-10](Isa.35.6-Isa.35.10); [41:18-20](Isa.41.18-Isa.41.20); [43:17-20](Isa.43.17-Isa.43.20); [49:10](Isa.49.10)).

Both kings and priests were **anointed** to dedicate them for service (see [132:17](Ps.132.17); [Exod 28:41](Exod.28.41); [1 Sam 9:16](1Sam.9.16); [16:1-13](1Sam.16.1-1Sam.16.13); cp. [Isa 61:1](Isa.61.1); [Acts 10:38](Acts.10.38)).
The psalmist viewed being in God’s presence as much **better than** being **anywhere else**.
Some people worshiped the **sun** as a god, but the true God provides all that anyone needs.

The psalmist leads the postexilic community in lament and prayer for full redemption. He ponders God’s past rescue of Israel from exile ([85:1-3](Ps.85.1-Ps.85.3)), longs for greater evidence of God’s goodness, and leads the community in prayer for full restoration ([85:4-7](Ps.85.4-Ps.85.7)). God responds with a message of peace ([85:8-9](Ps.85.8-Ps.85.9)), and the psalm concludes with a lyrical outburst at the grandeur of God’s salvation ([85:10-13](Ps.85.10-Ps.85.13)).
Though the psalmist gratefully acknowledges God’s goodness, he also asks God whether his wrath will last forever.
God **restored the fortunes** of Israel by bringing the nation back from exile (see [14:7](Ps.14.7); [126:1](Ps.126.1)).
When God **forgave the guilt** of **their sins***,* he gave the people the possibility of fellowship with him (see [32:5](Ps.32.5)).
This prayer for renewal is based on God’s **unfailing love** for his people.

When **God the** **LORD** speaks, **his faithful people** listen. He promises them **peace***,* meaning wholeness and well-being (see [37:11](Ps.37.11)). They fear the Lord and know that he and **his salvation** are **near** to them.
The Lord does not tolerate **foolish ways***,* such as those that resulted in the Exile.

In the glorious world of renewal and salvation, all the qualities of God’s care—**love***,* **truth***,* **righteousness***,* and **peace**—come together and transform the created order into something new (see [Isa 32:15-20](Isa.32.15-Isa.32.20)).
**Righteousness** is like a messenger preparing the world for God’s coming in response to the prayers of his people ([85:4-7](Ps.85.4-Ps.85.7); [89:14](Ps.89.14)).

The psalmist invokes God’s help and praises his character in a lament prompted by the presence of evil ([86:14](Ps.86.14), [17](Ps.86.17)). All people will worship the gracious and almighty God ([86:8-10](Ps.86.8-Ps.86.10)). To this end, the poet commits himself to a lifestyle of ethical integrity ([86:11](Ps.86.11)) and praising the Lord ([86:12-13](Ps.86.12-Ps.86.13)). The last stanza contrasts the qualities of evil people with those of the Lord ([86:14-17](Ps.86.14-Ps.86.17)).
God’s devoted servant prays for mercy. The psalmist sees himself as a member of the covenant community and as a citizen of the world.
86:title
This is the only psalm connected with **David** in Book Three.
The psalmist appeals to God to remain true to his character, which is the basis for hope.

The psalmist recounts the catalog of divine perfections ([Exod 34:6-7](Exod.34.6-Exod.34.7)), especially God’s willingness to forgive sin (see [Pss 32:5](Ps.32.5); [85:2](Ps.85.2); [145:7-10](Ps.145.7-Ps.145.10)).
**All the nations** must submit themselves to the Lord and worship him ([45:17](Ps.45.17); [117:1](Ps.117.1); [148:7-11](Ps.148.7-Ps.148.11)).
The poet responds to the Lord by seeking faithful instruction in the **truth**.
An individual with **purity of heart** has integrity and wholeness (see [73:1](Ps.73.1)).
In anticipation of God’s rescue, the psalmist praises him and trusts in his goodness.
The arrogant exist both inside and outside the community. The psalmist asks for a vision of God’s character; God is so great that just a glimpse of his goodness will shut the mouths of the wicked.

God has **mercy** on his people ([51:1](Ps.51.1)); he is gracious ([25:6](Ps.25.6)), **slow to get angry** ([103:8](Ps.103.8); [145:8](Ps.145.8)), and **filled with unfailing love and faithfulness** (Hebrew *khesed* and *’emeth*; [143:1](Ps.143.1)). This verse repeats a theme first expressed in [Exod 34:7](Exod.34.7); [Num 14:18](Num.14.18) (cp. [Pss 103:8](Ps.103.8); [145:8](Ps.145.8); [Neh 9:17](Neh.9.17); [Joel 2:13](Joel.2.13); [Jon 4:2](Jonah.4.2)).
This psalm envisions Jerusalem as the city of God where all the nations are citizens.
Jerusalem was Israel’s capital and the location of the Temple, God’s earthly palace (see [Ps 84](Ps.84.1-Ps.84.12)).
As great as Zion is, it will be even greater when it becomes an international city where believers from all the nations have citizenship.
God keeps a record of all who confess him as their Lord ([Dan 7:10](Dan.7.10); [Rev 13:8](Rev.13.8)).
**Jerusalem** becomes the international city where all God’s children are **citizens**.

In this lament, the psalmist sees himself as cast out from God’s presence. At first, he calls on the Lord. When he finds no relief from his suffering, he presents three charges against God ([88:6-7](Ps.88.6-Ps.88.7), [8-12](Ps.88.8-Ps.88.12), [13-17](Ps.88.13-Ps.88.17)).
The psalmist calls on the **LORD** for **salvation**.
88:title

**Heman the Ezrahite** might be a sage from Solomon’s time ([1 Kgs 4:31](1Kgs.4.31)), a descendant of Judah ([1 Chr 2:6](1Chr.2.6)), or a member of the Levitical family charged with singing at the Temple ([1 Chr 15:17](1Chr.15.17); [2 Chr 5:12](2Chr.5.12)).
In his first charge, the psalmist blames the Lord for his demise. God’s overpowering anger did not make sense.
The phrase **the darkest depths** implies the place of the dead ([143:3](Ps.143.3); see [Lam 3:6](Lam.3.6)) or the depths of the sea ([Pss 68:22](Ps.68.22); [69:1-2](Ps.69.1-Ps.69.2)).

In his second charge, the psalmist claims that God has isolated him and caused his loneliness (cp. [31:11](Ps.31.11); [38:11](Ps.38.11)). Loneliness was a curse in a culture where relationships were more important than personal achievement.
In his third charge, the psalmist accuses the Lord of rejecting him. The force and apparent cruelty of the psalmist’s suffering overwhelm him.
The psalmist restates his second and first charges.

Book Three ([Pss 73–89](Ps.73.1-Ps.89.52)) begins and ends with weighty questions. Though [Ps 89](Ps.89.1-Ps.89.52) begins with a praise-filled account of how the Lord exalted the throne of David ([89:1-37](Ps.89.1-Ps.89.37)), the psalmist protests the Lord’s apparent rejection of his covenant with David ([89:38-51](Ps.89.38-Ps.89.51); see [2 Sam 7:8-16](2Sam.7.8-2Sam.7.16)).
89:title
**Ethan the Ezrahite** was a wise man ([1 Kgs 4:31](1Kgs.4.31); cp. [Ps 88:title](Ps.88.1)).
God’s **unfailing love** gives reason to celebrate **forever**.
The psalmist restates God’s covenant with David (see also [89:19-37](Ps.89.19-Ps.89.37)).
The Lord has **sworn** by his own holiness ([89:35](Ps.89.35); see [110:4](Ps.110.4)).
God is the absolute standard of **faithfulness**, commitment, and order. The angelic beings and the heavens testify to his constancy.
Praise for God’s greatness (see [8:1](Ps.8.1)) comes from the inhabitants of **heaven** who witness his **faithfulness**.
**mightiest angel:** Literally *son of God* (see study note on 29:1-2).
In this hymn, the psalmist celebrates God’s comprehensive and powerful sovereignty over nature.
The Lord rules over all parts of the created order, including evil.
**You scattered your enemies:** The Lord will crush ([Luke 1:51](Luke.1.51)) evil powers that oppose him ([Ps 2:1-3](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.3)).
**with your mighty arm:** This phrase represents God’s strength ([89:13](Ps.89.13)).
**Mount Tabor** was in northern Israel. **Mount Hermon** formed the extreme northern border of the nation.
God rules wisely over creation. The qualities of **righteousness, justice,** and faithfulness fit the profile of a wise ruler. The **happy** people who live under his rule enjoy his **protection.**
Those who are wise **worship** God, **walk** in his **light***,* **rejoice** in their relationship with him, and **exult in** his character.
The Lord protects his people with the same power by which he established the created order.
The Lord chose David as his son and as king of Israel (see [2:4-6](Ps.2.4-Ps.2.6); [2 Sam 7:8-16](2Sam.7.8-2Sam.7.16)) to provide protection for his people.
**I have anointed him:** This is the verb from which *anointed one* (Hebrew *mashiakh*, “messiah”) is derived.

The Lord adopted David as his **son,** appointed him as his commander over the nations, and promised to support him **forever.** Verse 26 recalls a verse from David’s song of praise ([2 Sam 22:47](2Sam.22.47)).
David would be the most eminent of earthly kings. The Hebrew word translated **mightiest** is the same as the designation for God as “Most High” (*‘elyon*).
The Lord writes his faithfulness in **heaven***,* on the canvas of his universe (see [89:2](Ps.89.2)). He records his commitment to the dynasty of David in the same way.

The Lord disciplines but does not reject his erring children. He foresees violation of trust and subsequent punishment, but he commits himself to uphold the covenant. His fidelity to David corresponds to his faithfulness to the created order.

**holiness:** The Lord is wholly distinct from the created order ([22:3](Ps.22.3)); his character is totally pure. He does as he pleases ([115:3](Ps.115.3)), and he chooses to be faithful ([89:1](Ps.89.1); [115:1](Ps.115.1)); therefore, he **cannot lie.**
**You are angry:** The harshness of God’s wrath perplexes the psalmist.
**broken down the walls:** The Lord’s people are completely vulnerable.
Although the Lord promised to strengthen David, he secretly **strengthened** David’s **enemies**.
The psalmist wonders if he will live to see the end of the Lord’s **anger**. Our lifetimes are **short***,* like a day in the Lord’s sight ([90:4](Ps.90.4), [10](Ps.90.10)).
The phrase **your servants** refers to the community loyal to the Lord.

This doxology concludes all of Book Three ([Pss 73–89](Ps.73.1-Ps.89.52)); it is not intended to be read as part of [Ps 89](Ps.89.1-Ps.89.52). It stands in stark contrast to the anguish and questioning of [Ps 89](Ps.89.1-Ps.89.52). Cp. [41:13](Ps.41.13); [106:48](Ps.106.48).

Although the Lord’s people have made their home in him for generations, their sin widens the gap between them and their infinite Lord. The Lord’s wrath against a person’s sin might last a lifetime and yet be only a taste of his displeasure with sin. This lamentable situation calls the community to seek the Lord’s light. Taking the first step means seeking restoration with the Lord on the basis of his compassion and love ([90:13-14](Ps.90.13-Ps.90.14)). He alone makes his servants glad and blesses their future generations ([90:16-17](Ps.90.16-Ps.90.17)).

The Lord becomes the **home** of the godly; he has provided shelter for countless **generations.** The word translated *home* is not used frequently in the Psalter. It describes a place of safety where the Lord meets his needy people and cares for them ([68:5](Ps.68.5); [71:3](Ps.71.3)).
90:title
**Moses** led God’s people from slavery in Egypt to Mount Sinai, where he received the law and established God’s covenant with Israel.
**the man of God:** Moses enjoyed a special relationship with God ([Deut 33:1](Deut.33.1)).
The Lord is the eternal God.
The Lord **gave birth to the earth** by creating it.
Unlike God, humans are mortal and transitory.
Sinners cannot escape God’s wrath because the Lord sees their **sins.** Their fleeting **lives** are filled with afflictions.
A **groan** of sorrow ([Ezek 2:10](Ezek.2.10)) sums up a life spent in facing the consequences of sin.
Humans cause **trouble** (see [Ps 10:6](Ps.10.6)) and receive **pain** in return.

In the search for wisdom, no one **can comprehend** the Lord (see [Isa 40:13](Isa.40.13)). The appropriate human response to the Lord is godly **fear** (see [Ps 60:4](Ps.60.4)). The Lord alone can **teach** humans to follow the path of **wisdom** ([25:4-6](Ps.25.4-Ps.25.6)).
The psalmist prays for the Lord’s favor and restoration.
The phrase **your servants** refers to the community of those loyal to the Lord.
The psalmist calls upon the Lord to **give** the people **gladness** to replace their mourning (see [92:4-5](Ps.92.4-Ps.92.5)).
The **children** represent future generations in contrast to the generations past ([90:1](Ps.90.1)).
Humans waste their **efforts** unless the Lord makes them **successful** ([44:3](Ps.44.3)).

This wisdom psalm expresses confidence in the Almighty God, who provides a shelter for those who take refuge in him. They receive redemption, life, and glory from the Lord, who loves and cares for those who seek him.
The Lord is an ancient **shelter** (see [90:1](Ps.90.1)), open to those who seek **refuge** in him.
The **Most High** is an ancient title that expresses the Lord’s exalted status as the ruler and protector of the godly (see [Gen 14:19](Gen.14.19)).
The psalmist invites the godly to trust in the Lord and find protection in him.
God protects the godly from **deadly disease** and even a destructive word.
The **armor** might refer to a body shield, while **protection** refers to a small shield worn on the arm.
The godly should **not be afraid***,* because the Lord watches over them. These promises do not guarantee an escape from trouble, but they create an expectation of the Lord’s goodness.
The reference to **disease** represents any kind of affliction.
The poet again invites the godly to seek refuge in the Lord and enjoy the benefits of divine protection.

**he will order his angels:** Satan cited these words when he tempted Jesus ([Matt 4:6](Matt.4.6); [Luke 4:10-11](Luke.4.10-Luke.4.11)), but God makes this promise for those who obey him ([Ps 91:14](Ps.91.14)), not for those who arrogantly test him ([Matt 4:4](Matt.4.4), [7](Matt.4.7)).
The godly can trust the Lord’s protection and provision.
Those who **love** the Lord will obey him ([Deut 30:20](Deut.30.20); [1 Jn 5:3](1John.5.3)) and seek his protection ([Pss 91:1](Ps.91.1); [145:18](Ps.145.18)).
The Lord promises to **answer** the prayers of his people.

The Psalter often speaks of people honoring the Lord ([50:15](Ps.50.15)); here, God promises to **honor** the godly who risk everything for his sake ([62:7](Ps.62.7); [71:21](Ps.71.21); [84:11](Ps.84.11)).
A **long life** on earth represents just a small part of the Lord’s goodness and eternal friendship ([23:6](Ps.23.6)).

Thanksgiving and praise open this psalm. The Lord—the Most High—is faithful and just in discerning between the godly and the wicked. The godly will enjoy a glorious, vigorous future, while the wicked will perish. The wise see and understand the Lord’s works as they reveal his justice ([92:6-7](Ps.92.6-Ps.92.7), [11](Ps.92.11), [15](Ps.92.15)). The wicked, like grass, are quickly destroyed ([92:7-10](Ps.92.7-Ps.92.10)).
The psalmist offers praise and thanksgiving for God’s unfailing love and faithfulness.
92:title

**on the Sabbath Day:** Jewish tradition assigned one psalm to each day of the week: Sunday ([Ps 24](Ps.24.1-Ps.24.10)), Monday ([Ps 48](Ps.48.1-Ps.48.14)), Tuesday ([Ps 82](Ps.82.1-Ps.82.8)), Wednesday ([Ps 94](Ps.94.1-Ps.94.23)), Thursday ([Ps 81](Ps.81.1-Ps.81.16)), Friday ([Ps 93](Ps.93.1-Ps.93.5)), and the Sabbath ([Ps 92](Ps.92.1-Ps.92.15)). This is the only psalm that indicates this use in its title.
Fools perish because they do not understand the Lord’s marvelous works and eternal plans.
The Lord acts and the psalmist responds in praise ([92:4](Ps.92.4)). God’s actions spring from his thoughts ([92:5](Ps.92.5)).
The Lord’s **thoughts** do not make sense to the **simpleton** or the **fool***,* the immoral person who desires no wisdom ([Prov 1:22](Prov.1.22); [10:23](Prov.10.23)).
Even when the ungodly seem to grow luxuriantly ([73:3-5](Ps.73.3-Ps.73.5)), they have no future ([92:9](Ps.92.9); see [1:6](Ps.1.6); [90:5-6](Ps.90.5-Ps.90.6); [Isa 40:6-8](Isa.40.6-Isa.40.8)).
The glory of the Lord provides the reason for the poet’s renewed strength and glory, and for the imminent defeat of the enemy.

The transcendent Lord stays above the world of human experience. From this **exalted** place, he rules and judges ([7:7](Ps.7.7)), celebrates his victories ([68:18](Ps.68.18); see [Ps 47](Ps.47.1-Ps.47.9)), comes to rescue the needy ([102:19](Ps.102.19)), brings an end to the wicked ([92:7-8](Ps.92.7-Ps.92.8)), and receives praise ([148:1](Ps.148.1)).
**as strong as a wild ox:** The Lord allows the psalmist to share his exaltation ([92:8](Ps.92.8)), thus ensuring victory.
The psalmist understands the Lord’s mighty acts. He shares in the glory of the wise of heart.

Carvings of **palm trees** ([1 Kgs 6:29](1Kgs.6.29), [32](1Kgs.6.32), [35](1Kgs.6.35); [7:36](1Kgs.7.36)) adorned the Temple, and builders made rich use of **cedars** ([1 Kgs 5:6](1Kgs.5.6)). The trees represent the godly, who are planted in the very courts of the Temple.
The Temple area consisted of **the** **LORD’s own house** and the **courts** that surrounded it.
**There is no evil in him!** The Lord is consistently just; he rightly judges everyone (see [Zeph 3:5](Zeph.3.5)).

These psalms challenge the doubts created by the Exile (see [Ps 89](Ps.89.1-Ps.89.52)) and answer the questions asked in [90:11](Ps.90.11), [13](Ps.90.13). The Lord has established a kingdom ([Ps 93](Ps.93.1-Ps.93.5)) that is characterized by the punishment of the wicked ([Ps 94](Ps.94.1-Ps.94.23)), reverent obedience among his people ([Ps 95](Ps.95.1-Ps.95.11)), justice for the poor ([Ps 96](Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13)), celebration in Zion ([Ps 97](Ps.97.1-Ps.97.12)), salvation for Israel ([Ps 98](Ps.98.1-Ps.98.9)), holiness ([Ps 99](Ps.99.1-Ps.99.9)), and praise ([Ps 100](Ps.100.1-Ps.100.5)).
The everlasting Lord gloriously establishes his kingship (cp. [Pss 47](Ps.47.1-Ps.47.9), [99–100](Ps.99.1-Ps.100.5)).
**robed in majesty:** The Lord stands victorious both before and after battle (see [45:3](Ps.45.3)).
God’s victory over natural chaos gives the psalmist confidence that the Lord will also defeat his present enemies (cp. [Jer 46:8](Jer.46.8); [47:2](Jer.47.2)).
Through his stable rule and **royal laws***,* the Lord orders the world.
**Your reign** (literally *your house*): The *house* from which God reigns might be the Lord’s heavenly palace or the earthly Temple.

This plea for the Lord’s justice includes both communal and individual expressions of lament ([94:1-7](Ps.94.1-Ps.94.7), [16-23](Ps.94.16-Ps.94.23)). The psalmist gives voice to the pain and suffering caused by the wicked, but he also depicts the comfort and stability of the Lord’s protection. He calls on the Lord to avenge the needy against the arrogant and foolish, he rebukes such people for their folly ([94:8-11](Ps.94.8-Ps.94.11)), and he pronounces a blessing on the wise ([94:12-15](Ps.94.12-Ps.94.15)).
After the community falls victim to the **wicked** ([94:5-7](Ps.94.5-Ps.94.7)), they pray that the Lord will render **justice** (see [7:11](Ps.7.11); [9:12](Ps.9.12)).
Just as the Lord’s enemies rise up against him and his people ([3:7](Ps.3.7); [93:3](Ps.93.3)), he must **arise** and make retribution against the enemy (see [79:12](Ps.79.12); [Isa 65:6](Isa.65.6)).
**widows . . . foreigners . . . orphans:** The Lord’s law protects needy people ([Deut 24:17](Deut.24.17); [27:19](Deut.27.19)), but they remain vulnerable in society.
The wicked think that they can get away with their vile acts and speech, foolishly assuming that God **isn’t looking** or **doesn’t care**.
The psalmist rebukes human folly.
It is preposterous that those with **ears** and **eyes** would imagine their Creator to be **deaf** and **blind**.

**punishes:** This word also carries the idea of “warns” ([2:10](Ps.2.10)), “disciplines” ([6:1](Ps.6.1); [94:12](Ps.94.12)), or “instructs” ([16:7](Ps.16.7)). The Lord disciplines his people to purify their character ([Prov 3:11-12](Prov.3.11-Prov.3.12); [Heb 12:6-11](Heb.12.6-Heb.12.11)). He punishes his enemies by giving them what they deserve ([Ps 1:6](Ps.1.6); [Rom 6:23](Rom.6.23)).
While the Lord’s thoughts are deep, **people’s thoughts** are **worthless** (cp. [92:5](Ps.92.5); [1 Cor 3:20](1Cor.3.20)).
True to his nature, the Lord rewards those who live by his wise instruction and makes them happy according to his promises.
God’s **relief** includes his comfort and rescue.
Even when it seems that he has, **the** **LORD will not reject his people.**
The psalmist’s prayer resumes (see [94:1-7](Ps.94.1-Ps.94.7)) with a desperate cry for the Lord’s justice; it concludes with the hopeful expectation that evil will end.
Only God has the power to **stand up** to the wicked (see [2:2](Ps.2.2)).
The psalmist’s experience of **slipping** contrasts with God’s promise to stand with him ([94:12-13](Ps.94.12-Ps.94.13); see [15:5](Ps.15.5); [93:1](Ps.93.1)).

This call to worship urges the people to respond to the Lord, the Shepherd, and to follow him faithfully. The previous generation, who refused to obey, did not receive the blessings of the Promised Land.
The Lord is the **great King** over the whole universe.
**above all gods:** The psalmist refutes idolatry and paganism ([96:4-6](Ps.96.4-Ps.96.6); [135:15-18](Ps.135.15-Ps.135.18); see also [Isa 46:5-7](Isa.46.5-Isa.46.7)).
The whole created order owes its existence to the sovereign Lord alone—not to various gods.
The great King cares for his people as a shepherd cares for his **flock** ([Isa 40:11](Isa.40.11)).
The **LORD our maker***,* the Creator of heaven and earth, also made a people for himself ([Isa 45:9-12](Isa.45.9-Isa.45.12); [51:12-16](Isa.51.12-Isa.51.16)).
If people want to enter into the Lord’s rest, they need to respond immediately (see [Heb 3:7–4:11](Heb.3.7-Heb.4.11)).

To **harden your hearts** means to be stubborn and resist the Lord’s grace (see [Num 20:2-13](Num.20.2-Num.20.13); see also [Matt 13:3-23](Matt.13.3-Matt.13.23); [John 12:37-43](John.12.37-John.12.43); [Eph 4:17-32](Eph.4.17-Eph.4.32); [Heb 3:6-19](Heb.3.6-Heb.3.19); [4:6-11](Heb.4.6-Heb.4.11)).
Israel’s **ancestors . . . saw** the wonders of the Lord, but they foolishly did not try to grasp their significance (see [92:5-6](Ps.92.5-Ps.92.6)).

The generation of Israel that wandered in the wilderness for forty years failed to enter the **place of rest** that Israel enjoyed after the conquest of the land ([1 Kgs 8:56](1Kgs.8.56); see [Deut 12:9](Deut.12.9)). The Lord promised them the land and gave it to them ([Isa 28:12](Isa.28.12)), but they did not obey him ([Isa 28:1](Isa.28.1)). The warning reminds every generation of the need to obey in faith.

The rest that God provides includes peace, provision, and protection ([Ps 132:14-18](Ps.132.14-Ps.132.18)). The author of Hebrews challenged a new generation to enter the rest provided by Jesus Christ ([Heb 3:7–4:13](Heb.3.7-Heb.4.13)).

This psalm establishes the Lord’s universal kingship (see [Ps 93](Ps.93.1-Ps.93.5)) and prepares for the coming of the Lord to bring justice and righteousness into the world. The psalmist invites everyone to worship the Lord ([96:1-3](Ps.96.1-Ps.96.3)), the glorious Creator of all the earth ([96:4-6](Ps.96.4-Ps.96.6)), because worship is due to him alone ([96:7-9](Ps.96.7-Ps.96.9)). The universe joins in praise as the righteous Judge establishes a new order ([96:10-13](Ps.96.10-Ps.96.13)).
This psalm (along with [105:1-15](Ps.105.1-Ps.105.15); [106:1](Ps.106.1), [47-48](Ps.106.47-Ps.106.48)) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in [1 Chr 16:1-43](1Chr.16.1-1Chr.16.43).

Three psalms open with the exhortation to **sing a new song** ([Pss 96](Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13), [98](Ps.98.1-Ps.98.9), [149](Ps.149.1-Ps.149.9)); the song celebrates the Lord’s universal kingship (see [33:3](Ps.33.3)).
The gods of the nations are as nothing before the glorious and majestic Creator of the earth.

**Great is the** **LORD! . . . most worthy of praise:** With this refrain, the poet exalts the Lord over all the gods ([95:3](Ps.95.3)) and nations ([99:2](Ps.99.2)). He inspires awe more than anyone or anything else ([76:7](Ps.76.7), [12](Ps.76.12); [89:7](Ps.89.7); [99:3](Ps.99.3); [111:9](Ps.111.9)). He is beyond human possession or comprehension. The story of what he does to redeem his people causes them to praise him.
The **LORD made the heavens***,* an even greater task than creating the earth. The **idols***,* made by human hands ([115:4](Ps.115.4)), created nothing.

**Honor and majesty:** The Lord is glorious ([96:6](Ps.96.6); [104:1](Ps.104.1); [148:13](Ps.148.13)), and so are his works in nature ([8:1](Ps.8.1)) and in redemption ([111:3](Ps.111.3); [145:5](Ps.145.5)).
**nations of the world** (literally *families of the nations*): Families and clans represent subdivisions of the nations (see [Gen 12:3](Gen.12.3)).
The nations must respond to the Lord’s glory ([Pss 8:1](Ps.8.1); [19:1-4](Ps.19.1-Ps.19.4); [24:7](Ps.24.7)).

The **courts** of God’s sanctuary were usually off-limits to non-Jewish people. In this psalm the nations of the world—the non-Jews—are invited in ([65:4](Ps.65.4); [84:2](Ps.84.2), [10](Ps.84.10); [100:4](Ps.100.4); [116:19](Ps.116.19); [135:2](Ps.135.2); [Isa 1:12](Isa.1.12)).
Worshipers should **tremble** in awe ([96:4](Ps.96.4); see [18:7-15](Ps.18.7-Ps.18.15); [97:4](Ps.97.4)) at the **splendor** of the Lord’s majesty and holiness ([Heb 12:25](Heb.12.25)).
The Lord’s coming means the end of injustice. He rules fairly ([9:8](Ps.9.8); [96:13](Ps.96.13); [98:9](Ps.98.9)) and inaugurates an era of harmony and order not experienced since Eden.
The Lord’s reign over **the world** is founded on the strong pillars of “righteousness and justice” ([89:14](Ps.89.14)), so it **cannot be shaken** (cp. [11:3](Ps.11.3)).
The psalmist exhorts the created order to respond with joy to the news of the Lord’s coming. Cp. a similar theme in [98:7-9](Ps.98.7-Ps.98.9).
All of nature will experience renewal in God’s presence ([65:13](Ps.65.13); [72:6](Ps.72.6), [16](Ps.72.16); [Isa 44:23](Isa.44.23); [55:12](Isa.55.12); [Rom 8:21-22](Rom.8.21-Rom.8.22)).

God is greatly exalted over the gods and over all the earth. Awe-inspiring phenomena accompany his coming. Even the created order is visibly affected and the wicked perish, but the people of Zion love his coming and rejoice.
The **farthest coastlands** represent the most remote parts of the world.
**Dark clouds . . . Fire . . . lightning:** This language shows that the Lord is coming in judgment.
The created order stirs at the coming of its King. He alone deserves worship.
As the Lord enters the world, the testimony of his righteousness resounds from above ([50:6](Ps.50.6)).
**Every nation** will view the open display of the Lord’s **glory** (see [8:1](Ps.8.1); [19:1-4a](Ps.19.1-Ps.19.4); [24:7](Ps.24.7); [Isa 40:5](Isa.40.5)).
At the Lord’s coming, when **every god must bow** to him, those who worship other gods will face their own folly (see [95:3-5](Ps.95.3-Ps.95.5)).
**Jerusalem** rejoices at the news of the Lord’s coming, for he brings justice and rescues the upright of heart.

The godly people of integrity (see [Prov 2:7](Prov.2.7), [21](Prov.2.21); [3:32](Prov.3.32); [11:6](Prov.11.6), [11](Prov.11.11); [14:2](Prov.14.2)), **whose hearts are right***,* maintain a relationship with the Lord and with others ([Pss 94:15](Ps.94.15); [125:4](Ps.125.4)). The wicked plan the downfall of the godly ([11:2](Ps.11.2)), but the Lord rescues them ([11:1](Ps.11.1); [36:10](Ps.36.10)). Then the sorrows of the godly turn to joy and praise ([32:11](Ps.32.11); [64:10](Ps.64.10); [111:1](Ps.111.1); [119:7](Ps.119.7)).

This psalm celebrates the Lord’s kingship. The Lord is Israel’s true King, its champion and savior. His people sing a new song celebrating his victorious power and faithfulness to them. The Lord displays his righteous rule to all the nations throughout the earth, which will culminate in a worldwide kingdom of justice ([98:2](Ps.98.2), [9](Ps.98.9)). Consequently, all the earth must worship and rejoice together because the Lord is coming ([98:4-6](Ps.98.4-Ps.98.6)).
The Lord makes known his righteousness and faithfulness (see also [Isa 52:10](Isa.52.10)).
The psalmist invites the whole earth to worship the King (see [96:1](Ps.96.1)).
The Temple musicians used **trumpets** to call people together for meetings (cp. [81:3](Ps.81.3)).
The created order is personified as rejoicing at the coming of the righteous Judge (see [93:3-4](Ps.93.3-Ps.93.4); [96:11-13](Ps.96.11-Ps.96.13)).
The psalmist calls the nations to worship the Lord, the king of the earth who rules from Zion.

The Lord is the holy and righteous King ([Isa 6:1-5](Isa.6.1-Isa.6.5)). Mount Zion, the location of the Lord’s Temple, metaphorically stands as the highest point on earth ([Ps 113:4](Ps.113.4); [Isa 2:2](Isa.2.2); [6:1](Isa.6.1)). From this summit, the Great King ([Ps 47:2](Ps.47.2)) can see, rule over, and receive praise from all nations and peoples.
It is fitting to **tremble** and **quake** in response to the Lord’s holiness (see [96:9](Ps.96.9)).
The **throne between the cherubim** refers to the cover of the Ark of the Covenant ([Exod 25:17-22](Exod.25.17-Exod.25.22)).

The qualities of the Lord’s rule include strength, **justice***,* love, **fairness***,* and **righteousness** (see [93:4](Ps.93.4); [97:2](Ps.97.2), [6-7](Ps.97.6-Ps.97.7), [12](Ps.97.12); [98:2-3](Ps.98.2-Ps.98.3), [9](Ps.98.9); [138:6](Ps.138.6)).
God showed favor by responding to his people in the past, while holding sinners accountable.
**Moses** and **Samuel** were great models and leaders who had prayed on behalf of the Lord’s people ([Exod 32:31-32](Exod.32.31-Exod.32.32); [1 Sam 12:23](1Sam.12.23)).
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron from **the pillar of cloud** ([Exod 33:9](Exod.33.9); [Num 12:5-6](Num.12.5-Num.12.6)), and for a time, the people responded to the revelation.
This psalm calls all nations to come to Jerusalem to worship the Lord and acknowledge his goodness to Israel.
**The** **LORD** is the one who determines who **his people** are.
**the sheep of his pasture:** God will guide and protect his people ([23:1](Ps.23.1), [4](Ps.23.4)).
**Gates** and **courts** were part of the Temple in Jerusalem.
This hymn expresses a commitment to live with integrity and to avoid evil. Jesus meets this ideal.

**in my own home** (literally *in my house*): This commitment to **integrity** might refer to private life at home. Some interpreters view *my house* as referring to the king’s palace; the commitment would then refer to the policies of his administration.
Leading a **life of integrity** means choosing a wise lifestyle.
The psalmist hates what the Lord hates ([Prov 6:16-19](Prov.6.16-Prov.6.19); see [Pss 5:5](Ps.5.5); [11:4-5](Ps.11.4-Ps.11.5)).
**Perverse ideas** come from corrupt human hearts (cp. [18:26](Ps.18.26)).
The psalmist surrounds himself with people who are also committed to integrity ([101:2](Ps.101.2)).
The psalmist commits himself to ridding his **house** and **the city of the** **LORD**—representing the entire kingdom—of all evil.
A frail and afflicted human being prays for the Lord’s compassion on Jerusalem and for his presence with its inhabitants.
The psalmist appeals to the Lord not to **turn away** (or *hide your face*). Israel experienced his turning his face away during their exile.
**Smoke** is an image of transitory life ([37:20](Ps.37.20); [68:2](Ps.68.2)).
The psalmist’s **bones** represent his whole being (see [6:2](Ps.6.2); [34:19-22](Ps.34.19-Ps.34.22)).
**Like** dried **grass***,* the psalmist senses his life ebbing away.
**skin and bones:** The psalmist has wasted away because of his anguish (see [102:9](Ps.102.9); [109:24](Ps.109.24)).
The **owl** was associated with ruin and desolation ([Isa 34:11](Isa.34.11), [15](Isa.34.15)).
The psalmist cannot sleep (see [63:6-8](Ps.63.6-Ps.63.8)). Like a **bird on the roof***,* he feels isolated from both friends (see [88:8](Ps.88.8)) and **enemies**.
The psalmist blames the Lord for his troubles.
The psalmist’s existence seems empty and transitory ([102:4](Ps.102.4); [109:23](Ps.109.23); [144:4](Ps.144.4)).
The topic changes from the psalmist’s miseries to the Lord’s glory. A vision of the Lord’s compassionate kingship gives him confidence in Zion’s future.
**forever . . . to every generation:** The frailty of humans ([102:3-11](Ps.102.3-Ps.102.11)) contrasts with the permanence of the Lord.
**Now is the time** for the Lord to restore Jerusalem from exile (see [75:2](Ps.75.2); [Jer 29:10](Jer.29.10); [Dan 9:1-19](Dan.9.1-Dan.9.19)).

When the Lord arises ([102:13](Ps.102.13)), **the nations will tremble** with fear because they will see **his glory** (see [8:1](Ps.8.1); [19:1-4a](Ps.19.1-Ps.19.4); [24:7](Ps.24.7)). The rebuilding of Zion and the Temple portray God’s glory and fulfill this promise. An even greater fulfillment will come with the New Jerusalem ([Rev 21](Rev.21.1-Rev.21.27)).
The people of Israel were **destitute** (or *naked*) during the Exile.
The Lord will have mercy; Jews and Gentiles alike will worship him.
**Let this be recorded:** The written record stands as a memorial to the Lord’s goodness.
The **heavenly sanctuary** refers to God’s holy place on high (see [92:8-10](Ps.92.8-Ps.92.10)).

The **multitudes**—both Jews and Gentiles—will join in the worship of the Lord (see [96:7](Ps.96.7), [9](Ps.96.9); [106:48](Ps.106.48); [Isa 2:2-4](Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4); [43:10-13](Isa.43.10-Isa.43.13); [57:15](Isa.57.15); [60:3-7](Isa.60.3-Isa.60.7)).
Although the psalmist suffers in the present, he bases his hope for the future on the Lord’s past faithfulness.
The psalmist draws a contrast between his days ([102:23](Ps.102.23)) and God’s years (cp. [90:4](Ps.90.4)).
In contrast with the permanence of the Creator, the created order **will wear out like** a piece of **clothing** (see [Isa 40:28](Isa.40.28)).
The writer to the Hebrews describes this passage as having been addressed to Jesus, the Son ([Heb 1:10-12](Heb.1.10-Heb.1.12)).
The Lord’s **presence** provides the basis for the security and happiness of his **people** ([23:6](Ps.23.6)).
This psalm celebrates the Lord’s perfection, compassion, forgiveness, and goodness.
The psalmist offers praise for the Lord’s goodness.

**Let all that I am praise the** **LORD:** [Pss 103](Ps.103.1-Ps.103.22) and [104](Ps.104.1-Ps.104.35) each open and close with this commitment ([103:1-2](Ps.103.1-Ps.103.2), [22](Ps.103.22); [104:1](Ps.104.1), [35](Ps.104.35); see also [146:1](Ps.146.1)).
The Lord **revealed** himself **to Moses** in distinctive ways that ensured his relationship with his people (see [Exod 34:6-7](Exod.34.6-Exod.34.7); [Num 14:18](Num.14.18)).
If the Lord were to **constantly accuse** or **remain angry forever***,* no one would be left (see [Isa 54:7-8](Isa.54.7-Isa.54.8); [57:16](Isa.57.16)).
The Lord’s **love** and forgiveness are infinite and complete.

**The** **LORD is like a father to his children:** This analogy forms the basis for Jesus’ teaching about God’s fatherhood (see [Matt 5:43-48](Matt.5.43-Matt.5.48); [6:1](Matt.6.1); [10:19-20](Matt.10.19-Matt.10.20); [12:50](Matt.12.50); [Luke 6:36](Luke.6.36); [12:29-32](Luke.12.29-Luke.12.32); [John 8:31-59](John.8.31-John.8.59); [15:1-8](John.15.1-John.15.8); see also [2 Sam 7:14](2Sam.7.14); [Jer 3:19](Jer.3.19); [31:9](Jer.31.9); [Mal 1:6](Mal.1.6); [2 Cor 6:16-18](2Cor.6.16-2Cor.6.18)).
The Lord compassionately cares for frail humans (see [37:2](Ps.37.2); [90:5](Ps.90.5); [92:7](Ps.92.7); [102:4](Ps.102.4); [Isa 40:6-8](Isa.40.6-Isa.40.8)).
**the love of the** **LORD remains forever:** The Lord’s kingdom is everlasting, so he commits himself to his people across many generations.
To **obey** God means to be **faithful** and loyal to him.
The psalmist exhorts the Lord’s angels, his servants and messengers, to praise the Lord.
God’s **kingdom** extends over all things, so all things are called to praise the Lord.
The concluding phrase takes us back to [103:1-2](Ps.103.1-Ps.103.2).

This creation hymn (see also [Pss 8](Ps.8.1-Ps.8.9), [33](Ps.33.1-Ps.33.22), [145](Ps.145.1-Ps.145.21)) exalts God’s goodness and majesty. The psalmist reflects on the present world, the original creation, and a future new creation. He sees both creations as marvelously and wisely made (cp. [139:14](Ps.139.14)), as the work of the Lord’s Spirit ([104:30](Ps.104.30); [Gen 1:2](Gen.1.2); [2 Cor 3:6](2Cor.3.6)).

**Let all that I am praise the** **LORD:** [Pss 103](Ps.103.1-Ps.103.22) and [104](Ps.104.1-Ps.104.35) each open and close with this commitment to praise ([103:1-2](Ps.103.1-Ps.103.2), [22](Ps.103.22); [104:1](Ps.104.1), [35](Ps.104.35)).
**how great you are!** This acclamation expresses praise for rescue (see also [35:27](Ps.35.27); [40:16](Ps.40.16); [70:4](Ps.70.4)).
The psalmist interacts with two of the days of creation (see [Gen 1:1-8](Gen.1.1-Gen.1.8)), when God created the heavens and light.
This poetic portrayal envisions **the clouds** as beams that support heaven.

Wind and lightning are seen as divine **messengers**. The Lord uses weather phenomena as he desires ([77:17-18](Ps.77.17-Ps.77.18); [78:26](Ps.78.26); [135:7](Ps.135.7); [148:5-6](Ps.148.5-Ps.148.6)).
The psalmist interacts with day three of creation ([Gen 1:9-13](Gen.1.9-Gen.1.13)). The Lord is master of water and earth.
At first, **water** covered the earth.
The Lord created dry ground on day three of creation ([Gen 1:9-13](Gen.1.9-Gen.1.13)).
The earth originates in God’s will.

The Lord reigns over all bodies of water, including those on land. He replaced chaotic waters with order and abundance, and the earth became a splendid place for animals and humans, with water refreshing the ground, the birds, and the animals.

The Lord **set a firm boundary for the seas** to protect the land. God’s sovereignty over sea and land was an argument against the existence of Baal, whom the Canaanites celebrated as victorious over the waters (see [Ps 29](Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11)).
The psalmist celebrates animal, plant, and human life, as well as the Lord’s abundant provision for all of it ([Gen 1:9-30](Gen.1.9-Gen.1.30)).
**people to use:** People are the managers of the created order, and they receive nourishment from the work of their hands.
While both can be misused (cp. [Prov 21:17](Prov.21.17)), the Lord provides **wine** and **olive oil** as gifts to enhance life. Life is sustained by basic food, represented by **bread**.
The **storks** migrated from northern Europe and resided in Palestine during the winter.
**hyraxes:** These animals are about the size of a rabbit and live in rocky places.
The psalmist rejoices in the order of night and day, marking day four of creation ([Gen 1:14-19](Gen.1.14-Gen.1.19)). This cycle gives all creatures an opportunity to live.
**the moon to mark the seasons:** Ancient Israel based its calendar on the cycles of the moon.
**the sun knows when to set:** This is a poetic description from the perspective of normal observation. The sun goes down at a regular time every evening.
Cycles of **darkness** and **dawn** mark the days on earth.
The Lord’s works testify to his wisdom. All parts fit together—land and sea, night and day, land creatures and sea creatures. The Lord’s wisdom makes life orderly and wonderful.
The **ocean, . . . teeming with life of every kind** (see [Gen 1:20-21](Gen.1.20-Gen.1.21)), exemplifies the Lord’s creative activities.
**ships sailing:** Commercial vessels engaged in sea trade were one of the wonders of the ancient Near East (see [Isa 2:16](Isa.2.16); [23:1](Isa.23.1), [3](Isa.23.3)).
**Leviathan:** The psalmist says that this feared creature is nothing but the Lord’s pet.
All life depends on the gracious sustenance of the Lord of life and death (cp. [Matt 6:11](Matt.6.11)).

**When you give them your breath:** Life on earth is only possible as the Lord’s gift, symbolized by his breath (Hebrew *ruakh,* “breath, wind, spirit”). The Lord’s Spirit is the agent of renewal ([Isa 32:15-20](Isa.32.15-Isa.32.20)).
The psalmist moves from describing the known creation to anticipating the new creation, when the Lord will renew the created order into a world without sinners.
The Lord reveals his presence in the created order (see [8:1](Ps.8.1); [19:1-4](Ps.19.1-Ps.19.4); [24:7](Ps.24.7)) and takes **pleasure** in his new creation (see [Isa 65:19](Isa.65.19)).
The trembling **earth** and the smoking **mountains** represent the Lord’s coming in judgment against sinners and salvation for his faithful people (see [18:7-15](Ps.18.7-Ps.18.15)).
The Lord will remove all forms of evil that defile his creation.
The concluding phrase takes us back to [104:1](Ps.104.1) (see also [103:1-2](Ps.103.1-Ps.103.2), [22](Ps.103.22); [146:1](Ps.146.1)).

This hymn praises the Lord’s faithfulness to Abraham and his descendants in all their journeys—from Ur to Canaan ([105:12](Ps.105.12)), to Egypt ([105:17](Ps.105.17), [23](Ps.105.23)), through the wilderness ([105:37](Ps.105.37), [41](Ps.105.41)), and back to Canaan ([105:44](Ps.105.44)). All of this fulfilled the Lord’s promise to Abraham ([105:9](Ps.105.9), [42](Ps.105.42)), which was the basis for Israel’s very existence. Joseph, whose suffering was changed into glory, is a paradigm of encouragement for Israel ([105:16-25](Ps.105.16-Ps.105.25)).
[Psalm 105:1-15](Ps.105.1-Ps.105.15) (along with 96; [106:1](Ps.106.1), [47-48](Ps.106.47-Ps.106.48)) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in [1 Chr 16](1Chr.16.1-1Chr.16.43).

The poet begins with the exhortation **Give thanks** (see also [106:1](Ps.106.1); [107:1](Ps.107.1); [118:1](Ps.118.1); [136:1](Ps.136.1)). The other psalms continue with the refrain “for he is good!” The rest of [Ps 105](Ps.105.1-Ps.105.45) tells of God’s goodness.

The story of Israel is based on the Lord’s commitment to Abraham. Even when a question arises about the future of God’s covenant with David ([Ps 89](Ps.89.1-Ps.89.52)), God’s covenant with Abraham stands, as does the spiritual bond between God and Israel, Abraham’s descendants.
The **covenant** is the Lord’s irrevocable oath to be the Father of Abraham and his descendants (see [Gen 12:1-9](Gen.12.1-Gen.12.9); [15:1-21](Gen.15.1-Gen.15.21)).

God promised **the land of Canaan** to Abraham’s descendants as their **special possession***,* where they could live as God’s people ([105:44-45](Ps.105.44-Ps.105.45); [Gen 12:7](Gen.12.7); [15:7-21](Gen.15.7-Gen.15.21)).
The Lord protected Israel’s patriarchs.
Abraham was one of the nation’s **prophets** ([Gen 20:7](Gen.20.7)).
These verses tell the story of Joseph (see [Gen 37–41](Gen.37.1-Gen.41.57)).
**tested Joseph’s character:** See [Gen 39:6-12](Gen.39.6-Gen.39.12).
These verses tell the story of Israel’s affliction in Egypt (see [Exod 1:1-14](Exod.1.1-Exod.1.14)).
**Egypt** (Hebrew *mitsrayim*) is called **the land of Ham**.
The psalmist recounts the story of Moses and the plagues in Egypt ([Exod 7:20–12:30](Exod.7.20-Exod.12.30)).

The Exodus and the conquest of Canaan fulfilled God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob ([105:9-10](Ps.105.9-Ps.105.10)). Unlike [Ps 78](Ps.78.1-Ps.78.72), the poet recites the Lord’s goodness without commenting on Israel’s history of rebellion (cp. [Ps 106](Ps.106.1-Ps.106.48)).
**not one . . . stumbled:** The Lord protected all of his people (cp. [9:3](Ps.9.3)).
The Lord’s presence was as evident to all as a **fire** in the **darkness** ([Exod 13:22](Exod.13.22)).
The story of redemption is also the story of the Lord’s faithfulness.

Canaan was a land of **pagan nations** (see [111:6](Ps.111.6)). The psalmist might also be reflecting on God’s promise to Abraham ([Gen 24:60](Gen.24.60)) regarding the lands given to Isaac ([Gen 26:3](Gen.26.3)).
The Lord planned for Israel to testify about him by obeying him; Israel was to be his model people.

The Israelite community in exile confessed the Lord’s goodness and justice and their own historic sinfulness. From the humble state of exile, they pleaded for redemption and restoration, asking to be gathered back from all the places the Lord had scattered them in his wrath. The psalm does not end in despair but with the memory of the Lord’s former mercy and the hope that his mercy will be renewed ([106:44-48](Ps.106.44-Ps.106.48)). Israel failed, but the Lord is constant.
Verses 1, [47-48](Ps.47.1-Ps.48.14) (along with [Pss 96](Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13); [105:1-15](Ps.105.1-Ps.105.15)) are included in David’s song of praise recorded in [1 Chr 16:1-43](1Chr.16.1-1Chr.16.43).

**Praise the** **LORD!** This refrain (Hebrew *haleluyah*) characterizes four small subgroups in the psalms: [104–106](Ps.104.1-Ps.106.48), [111–113](Ps.111.1-Ps.113.9), [115–117](Ps.115.1-Ps.117.2), [146–150](Ps.146.1-Ps.150.6).
Wise people who practice justice and righteousness receive encouragement to proclaim the Lord’s great acts.
The poet prays individually for the Lord’s favor before leading the community confession that follows.
The community joins together to confess their sins and their ancestors’ many acts of unbelief.

The story of Israel’s redemption encompasses their sinful response from the days of the **ancestors** to the present ([106:43](Ps.106.43)). The themes of sin and divine wrath both open and close Book Four ([90:1-9](Ps.90.1-Ps.90.9); [106:6](Ps.106.6), [23](Ps.106.23), [43](Ps.106.43)).
**Red Sea:** See [Exod 14:15-31](Exod.14.15-Exod.14.31).

**They wouldn’t wait:** God’s impatient people did not trust him to work according to his will (e.g., see [Exod 15:24](Exod.15.24); [16:2-3](Exod.16.2-Exod.16.3); [17:1-3](Exod.17.1-Exod.17.3); [Num 14:26-45](Num.14.26-Num.14.45); [21:4-9](Num.21.4-Num.21.9)).
**he sent a plague:** See [Exod 32:35](Exod.32.35); [Num 11:33](Num.11.33).
The people became **jealous** because they presumed to have the same privileges as God’s appointed priests (see [Num 16:1-35](Num.16.1-Num.16.35)).
**the earth opened up:** See [Num 16:28-33](Num.16.28-Num.16.33).
**they bowed before an image:** The people forgot their Savior and committed the sin of idolatry (see [Exod 32:1-6](Exod.32.1-Exod.32.6)).
**The land of Ham** here means Egypt ([106:21](Ps.106.21)).
The people disobeyed God’s command when they **refused to enter the pleasant land** (the Promised Land; see [Jer 3:19](Jer.3.19)).
**they wouldn’t believe his promise:** See [Num 13:25–14:12](Num.13.25-Num.14.12).

God’s judgment when Israel refused to obey was death and exile ([Num 14:26-30](Num.14.26-Num.14.30)). The occasion for these severe judgments seems to have been disobeying God’s word ([Ps 106:24-25](Ps.106.24-Ps.106.25)) and provoking the Lord’s wrath ([106:28-46](Ps.106.28-Ps.106.46)).
Israel’s idolatry outside of the land came with them into the land. Their nature did not change; they continued to provoke the Lord to anger by their actions.
**the worship of Baal at Peor:** See [Num 25:3](Num.25.3); [Deut 4:3](Deut.4.3).

**Phinehas**, who executed a flagrantly apostate Israelite man ([Num 25:3-8](Num.25.3-Num.25.8)), is an even better model of **a righteous** man than **Moses**, who failed **at Meribah** ([Num 20:11-13](Num.20.11-Num.20.13)).

Israel continued to disobey the word of the Lord while living in the Promised Land. Rather than destroying the nations, Israel accepted them and their ways (see [Judg 2:1-3](Judg.2.1-Judg.2.3), [11-15](Judg.2.11-Judg.2.15); [3:5-6](Judg.3.5-Judg.3.6)).
Pagan gods were **demons** (see [Deut 32:17](Deut.32.17)).
Idolatry, like **adultery***,* defiles God’s people (see [Lev 18:24](Lev.18.24); [Hos 5:3](Hos.5.3)).
The psalmist returns to the Babylonian exile ([106:26-27](Ps.106.26-Ps.106.27)). The Lord judged Israel severely, but he also restrained his wrath, remembering the covenant he had made with Abraham.
God **abhorred** Israel’s sin, as he does all sin.
When Israel was **finally destroyed***,* the destruction was not complete. The Lord **pitied them***,* so he left a remnant.
**He remembered . . . and relented:** Unlike Israel, the Lord is faithful to his **covenant** ([105:8](Ps.105.8)).
As harsh as the Exile was, the Lord still protected his people (see [2 Kgs 25:27-29](2Kgs.25.27-2Kgs.25.29)).
This doxology concludes Book Four (cp. [41:13](Ps.41.13); [89:52](Ps.89.52)).
**from everlasting to everlasting!** The reference to God’s eternal nature links to the opening of Book Four ([90:1-2](Ps.90.1-Ps.90.2)).
**Let all the people say, “Amen!”:** The Hebrew word *’amen* means “It is true.” The godly accept the Lord’s will in exile and his promise to be their God.

This psalm is a hymn of praise to God the Redeemer. After an introduction exhorting the redeemed to praise God for his goodness ([107:1-3](Ps.107.1-Ps.107.3)), the psalmist brings together four case studies of people whom the Lord redeemed from adversity ([107:4-32](Ps.107.4-Ps.107.32)). He then sums up the Lord’s sovereignty ([107:33-42](Ps.107.33-Ps.107.42)) and concludes with an invitation to discern God’s unfailing love in all areas of life ([107:43](Ps.107.43)).
The **redeemed** might be all who came out of exile.
**exiles:** People came from all nations where the people of Israel and Judah had been scattered.
