Those who were lost in the **wilderness** thank God for his rescue. The wilderness might be a metaphor for leaving the path of wisdom ([1:1](Ps.1.1); [Prov 4:10-15](Prov.4.10-Prov.4.15)).
The psalmist does not specify the occasion of his **trouble** and **distress**. The generic nature of the adversity permits readers in a variety of circumstances to identify with the laments.
God **led them** like a shepherd (see [23:1](Ps.23.1)).
Verse 8 is a refrain that is repeated in [107:15](Ps.107.15), [21](Ps.107.21), [31](Ps.107.31).
The psalmist calls for thanksgiving and praise from people in despair over the consequences of their rebellion.
God’s **counsel** includes his instruction and will.

Exhausted by their **hard labor** ([Lam 5:13](Lam.5.13)), the people **fell**. While this might be expected of the wicked ([Pss 9:3](Ps.9.3); [27:2](Ps.27.2)), it was unlike the Israelites’ flight from Egypt ([105:37](Ps.105.37)).
Fools who received what they deserved but were rescued from death offer thanksgiving to the Lord.
The Lord creates ([Gen 1:3](Gen.1.3)) and sustains the universe ([Heb 1:3](Heb.1.3)) simply by speaking ([Ps 147:18](Ps.147.18)); when he speaks, people are also **healed** ([Matt 8:8](Matt.8.8)).
Sailors give thanks to the Lord when he saves them from the chaos and peril of the sea.
The same God who speaks and brings about the sailors’ distress can also calm the storm with just a word (cp. [Jon 1:4](Jonah.1.4); [Matt 8:26](Matt.8.26)).
This call for public praise expands the refrains in [107:21-22](Ps.107.21-Ps.107.22) and [107:31](Ps.107.31).
These two sections ([107:33-38](Ps.107.33-Ps.107.38), [39-42](Ps.107.39-Ps.107.42)) expand the theme of the Lord’s sovereignty over things that humans cannot control.
The Lord can choose to make the earth fertile or barren ([74:15](Ps.74.15); [Isa 35:6-7](Isa.35.6-Isa.35.7)).
God’s presence can be seen in the abundance of his people’s **families** and **herds** ([127:3](Ps.127.3); [133:3](Ps.133.3); cp. [109:8](Ps.109.8)).
People often **become impoverished** when their rulers practice **oppression**.
In his **contempt** for human rulers, the Lord rectifies their corruption on earth.
The large **families** of **the poor** are evidence of God’s blessing.
Justice prevails in God’s world ([1:6](Ps.1.6)), and Israel’s history demonstrates God’s faithful love.
This psalm combines two excerpts from David’s other psalms (cp. [57:5](Ps.57.5), [7-11](Ps.57.7-Ps.57.11); [60:5-12](Ps.60.5-Ps.60.12)).

The psalmist begins this lament with a general charge against his accusers: They do evil in return for good ([109:1-5](Ps.109.1-Ps.109.5)). At the end of the psalm, he turns to the Lord in prayer, asking for his protection ([109:21-25](Ps.109.21-Ps.109.25)) and vengeance ([109:26-31](Ps.109.26-Ps.109.31)).
The psalmist sees no evidence that God cares (see [28:1](Ps.28.1)).
The psalmist’s acts of kindness and godliness (see [35:12-14](Ps.35.12-Ps.35.14)) have only met with stubborn opposition and expressions of hatred.
The NLT translates these verses as the words of the psalmist’s accusers; Hebrew lacks **They say***,* which makes it unclear who is speaking.

Family members of those guilty of capital crimes often died with the perpetrator ([Num 16:1-33](Num.16.1-Num.16.33); [Josh 7:1-25](Josh.7.1-Josh.7.25)) or had their property confiscated ([1 Kgs 21:13-16](1Kgs.21.13-1Kgs.21.16)).
The wicked person apparently held a **position** of leadership. Peter referred to this psalm in regard to Judas Iscariot ([Acts 1:20-26](Acts.1.20-Acts.1.26)).
If one’s **family name** was **blotted out***,* it meant there was no **offspring** to carry on the family name or remember its history (see [Prov 10:7](Prov.10.7)).

Children inherit the sinful nature of their parents ([51:5](Ps.51.5); [Exod 20:5](Exod.20.5); [Eph 2:3](Eph.2.3)). The speaker wants the Lord to punish the perpetrator for the guilt of family members who went before him (cp. [Matt 23:35-36](Matt.23.35-Matt.23.36)).
The defendant committed capital crimes and did not exercise even basic decency.
**Cursing** is the accused person’s whole way of life.
The psalmist appeals to the principle of retribution (see [94:23](Ps.94.23)).
Vulnerable and miserable, the psalmist appeals to his Lord for help. The accusations have killed his inner spirit and even his physical stamina.
The Lord’s **reputation** is at stake. If the wicked triumph, others could think that the Lord is also wicked and be drawn to that wickedness ([1:1](Ps.1.1)).
A **shadow at dusk** suggests a transitory, empty existence ([102:11](Ps.102.11); [144:4](Ps.144.4)); a single **locust** could easily be **brushed off** one’s clothing.
These verses form a prayer for God’s presence and for vindication. The psalmist wants everyone to see that he is vindicated by the Lord, not by any human agent.
The Lord’s **servant** demonstrates loyalty and obedience.
The psalmist had been accused of being clothed with curses ([109:18](Ps.109.18)); now he asks that his accusers be **clothed with disgrace** and **humiliation**.

Jesus and the apostles cite this psalm to explain Jesus’ unique ministry and status as the Messiah ([Matt 22:43-45](Matt.22.43-Matt.22.45); [Acts 2:32-36](Acts.2.32-Acts.2.36)). It reaffirms God’s covenant with David and gives hope for the future (see [2 Sam 7:8-16](2Sam.7.8-2Sam.7.16)).

The king of Israel had the great privilege of being the Lord’s adopted son ([Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12); [1 Chr 22:10](1Chr.22.10)), but he fell ([Ps 89](Ps.89.1-Ps.89.52)). This decree restores and heightens his position.
**The** **LORD:** Hebrew *Yahweh,* the name of God (see [Exod 3:6-14](Exod.3.6-Exod.3.14); [6:2-8](Exod.6.2-Exod.6.8); [20:2](Exod.20.2)).

**my Lord** (Hebrew *’adoni*) means “my master” or “my superior.” The psalmist viewed God’s messianic ruler as his superior. The New Testament frequently cites this psalm to validate Jesus’ claim to be the Messiah ([Matt 22:44-45](Matt.22.44-Matt.22.45); [Mark 12:36-37](Mark.12.36-Mark.12.37); [Luke 20:42-44](Luke.20.42-Luke.20.44); [Acts 2:34-35](Acts.2.34-Acts.2.35); [Heb 1:13](Heb.1.13)).

The Lord’s **right hand** represents his authority, strength, presence, and benefits. The Lord chose the descendant of David and raised him up to be close to him ([Ps 80:17](Ps.80.17)). Jesus claimed this position for himself ([Matt 26:64](Matt.26.64); [Mark 14:62](Mark.14.62); [16:19](Mark.16.19); [Luke 22:69](Luke.22.69)), and the apostles announced that Jesus, having ascended to heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father ([Acts 2:33](Acts.2.33); [5:31](Acts.5.31); [7:55-56](Acts.7.55-Acts.7.56); [Rom 8:34](Rom.8.34); [Eph 1:20](Eph.1.20); [Col 3:1](Col.3.1); [Heb 1:3](Heb.1.3); [8:1](Heb.8.1); [10:12](Heb.10.12); [12:2](Heb.12.2)).
Ancient Near Eastern kings were sometimes portrayed as placing their feet on the backs of their conquered **enemies** as on a **footstool** (see [Heb 10:12-13](Heb.10.12-Heb.10.13)).
The **kingdom** will expand and increase, beginning from Jerusalem, until all enemies are conquered.

The Lord had made an unbreakable **oath** and covenant, so his apparent rejection of David’s dynasty ([89:38](Ps.89.38)) in the Exile had led to a crisis. The placement of [Ps 110](Ps.110.1-Ps.110.7) in Book Five reaffirms the future of the dynasty: David’s descendant must conform to God’s standard of integrity ([Ps 101](Ps.101.1-Ps.101.8)). His ministry will be transformed as he serves under God’s kingship ([Pss 93–100](Ps.93.1-Ps.100.5)).

**You are a priest forever:** The role of God’s messianic ruler changes. The priestly kingship of David and his descendants extended to serving as patrons of the Temple. David had the Ark brought to Jerusalem ([2 Sam 6:15](2Sam.6.15)) and arranged for the Temple service ([1 Chr 6:31-48](1Chr.6.31-1Chr.6.48); [15:11-26](1Chr.15.11-1Chr.15.26); [16:4-42](1Chr.16.4-1Chr.16.42); [23:4-32](1Chr.23.4-1Chr.23.32); [25:1](1Chr.25.1)). Solomon supervised the Temple construction ([1 Kgs 5:1–7:51](1Kgs.5.1-1Kgs.7.51)). Even so, Israel’s kingship was separate from its priesthood. In the messianic kingdom, the king would also minister as priest, as **Melchizedek***,* king of Salem ([Gen 14:18](Gen.14.18)), had done. The New Testament develops the ministry of Jesus Christ as a fulfillment of this new order (see [Heb 5:6-10](Heb.5.6-Heb.5.10); [6:20–7:25](Heb.6.20-Heb.7.25)).

The new priestly role of David’s descendant does not rescind his old role as conquering ruler. He must still bring the nations under his rule ([110:2-3](Ps.110.2-Ps.110.3); see [Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12)).
**at your right hand:** This position brings help and protection (see [16:7-8](Ps.16.7-Ps.16.8); [108:13](Ps.108.13)).
The Lord **will strike down** rebellious **kings**. Rebellion against the Lord is a capital offense ([Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12); [Rom 6:23](Rom.6.23)).
God’s messianic ruler obtains victory as a vigorous person, as if he had received nourishment **from brooks along the way** ([110:3](Ps.110.3)).
The refrain **Praise the** **LORD!** (Hebrew *haleluyah*) characterizes this group of psalms.

This wisdom psalm contains many references to the works of the Lord that reveal his character. God is righteous, gracious, compassionate, faithful, just, trustworthy, upright, holy, and awe-inspiring ([111:3](Ps.111.3), [4](Ps.111.4), [7](Ps.111.7), [8](Ps.111.8), [9](Ps.111.9)). God’s character gives hope in the covenant relationship ([111:5](Ps.111.5)). He rescued Israel from Egypt ([111:9](Ps.111.9)), gave them the land ([111:6](Ps.111.6)), and provides for his people ([111:5](Ps.111.5)). However, God demands that the beneficiaries of this relationship also be people of righteousness and integrity.

The godly praise God and delight themselves in his great works. His mighty acts reflect his righteousness, grace, and compassion (see [116:5-7](Ps.116.5-Ps.116.7)). All who submit themselves to him experience his glory.
God takes care of his people’s needs, even providing **food**. He **remembers his covenant** with Abraham (see [105:8-11](Ps.105.8-Ps.105.11)).

Giving Israel **the lands of other nations** was **just and good** because the Lord was executing his justice on those he dispossessed and showing grace to the Israelites. However, if the Israelites do not live **faithfully and with integrity***,* they will also be dispossessed. The Lord’s people must reflect his character.
The people of the Exodus generation went free because of God’s grace.
**True wisdom** is the source of life ([Prov 3:18](Prov.3.18); [9:11](Prov.9.11); [Eccl 7:12](Eccl.7.12)); it begins with the **fear of the** **LORD** ([Prov 9:10](Prov.9.10)).

This psalm reiterates the themes of wisdom and the fear of the Lord ([Ps 111](Ps.111.1-Ps.111.10)). The wise have reason to be happy ([112:1-5](Ps.112.1-Ps.112.5)) and vigorous ([112:6-10](Ps.112.6-Ps.112.10)).
The fear of the Lord leads to a life of wisdom that honors God and blesses the family and community. The godly joyfully imitate God; their obedience is not slavish.
**successful:** All will know the **children** of **godly people** (see [127:4](Ps.127.4)) because the godly leave a legacy for their children (see [1:3](Ps.1.3); cp. [Matt 6:20](Matt.6.20)).

The godly imitate God by being **generous, compassionate, and righteous** ([51:1](Ps.51.1); [111:1-10](Ps.111.1-Ps.111.10); [2 Cor 9:9](2Cor.9.9)). They **lend money** to the poor without charging interest ([Pss 15:5](Ps.15.5); [112:9](Ps.112.9); [Exod 22:25](Exod.22.25)).
The honesty and compassion of the wise keeps them from stumbling ([15:5](Ps.15.5); [37:23-24](Ps.37.23-Ps.37.24)), ensuring that they **will be long remembered** ([Prov 10:7](Prov.10.7)).
Because the godly joyfully expect God to prevail and rescue them, they **face their foes triumphantly** ([59:10](Ps.59.10); [112:4](Ps.112.4); [118:7](Ps.118.7)).
Paul quotes this verse in his instructions about generous giving ([2 Cor 9:9](2Cor.9.9)).
The **wicked . . . grind their teeth in anger** out of their bitter envy ([35:16](Ps.35.16); [37:12](Ps.37.12)). The vigor and reputation of the godly cause conflict with those who want them dead.
The wicked **will slink away** out of fear and shame.

These psalms form what is known as the “Egyptian Hallel” (*hallel* means “praise”) because Jews use the collection in the celebration of Passover, which was instituted at the beginning of the exodus from Egypt. [Psalms 113–114](Ps.113.1-Ps.114.8) are recited before the Passover meal and [Pss 115–118](Ps.115.1-Ps.118.29) afterward.

This hymn of praise exalts the greatness of the Lord’s name and glory. God is greatly exalted and glorious in heaven ([113:4](Ps.113.4)); he also stoops down to take care of the lowly and needy on earth ([113:5-9](Ps.113.5-Ps.113.9)).

**The name of the** **LORD** (Hebrew *Yahweh;* see [Exod 3:15](Exod.3.15)) reveals his being, character, and reputation. He is exalted in time (**now and forever**) and in space (**from east to west**).

The Lord’s glory reaches to the **heavens** ([57:5](Ps.57.5), [11](Ps.57.11); [99:2](Ps.99.2); [108:5](Ps.108.5); [138:6](Ps.138.6); [Isa 6:1](Isa.6.1); [57:15](Isa.57.15)) and throughout the world of human relationships.
The incomparable Lord intimately involves himself in caring for people on earth.
The Lord **stoops** to the world’s level to be directly involved with his people (see [138:6](Ps.138.6); [Phil 2:6-8](Phil.2.6-Phil.2.8)).
These phrases are a quotation from Hannah’s prayer of praise ([1 Sam 2:8-9a](1Sam.2.8-1Sam.2.9)).

A **childless woman** was customarily treated with disdain ([Gen 16:4](Gen.16.4)); the Lord has the power to make her **a happy mother***,* as he made Sarah ([Gen 21:2](Gen.21.2)), Rebekah ([Gen 25:21](Gen.25.21)), Rachel ([Gen 30:23](Gen.30.23)), and Hannah ([1 Sam 1:20](1Sam.1.20)).
God’s greatness and goodness provide ample reason to **praise** him.

This lyrical celebration of the Lord’s power in nature recalls Israel’s beginning as a nation at the Exodus ([114:1-2](Ps.114.1-Ps.114.2)) and upon their entry to the Promised Land ([114:3-6](Ps.114.3-Ps.114.6)). It promotes reverence for the God of Jacob ([114:7-8](Ps.114.7-Ps.114.8)).
At the time of Israel’s exodus from Egypt and their entrance into the Promised Land, Israel was one holy **kingdom** ([Exod 19:5-6](Exod.19.5-Exod.19.6)).

The separate references to **the land of Judah** and **Israel** indicate that the psalm was composed after the kingdom was divided ([1 Kgs 12:16-17](1Kgs.12.16-1Kgs.12.17); cp. [1 Sam 11:8](1Sam.11.8); [1 Kgs 1:35](1Kgs.1.35)), and probably after the Exile. The **land of Judah became God’s sanctuary** because the people worshiped God; his Tabernacle and later his Temple were located there.
**hurried out of their way!** The waters divided for Israel to escape Egypt ([77:17-18](Ps.77.17-Ps.77.18); [Exod 14](Exod.14.1-Exod.14.31)).
**The Jordan River turned away** when Israel arrived to cross over (see [Josh 3](Josh.3.1-Josh.3.17)).
**skipped like rams:** God’s presence caused the mountains to quake ([Exod 19:16-20](Exod.19.16-Exod.19.20)).
The Lord miraculously provided for his people in hard times after the Exile, just as he had done in the wilderness after the Exodus.

In this hymn of thanksgiving for God’s blessings, the community ascribes all glory to the name of the Lord, who is the true source of hope and blessing. Meanwhile, those who trust in idols are greatly disappointed. The blessing of the Creator of heaven and earth extends to future generations ([115:14](Ps.115.14)), and especially to the priesthood ([115:12](Ps.115.12)).
The community confesses their faith that God will rescue them for the glory of his name.

**Where is their God?** People deny God’s presence or power when he does not act as they think he should (cp. [14:1](Ps.14.1); [42:3](Ps.42.3), [10](Ps.42.10)). However, **God is in the heavens**—he has all power, authority, and knowledge. He **does as he wishes***,* not what people think he should do. He works out his plans in accord with his will ([Eph 1:11](Eph.1.11)) and acts in his own time and in ways he chooses.
This entire section is repeated in [135:15-20](Ps.135.15-Ps.135.20).
Unlike the Lord ([95:3-5](Ps.95.3-Ps.95.5)), **idols** cannot do anything; they are good for nothing.
Worshiping idols leads one astray and corrupts those **who trust in them** ([Isa 44:20](Isa.44.20)).

**Israel . . . priests . . . you who fear the** **LORD:** The psalmist calls on all those in the God-fearing community to commit their ways to the living God. The threefold address assures them that the Lord is their true **helper** and **shield** (cp. [118:2-4](Ps.118.2-Ps.118.4)).
The groups named in [115:9-11](Ps.115.9-Ps.115.11) receive assurance of the Lord’s blessing, regardless of their social status (see [113:8](Ps.113.8)).
The psalmist blesses ([107:37-38](Ps.107.37-Ps.107.38), [41](Ps.107.41)) all who trust in and fear the Lord. The Creator will care for the families of those who fear him.
**who made heaven and earth:** This statement speaks of the Lord’s all-encompassing power in creation.

**The heavens belong to the** **LORD:’s:** God’s exaltation begins in heaven ([113:4](Ps.113.4)), far above the gods of the nations. Of course, the earth also belongs to him ([47:9](Ps.47.9); [95:4](Ps.95.4)).
The **dead** cannot participate in God’s blessings. The living **praise** God in thanksgiving for his blessings ([79:13](Ps.79.13)).

This hymn of thanksgiving rejoices in God’s character and in rescue from death ([116:1-11](Ps.116.1-Ps.116.11)). It gives an assurance of God’s protection in life and reminds the godly that the Lord watches over them even at death. The psalmist commits to living as God’s servant and resolves to honor him publicly ([116:12-19](Ps.116.12-Ps.116.19)).
The psalmist praises the Lord for answering his prayers and rescuing him from death.
**I love the** **LORD:** This unique opening expresses affection for and commitment to the Lord (see [18:1](Ps.18.1); [Deut 6:5](Deut.6.5)) on the basis of what the Lord has done.
Because the Lord responds to the cry of his people ([107:41](Ps.107.41); [113:6-8](Ps.113.6-Ps.113.8)), the psalmist now strongly believes in prayer.
It isn’t clear if the psalmist’s crisis was a literal near-death experience or if he was using the term figuratively.
This is the first of three times that the psalmist calls on the Lord’s **name** (i.e., reputation).
The gracious, righteous, and compassionate Lord (see [111:1-5](Ps.111.1-Ps.111.5)) rescued and gave rest to the psalmist.
People with **childlike faith** readily receive his wisdom and instruction ([19:7-11](Ps.19.7-Ps.19.11); [Matt 18:3-4](Matt.18.3-Matt.18.4)).
The psalmist’s near-death crisis made him more aware of life and of walking before the Lord. Though he had been in anguish, the Lord was faithful. However, **people are all liars**.

**I walk in the** **LORD’s presence:** The psalmist already lived with integrity, but since his experience of deep distress, he now enjoys open fellowship with the Lord (see [56:13](Ps.56.13); cp. [Job 42:5](Job.42.5)).
**I believed in you:** Paul quotes this phrase in [2 Cor 4:13](2Cor.4.13).
The Lord’s gracious gifts are so great that the psalmist can do nothing to repay his debt. Keeping his promises publicly demonstrates his gratitude.
**All he has done for** the psalmist includes answers to prayer, rescue, and life.
The **cup of salvation** overflows with God’s blessings ([23:5](Ps.23.5)), unlike the cup of judgment ([75:8](Ps.75.8)).
The psalmist makes **promises** (“vows,” [116:18](Ps.116.18)) to praise the Lord publicly ([116:17-18](Ps.116.17-Ps.116.18)).
No one lives or dies outside of God’s will. Having been given a second chance at life, the poet readily commits himself to the Lord with renewed acts of public devotion.
This psalm, the shortest in the Psalter, invites **all . . . people of the earth** to **praise the** **LORD** because of his **unfailing love** and enduring **faithfulness**.
Paul quotes this verse to show that Gentiles would eventually praise the God of Israel ([Rom 15:11](Rom.15.11)).

With an exultant testimony, the psalmist gives thanks for the Lord’s goodness and encourages others to trust in his faithful love ([118:1-4](Ps.118.1-Ps.118.4), [29](Ps.118.29)). This poem is the last of the Egyptian Hallel ([Pss 113–118](Ps.113.1-Ps.118.29)).

**Israel . . . Aaron’s descendants . . . all who fear the** **LORD:** These three groups represent the whole of the covenant community (cp. [115:9-11](Ps.115.9-Ps.115.11); [135:19-20](Ps.135.19-Ps.135.20)).
The Lord alone is the psalmist’s helper.
**The** **LORD is for me:** Cp. [Rom 8:31](Rom.8.31); [Heb 13:6](Heb.13.6).
God’s presence cancels out the need to fear **mere people** ([Ps 56:11](Ps.56.11)). The psalmist joyfully expects God’s rescue ([59:10](Ps.59.10); [112:8](Ps.112.8)).
Trusting in the Lord is better than placing confidence in even the most powerful human leaders ([118:6](Ps.118.6); [146:3](Ps.146.3)).
Strength comes in the name of the Lord, declared by the threefold mention of the attackers, the Lord’s name, and victory.
Even when hostile people **blazed . . . like a crackling fire***,* the Lord caused them to subside like burning thorns (see [Isa 9:18](Isa.9.18); [10:17](Isa.10.17)).
The psalmist celebrates the victory of the Lord’s **strong right arm***,* which kept him from death.
God has restored the psalmist from death to life, so he praises the Lord publicly (cp. [116:6](Ps.116.6), [12-19](Ps.116.12-Ps.116.19)).
The psalmist sees his own salvation as the beginning of a new day in which the Lord will do great things.

The **cornerstone** (or *keystone*) of a building or an arch gives the structure its shape and foundation. It is the most important of all the stones. The Lord chooses and places this stone for his sanctuary ([Isa 28:16](Isa.28.16)). Jesus referred to himself as this cornerstone ([Matt 21:42](Matt.21.42); [Mark 12:10-11](Mark.12.10-Mark.12.11); [Luke 20:17](Luke.20.17); see [Acts 4:11](Acts.4.11); [Eph 2:20](Eph.2.20); [1 Pet 2:6-7](1Pet.2.6-1Pet.2.7)).
**This is the day the** **LORD has made:** The day of the Lord’s victory has already arrived, although its completion awaits another day ([118:25](Ps.118.25)).
The psalmist concludes with prayer and thanksgiving, anticipating an even greater revelation of God’s victory and rescue.
The **one who comes in the name of the** **LORD** brings the Lord’s complete victory (see [118:10-12](Ps.118.10-Ps.118.12)).

During Jesus’ triumphant entry into Jerusalem, the crowds called out various blessings, including phrases taken from this verse ([Matt 21:9](Matt.21.9); [Mark 11:9](Mark.11.9); [Luke 19:38](Luke.19.38); [John 12:13](John.12.13)). Jesus himself quoted this passage as he wept over Jerusalem ([Matt 23:39](Matt.23.39); [Luke 13:35](Luke.13.35)).

This psalm combines elements of wisdom, lament, praise, thanksgiving, and confession. Eight Hebrew words are used frequently, translated as “instructions,” “laws,” “words,” “regulations,” “statutes,” “commands,” “decrees,” “commandments,” and “promises.” Together, these words encourage love for and obedience to God’s instructions, as found in the Scriptures (see [2 Tim 3:14-17](2Tim.3.14-2Tim.3.17)). The expression of deep commitment to these instructions unifies the psalm.
*Aleph* (א): God, the author of these **instructions***,* commands that his followers live by them. The psalmist prays to be given the grace to live by that revelation.

The wise are happy. They are **people of integrity** (see [84:11](Ps.84.11)) who **follow** the path of divine instruction. They **obey** God’s revelation and **search** for it **with all their hearts** (see [27:7](Ps.27.7); [119:10](Ps.119.10), [45](Ps.119.45), [94](Ps.119.94), [155](Ps.119.155)), and they reject all forms of evil. Cp. [1:1-2](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.2).
To **keep** God’s **commandments** means to guard them by obeying them.
*Beth* (ב): The psalmist is determined to pursue purity and encourages the cultivation of wisdom through God’s principles ([119:9](Ps.119.9)) and instructions ([119:10-16](Ps.119.10-Ps.119.16)).

A **young person** tends toward foolishness ([Prov 22:15](Prov.22.15)) and can easily make mistakes that destroy his life ([Prov 7:6-23](Prov.7.6-Prov.7.23)). Youth is also the best time to develop personal discipline and pursue wisdom (see [Ps 34:11](Ps.34.11); [Prov 1:4](Prov.1.4)).
To **stay pure** means to remain uncorrupted by wickedness and sin and to develop the integrity of life defined in [Ps 15](Ps.15.1-Ps.15.5).
The student asks God the teacher to discipline him so that he will not **wander**.
God’s wisdom is far greater than any **riches** humans seek ([119:72](Ps.119.72), [127](Ps.119.127); [Prov 3:14-15](Prov.3.14-Prov.3.15)).
The way of wisdom includes meditating on God’s **ways** (see [119:1](Ps.119.1), [3](Ps.119.3)). The wise reflect on the implications of God’s word.
*Gimel* (ג): Like a **foreigner** in hostile territory, God’s **servant** needs God’s guidance.

The psalmist seeks to please the Lord with a full and obedient life of praise ([118:17](Ps.118.17); [119:25](Ps.119.25), [77](Ps.119.77), [116](Ps.119.116), [144](Ps.119.144), [175](Ps.119.175)). Only the Lord can remove his adversaries and enable him to **see** the wonderful truths found in God’s instructions.
The **arrogant** are probably those who mock the psalmist ([119:22-23](Ps.119.22-Ps.119.23)).
Those who **meditate** on God’s instructions receive **wise advice** from them.

*Daleth* (ד): Though the poet feels anguish and sorrow, he entreats the Lord to revive him because he wants to obey the Lord. Suffering and death may result from the Lord’s chastening ([118:17-18](Ps.118.17-Ps.118.18); [119:67](Ps.119.67), [71](Ps.119.71), [75](Ps.119.75)), but his instruction revives the weary soul (see [119:12](Ps.119.12)).
**lying to myself:** Self-deception is a fruit of sinful human nature ([Jer 17:9](Jer.17.9)); it leads to folly.
Access to God’s word is a **privilege**, not a right.
*He* (ה): As a student, the poet asks his teacher, God, to renew life and to transform disgrace into righteousness.
The **love for money** can lead to sin (cp. [Exod 18:21](Exod.18.21); [1 Tim 3:1-5](1Tim.3.1-1Tim.3.5); [6:10](1Tim.6.10)).
*Waw* (ו): The psalmist prays that God’s word would continue to be the source of his **love** and **salvation**.
The psalmist asks to be saved from enemies who speak harshly (see [42:10](Ps.42.10); [44:16](Ps.44.16); [89:50-51](Ps.89.50-Ps.89.51); [102:8](Ps.102.8)).
The psalmist is determined to obey the Lord.
The psalmist finds **delight** in God’s word in spite of pain ([119:92](Ps.119.92), [143](Ps.119.143)).
*Zayin* (ז): The psalmist asks God to **remember** his word as the psalmist also remembers God’s word and his name. Remembrance expresses devotion.
The **age-old regulations** are the Torah (God’s “instructions” or “law”), a term that refers to the books of Genesis—Deuteronomy.
*Heth* (ח): The psalmist seeks God’s favor and **unfailing love**. Although surrounded by evildoers, he remains a loyal servant of the Lord.
**Evil people try to drag** him **into sin***,* but the psalmist’s memory of God’s word keeps him standing firm (see [119:16](Ps.119.16)).
God’s goodness **fills the earth***;* the whole created order provides evidence of his goodness (see [Isa 6:3](Isa.6.3); [11:9](Isa.11.9)).
*Teth* (ט): The psalmist describes himself as a penitent sinner who gratefully accepts the Lord’s discipline.
**Good judgment and knowledge** come from wisdom ([111:10](Ps.111.10)).
The psalmist admits that he **used to wander off** like a stray sheep ([119:176](Ps.119.176)).
**you disciplined me:** See [119:25-29](Ps.119.25-Ps.119.29).
**You are good and do only good:** God’s character is perfect ([97:2](Ps.97.2); [Jas 1:17](Jas.1.17); [1 Jn 1:5](1John.1.5)).

*Yodh* (י): In this prayer for comfort and compassion, the psalmist commits himself to his Creator, who has afflicted him. He wants God to pay back his enemies for the wrongs they have done. He also prays to receive the gift of life. He not only prays for himself but also considers the whole community of the godly, asking that God’s answers to prayer would encourage them.
As God’s child, the psalmist asks for divine wisdom.
*Kaph* (כ): The psalmist is **worn out** from **waiting** for the Lord, but his **hope** is in God’s future **rescue**.
God’s word is **trustworthy***,* in contrast to the deceptions of the enemies **who hunt** the psalmist **down without cause** (see [119:78](Ps.119.78)).
*Lamedh* (ל): The stability of God’s wisdom gives understanding. God’s word provides order and a framework for living, even when under pressure from adversaries.
The **wicked** intended to **kill** the psalmist, but destruction ([1:6](Ps.1.6)) was their own fate.
**Even perfection has its limits:** Humans cannot fully understand God’s ways (see [Eccl 3:11](Eccl.3.11)).
*Mem* (מ): The instruction and wisdom of God through his word are far superior to the best that human teachers can offer.
**make me wiser:** God’s word provides wisdom and perspective. God is the true source of wisdom.
Wisdom is preferable to even the finest food ([19:10](Ps.19.10); [81:16](Ps.81.16)).
The psalmist had already rejected the delusion offered by the way of folly (see [119:18](Ps.119.18), [78](Ps.119.78), [86](Ps.119.86), [163](Ps.119.163)).
*Nun* (נ): The psalmist’s devotion to God’s word comes from within his being ([119:112](Ps.119.112)) and guides his external life.

The Lord’s **word is a lamp** that provides perspective, hope, and guidance in darkness ([18:25-29](Ps.18.25-Ps.18.29); [119:130](Ps.119.130)). Even more, this **light** gives life ([Prov 6:23](Prov.6.23)).
**offering of praise:** This Hebrew expression is unique in the Old Testament (cp. [50:23](Ps.50.23)).
The psalmist is vulnerable to his opponents because of his commitment to a wise life.
*Samekh* (ס): The psalmist declares his hatred of evil and his love for God and his ways.
The godly hate the wicked and their deeds ([5:4-6](Ps.5.4-Ps.5.6); cp. [Ezek 33:11](Ezek.33.11)).
*Ayin* (ע): The servant of the Lord strains to endure the evil around him. He boldly petitions the Lord to rescue him immediately!
Simply possessing God’s law does not provide any benefits. The psalmist knows that only as the Lord gives **discernment** will he **understand** it.
*Pe* (פ): The psalmist prays earnestly for God to speak to him as he suffers from his adversities.
*Tsadhe* (צ): God is righteous, and his word is right and just, especially in contrast to the deceptions of the wicked.
The psalmist’s **indignation** (cp. [69:9](Ps.69.9)) comes from seeing the wicked disregard God’s word.
The psalmist is greatly troubled by his oppressors (see [119:143](Ps.119.143); cp. [Isa 53](Isa.53.1-Isa.53.12)).
*Qoph* (ק): The psalmist prays to the Lord at night. Although God appears to be distant, he is nearby.
**I pray** and **I cry out** translate the same Hebrew verb.
**I rise early** and **I stay awake** translate the same Hebrew verb.

**Coming to attack me** (or *are coming near to me*) is a Hebrew wordplay on **but you are near**. The wicked remain far from God’s instructions, whereas the psalmist stays near, so he does not need to fear.
*Resh* (ר): This petition for **life** can be found throughout [Ps 119](Ps.119.1-Ps.119.176), but it is concentrated in this stanza.
*Shin* (ש): The psalmist looks beyond his adversaries to the peace of God. This perspective allows him to praise God throughout the day.
**my heart trembles . . . I rejoice:** Fear, trembling, and joy mark the psalmist’s devotion to God.
God’s word is a **treasure**.
In the Old Testament, **seven** signifies wholeness.
*Taw* (ת): God’s servant petitions the Lord one final time; he still feels like a lost sheep.
God, the Great Shepherd, seeks out his **lost sheep** ([23:1](Ps.23.1); [Luke 15:4-6](Luke.15.4-Luke.15.6)).

These short, appealing songs were sung during pilgrims’ journeys to Jerusalem for the national festivals three times per year ([Deut 16:16](Deut.16.16)). The title of these psalms includes the Hebrew word for stairs, which some take to mean “ascending to Jerusalem.” These psalms (sometimes called the Songs of Ascents) take the reader on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem to praise God for his goodness to Israel throughout history.

This short, individual lament expresses the psalmist’s trust that the Lord will deal with deceptive evildoers. It also laments living as a stranger among hateful liars. The psalmist’s picture of his life in a foreign land might have been a reality as he set out for Jerusalem, or it might depict his feelings and concerns as he begins his pilgrimage. Overwhelmed with injustice, he trusts God and looks forward to arriving in the Lord’s presence.
The psalmist is surrounded by **liars***,* so he makes his lament **to the** **LORD***,* the only one who can help him.
The psalmist dialogues with the liars who surround him. He feels reassured that the Lord will judge them.
The Divine Warrior (see [7:12-13](Ps.7.12-Ps.7.13); [11:4-6](Ps.11.4-Ps.11.6)) will throw **sharp arrows** and **glowing coals** on the liars.
The psalmist feels the anguish of alienation, isolation, and perpetual conflict.

**Meshech** was a Japhethite territory far to the north of Canaan. **Kedar** was an Ishmaelite territory in Arabia. Violent people lived in both locations. Meshech was the home of a famous slave trade ([Ezek 27:13](Ezek.27.13); cp. [Exod 21:16](Exod.21.16)) and Kedar of renowned warriors ([Isa 21:16-17](Isa.21.16-Isa.21.17)). These places can be understood as representative of the apostate, violent land where the psalmist suffered.
The leader of the group of pilgrims uses word pictures to assure the group of the Lord’s presence during the journey.

**The mountains** were known for their idolatrous worship ([Deut 12:2](Deut.12.2)), and Israel was enticed to the hilltop shrines ([Hos 4:13](Hos.4.13)). This verse can be understood as a rhetorical question expecting a negative answer: The gods of the hilltop shrines cannot rescue anyone. Others understand the mountains to be a symbol of the Lord’s strength ([Ps 95:4](Ps.95.4)). In that case, the question would be interpreted literally (*Where does my help come from?*), with the answer given in the next verse
The Creator ([121:2](Ps.121.2)) is the guardian of Israel.
God **stands beside** Israel, supporting and caring for the godly (see [16:7-8](Ps.16.7-Ps.16.8)).
Both the **sun** and the **moon** were regarded as deities in the ancient Near East, but the Creator limits their power. They, too, praise the Lord ([148:3](Ps.148.3)).
God **watches over** his own, even and especially when they face many troubles ([12:5](Ps.12.5), [7](Ps.12.7); [69:29](Ps.69.29); [91:14](Ps.91.14); [146:9](Ps.146.9)).

Jerusalem is here idealized as the city of God, the city of David, and the city of faith. A group of people on a pilgrimage joyfully arrive in the city ([122:1-2](Ps.122.1-Ps.122.2)). The psalmist sings an ode to Jerusalem ([122:3-5](Ps.122.3-Ps.122.5)) and prays for the city’s peace ([122:6-9](Ps.122.6-Ps.122.9)).
The central sanctuary was the **house of the** **LORD**. This phrase originally referred to the Tabernacle ([Exod 23:19](Exod.23.19); [34:26](Exod.34.26)).
Several psalms celebrate or look forward to being **inside** the **gates** of the city ([9:14](Ps.9.14); [87:2](Ps.87.2); [100:4](Ps.100.4); [118:19](Ps.118.19)).
Jerusalem is a metaphor for God’s heavenly dwelling. David was the archetype for God’s chosen rulers.
In the time of David and Solomon, **Jerusalem** was renowned as a place of security ([1 Kgs 10:6-7](1Kgs.10.6-1Kgs.10.7)).
Each of the people of **Israel** belonged to one of the tribes, and all of the **tribes** belonged to the Lord.
To **give thanks** is to present an offering acceptable to the Lord ([50:14](Ps.50.14), [23](Ps.50.23); [100:4](Ps.100.4); [118:19](Ps.118.19)).
**as the law requires of Israel:** See [Exod 23:17](Exod.23.17); [Deut 16:16](Deut.16.16).
**the thrones where judgment is given:** In the eras of **David** and Solomon ([1 Kgs 3:28](1Kgs.3.28)), Jerusalem was the home of wisdom and justice; it would be so again ([Isa 9:7](Isa.9.7)).
Prayers for the **peace** of Jerusalem are motivated by love of family and God’s sanctuary.

This lament on the psalmist’s lowly position expresses vivid trust in the Lord ([123:1-2](Ps.123.1-Ps.123.2)). The psalmist prays for God’s favor on the community, as the reality of evil surrounds them ([123:3-4](Ps.123.3-Ps.123.4)). The poet looks beyond Jerusalem ([Ps 122](Ps.122.1-Ps.122.9)) to God’s throne **in heaven.**
This thanksgiving song describes what might happen if the Lord were not present with his people.
The negative rhetorical questions emphasize the positive idea that the **LORD** was indeed on their side.
**the raging waters of their fury:** The enemies could have **overwhelmed** the Israelites and wiped them out if the Lord had not been with his people (cp. [69:15](Ps.69.15); [Jer 46:8](Jer.46.8)).

The enemies of God’s people, like lions or bears who **tear** their prey with their **teeth** (see [57:4](Ps.57.4); [Prov 28:15](Prov.28.15)), had their mouths shut by the Lord ([Dan 6:22](Dan.6.22)).
The psalmist expresses the community’s confidence in the Lord’s protection ([125:1-2](Ps.125.1-Ps.125.2)) and prays for peace ([125:3-5](Ps.125.3-Ps.125.5)).
**surrounds:** God guards and protects like a wall of fire ([Zech 2:5](Zech.2.5)).
The **godly might be tempted** through peer pressure and cultural domination.
People who reject the straight path of the upright are fools ([Prov 2:12-15](Prov.2.12-Prov.2.15)). God pours out his goodness on the godly (see [Ps 122:6-9](Ps.122.6-Ps.122.9)).
This hymn celebrates Israel’s return from exile ([126:1-3](Ps.126.1-Ps.126.3)). The psalmist prays for full restoration ([126:4-6](Ps.126.4-Ps.126.6)).

The Lord brought about Israel’s restoration from exile, just as he had brought Israel out of Egypt ([114:1](Ps.114.1)). The restoration transformed the weeping of the Lord’s people into **laughter** and showed the Lord’s character to the **nations** ([9:11](Ps.9.11); [64:9](Ps.64.9); [Isa 12:4](Isa.12.4)).

The prophets had spoken of the restoration as a time when the wilderness would change into the Garden of Eden ([Isa 51:3](Isa.51.3); [Ezek 47](Ezek.47.1-Ezek.47.23)); the reality fell far short of paradise. Here the restoration community prays for full redemption (see [Hag 2:19](Hag.2.19)).

**as streams renew the desert:** The seasonal rains filled the dry river beds (*wadis*), and the land turned green again. The prayer looks for a similar transformation of Israel’s **fortunes***,* a fulfillment of the imagery of the “Second Exodus” in Isaiah (see “The Promise of a Second Exodus” Theme Note).
The **harvest** represents God’s full restoration.

Blessing and protection come from God. Without his presence, there is no success ([127:1-2](Ps.127.1-Ps.127.2)). This is particularly true for children, who are God’s gift ([127:3-5](Ps.127.3-Ps.127.5)).
**Unless:** These conditional sentences emphasize the positive idea that the Lord will protect the city (cp. [124:1-2](Ps.124.1-Ps.124.2)).
Human effort is futile unless the Lord blesses it (see [44:3](Ps.44.3)).
**from early morning until late at night:** This depicts an aggressive and competitive lifestyle.
God’s **loved ones** enjoy a quiet night’s sleep ([3:5](Ps.3.5); [4:8](Ps.4.8)).
**Children** are one of God’s blessings. The words translated “children” (Hebrew *banim*) and “builders” (*bonim,* [127:1](Ps.127.1)) form a wordplay. Having children builds a family.
**like arrows:** God uses children to protect the reputation of his people against the wicked (cp. [120:4](Ps.120.4); [7:12-13](Ps.7.12-Ps.7.13)).

The godly, who fear the Lord, will know true happiness ([128:1-2](Ps.128.1-Ps.128.2)). The Lord is with them (see [127:1-2](Ps.127.1-Ps.127.2)), building their home life ([128:3-4](Ps.128.3-Ps.128.4)) and blessing them across the generations ([128:5-6](Ps.128.5-Ps.128.6)).
Enjoying **the fruit** of one’s **labor** means gaining benefit from whatever work one does.

Like **vigorous young olive trees***,* children are saplings filled with potential. Olive oil symbolizes God’s blessing ([104:15](Ps.104.15); [Num 18:12](Num.18.12); [Jer 31:12](Jer.31.12); [Hag 2:19](Hag.2.19)).
God will **continually bless** all who fear him ([133:3](Ps.133.3)) from his dwelling in **Zion** ([20:2](Ps.20.2); [50:2](Ps.50.2); [110:2](Ps.110.2)), no matter where they live.

**grandchildren:** God’s blessings extend from generation to generation for the faithful ([79:12-13](Ps.79.12-Ps.79.13); [89:1](Ps.89.1); [100:4-5](Ps.100.4-Ps.100.5); [103:17-19](Ps.103.17-Ps.103.19)).

The psalmist briefly reviews Israel’s history of trouble ([129:1-2](Ps.129.1-Ps.129.2)) and redemption ([129:3-4](Ps.129.3-Ps.129.4)). He concludes with curses against the enemies and blessings on the godly ([129:5-6](Ps.129.5-Ps.129.6)).
Israel’s **earliest youth** as a nation was during its sojourn in Egypt.
**the** **LORD is good:** He rescued Israel from Egypt, from many enemy attacks, and from the Babylonian exile.
**Grass on a rooftop** had shallow roots and would scorch easily. A crop was **ignored by the harvester** when the yield was low. The enemies who had sown hurt among God’s people would gain little.

Beginning with himself as a representative of the community, the psalmist cries for God’s mercy ([130:1-3](Ps.130.1-Ps.130.3)) out of deep distress. He places his hope in the Lord ([130:4-6](Ps.130.4-Ps.130.6)), knowing that the Lord will rescue when and as he chooses. Based on this confidence, the psalmist invites Israel to wait for the Lord ([130:7-8](Ps.130.7-Ps.130.8)).

A **cry** from **the depths** is from a place of deep distress (cp. [69:2](Ps.69.2), [14](Ps.69.14); [Isa 51:10](Isa.51.10); [Ezek 27:34](Ezek.27.34)). Out of the frailty of his being, the psalmist prays for divine favor.
The psalmist knows that his **sins** make him guilty and deserving of God’s judgment.
The good news comes in God’s readiness to forgive sinners. His grace encourages people to fear him and hope in him.

**Israel** is invited to **hope in the LORD** ([9:18](Ps.9.18); [27:14](Ps.27.14); [131:3](Ps.131.3)) because the Lord pays the costly price for **redemption** and covers whatever **sin** separates humans from him (see also [111:9](Ps.111.9); [Exod 6:6-8](Exod.6.6-Exod.6.8); [2 Sam 7:23-24](2Sam.7.23-2Sam.7.24); [Isa 43:1-4](Isa.43.1-Isa.43.4); [Titus 2:14](Titus.2.14); [Heb 9:12](Heb.9.12); [1 Pet 1:18](1Pet.1.18)).
Out of his contentment in the Lord, the psalmist invites Israel to seek their rest in God ([131:3](Ps.131.3)).
The **heart** represents the whole being (see [27:8](Ps.27.8)).
God hates arrogance, which is a foolish way of life ([Prov 6:16-19](Prov.6.16-Prov.6.19)).
The psalmist does not trouble himself with matters that properly belong to the Lord.
The psalmist **calmed and quieted** himself, surrendering his ambitions and taming his ego ([Gal 2:20](Gal.2.20)).
**like a weaned child:** The psalmist sees himself as a contented child.

This psalm celebrates the Lord’s faithfulness to David. When David wanted to bring the Ark into Jerusalem ([132:1-5](Ps.132.1-Ps.132.5)), the Lord granted the request and made Jerusalem his earthly home ([132:6-10](Ps.132.6-Ps.132.10)). The choice of Jerusalem marked God’s election of David’s line ([132:11-13](Ps.132.11-Ps.132.13)), of Zion ([132:14-17](Ps.132.14-Ps.132.17)), and of the priesthood ([132:9](Ps.132.9), [16](Ps.132.16)).
These verses form a recollection of David’s moving the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem ([2 Sam 6:1-15](2Sam.6.1-2Sam.6.15)) and of the Lord’s oath to David ([2 Sam 7:4-16](2Sam.7.4-2Sam.7.16)).
**Ephrathah** is Bethlehem ([Gen 35:19](Gen.35.19); [48:7](Gen.48.7)).
**Jaar** is the singular form of the plural “Jearim.” The Ark was at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years in Samuel’s time ([1 Sam 7:1-2](1Sam.7.1-1Sam.7.2)).
These verses are a quotation from Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the Temple ([2 Chr 6:41-42](2Chr.6.41-2Chr.6.42)).
The **priests** were to exhibit righteousness in their lives ([132:16](Ps.132.16); [Mal 2:6](Mal.2.6)).

The **LORD swore an oath to David** ([2 Sam 7:4-16](2Sam.7.4-2Sam.7.16)): God’s **promise** is unconditional, but the covenant is not (**If . . . then**). Those who break God’s covenant can expect the discipline of God’s judgment (see [Ps 89:30-37](Ps.89.30-Ps.89.37)).
The psalmist recounts the selection of Jerusalem and of the priests.

**anointed one:** The ruler God chose and established (see [Pss 1–8](Ps.1.1-Ps.8.9)) would never cease to provide **light for** the Lord’s **people.** This light would burn continually (see [1 Kgs 11:36](1Kgs.11.36); [2 Kgs 8:19](2Kgs.8.19); cp. [John 8:12](John.8.12); [Rev 21:23-24](Rev.21.23-Rev.21.24)).
The adversaries will be humiliated, in contrast to the **glorious king** ([132:9](Ps.132.9), [16](Ps.132.16)).
In this wisdom psalm (see [Ps 1](Ps.1.1-Ps.1.6)), peaceful and harmonious relationships manifest the presence of God.
The psalmist tells of the joy of consecrated relationships.
**Brothers** are related by blood, by profession, or by commitment.
The **anointing oil** was the oil used to ordain and consecrate Aaron for service in his office (see [Exod 29:7](Exod.29.7)).
**head . . . beard . . . border of his robe:** The oil consecrated Aaron completely.

The **dew** represents the richness of divine blessings; in Jerusalem, it comes from moist winds from the Mediterranean Sea. **Mount Hermon***,* which is capped with snow, is a place of abundant moisture.

A **blessing** is God’s life-giving power, a guarantee of his provision and protection ([5:12](Ps.5.12); [41:2](Ps.41.2)), secured by his presence ([21:6](Ps.21.6); [67:1](Ps.67.1)). Even the other nations will ultimately be blessed ([Pss 67](Ps.67.1-Ps.67.7); [72:17](Ps.72.17)). Zion is the focal point of God’s blessing ([134:3](Ps.134.3); [147:13](Ps.147.13)).
God gives **life everlasting** to human beings.
In the last of the pilgrims’ songs ([Pss 120–134](Ps.120.1-Ps.134.3)), the travelers call the Temple workers to praise the Lord. In return, they will receive a much-anticipated blessing.
Those **who serve at night** were the priests and Levites (see also [135:2](Ps.135.2)).
God, the Creator and the Lord of history, “made heaven and earth” ([134:3](Ps.134.3)). He deserves praise because, unlike idols, he redeems his people.

The synonyms **Jacob** and **Israel** include all twelve tribes. The Lord cherishes his chosen people. They are his **treasure** out of all the kingdoms of the world ([Exod 19:5-6](Exod.19.5-Exod.19.6)).
The Lord is superior to any real or imagined supernatural being (see [95:3-5](Ps.95.3-Ps.95.5); [115:4-8](Ps.115.4-Ps.115.8)).
God is sovereign over the whole created order—he **does whatever pleases him** him.
The phrase **heaven and earth** refers to all of creation.
The Lord was sovereign over the Exodus and the conquest of the Promised Land.
In the tenth and culminating plague against Egypt, God **destroyed the firstborn** of each family.
The **miraculous signs and wonders** are the ten plagues (see [Exod 7–11](Exod.7.1-Exod.11.10); [Deut 4:34](Deut.4.34); [Neh 9:10](Neh.9.10)).
The Lord’s name and character stand in contrast to idols.
This entire section is repeated in [115:4-11](Ps.115.4-Ps.115.11).

Idols corrupt the thinking because they are **merely things** made by humans; they cannot **speak, see, hear,** or **breathe** ([Isa 41:22-24](Isa.41.22-Isa.41.24); [44:9](Isa.44.9), [18](Isa.44.18); [Rom 1:21-23](Rom.1.21-Rom.1.23)).
The groups named here comprised the covenant community (see [115:9-11](Ps.115.9-Ps.115.11)).

This is the last of the Great Hallel psalms ([Pss 120–136](Ps.120.1-Ps.136.26)). It distinctively repeats the refrain **His faithful love endures forever** in every verse. The hymn is framed by a call to praise ([136:1-3](Ps.136.1-Ps.136.3), [26](Ps.136.26)). It proclaims the Lord as the Creator of all and the Redeemer of Israel, both in the distant ([136:10-22](Ps.136.10-Ps.136.22)) and in the recent past ([136:23-24](Ps.136.23-Ps.136.24)).
The psalmist invites the community to praise the Lord, who is good and full of love, the true Lord of humanity. Verse 1 alludes to the poetic expression in [2 Chr 5:13](2Chr.5.13).
The psalmist recounts the early history of Israel’s redemption.
The psalmist relates the recent history of Israel’s redemption, although the circumstances are not specified.
The Lord provides for all of his creatures.

The phrase **God of heaven** is an exilic and postexilic designation for the Lord; it is found in Ezra ([Ezra 1:2](Ezra.1.2); [5:11](Ezra.5.11), [12](Ezra.5.12); [6:9](Ezra.6.9), [10](Ezra.6.10); [7:12](Ezra.7.12); etc.), Nehemiah ([Neh 1:5](Neh.1.5); [2:4](Neh.2.4), [20](Neh.2.20); etc.), and Daniel ([Dan 2:18](Dan.2.18), [19](Dan.2.19), [37](Dan.2.37), [44](Dan.2.44)).

In response to the pain of exile ([137:1-4](Ps.137.1-Ps.137.4)), the psalmist resolves to remember Jerusalem even though the memories cause him pain ([137:4-6](Ps.137.4-Ps.137.6)). He also writes an astounding imprecation, or prayer for vengeance ([137:7-9](Ps.137.7-Ps.137.9)).

Because the music of Jerusalem was tied to the joys of life in the Promised Land, the Exile removed any occasion for singing joyous songs. The Babylonians wanted the Judeans to sing and dance for them, but the exiles’ grief made doing so either distasteful or impossible. The songs celebrating the Lord speak of his power and goodness, but his people were filled with doubts and questions. They hung their harps in trees, perhaps signifying the death of their joy under God’s curse ([Deut 21:23](Deut.21.23)).
The psalmist pledges his loyalty to **Jerusalem***,* the city at the center of God’s reign and the location of fellowship with him.

The poet witnessed the betrayal of God’s people from Judah by **the Edomites***,* so he curses Edom. The long rivalry between Edom and Judah came to a head during Judah’s last days, when the Edomites handed the Judeans over to the Babylonians ([Obad 1:10-11](Obad.1.10-Obad.1.11)) and rejoiced in Jerusalem’s fall.
This prayer for vengeance is shocking.

In this final collection of psalms of David, praise and wisdom psalms ([Pss 138–139](Ps.138.1-Ps.139.24), [145](Ps.145.1-Ps.145.21)) form a frame around five poems of lament ([Pss 140–144](Ps.140.1-Ps.144.15)).
In this wisdom psalm, the Lord is presented as the God of gods. He rescued his people and has a perfect plan for them as individuals. The nations will join Israel in glorifying God.
The Lord receives praise before the gods of the nations.

As the Lord’s **glory** fills the earth, the world’s population must willingly submit to him. **Every king** (cp. [Ps 2](Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12)) will join the community of praise as they hear **the** **LORD’s ways** of truth and love.
The exalted God takes care of the humble ([138:6](Ps.138.6)), especially his servant the psalmist ([138:7-8](Ps.138.7-Ps.138.8)).
God’s holiness and excellence are **great***,* beyond the scope of humanity (see [99:2](Ps.99.2); [113:4](Ps.113.4); [Isa 6:1](Isa.6.1); [57:15](Isa.57.15)).

The psalmist expresses confidence in the Lord’s **plans***,* which are perfect, and prays for God’s continued involvement. The psalmist sees himself as part of God’s plans (see [9:10](Ps.9.10); [139:14](Ps.139.14)).

In this wisdom psalm, the psalmist opens every aspect of his being, character, behavior, and speech to God’s examination. As hard as life is, he wants to ensure his own growth in wisdom so that he does not come under God’s judgment of the wicked ([141:5](Ps.141.5); [142:3](Ps.142.3); [143:8](Ps.143.8), [10](Ps.143.10); [144:3-4](Ps.144.3-Ps.144.4)). Further, the poet recognizes that he cannot escape from the Lord. His sense of stress disappears when he considers the Lord’s loving care for him, even before birth ([139:13-18](Ps.139.13-Ps.139.18)). He then invites the Lord to continue examining him as he walks in the path of wisdom ([139:23-24](Ps.139.23-Ps.139.24)).
The Lord knows the psalmist well; God has examined him thoroughly, in an inescapable examination that is painful at times ([Job 7:17-19](Job.7.17-Job.7.19)).
The phrase **sit down or stand up** refers to daily activities (cp. [Deut 6:6-9](Deut.6.6-Deut.6.9)).
The Lord’s omniscience and omnipotence provide comfort to the godly, but they imprison the hearts of the wicked ([2:3](Ps.2.3)).
The Lord’s **wonderful** understanding lies beyond the psalmist’s ability to comprehend (see [Judg 13:18](Judg.13.18)).
The psalmist expresses his awe at the Lord’s omnipresence.
**down to the grave:** God has total access to his entire creation—even the most hard-to-reach places.
**ride the wings of the morning:** This poetic expression describes traveling eastward, as far as the sunrise, if that were possible.
**the farthest oceans:** This expression takes the traveler in the opposite direction, far to the west.
The **delicate, inner parts** of the **body** include a person’s very being.
Even when hidden in his **mother’s womb***,* the psalmist was guided by the Lord.
**How precious are your thoughts about me:** God’s investigation reveals loving care. Fellowship with the Lord provides riches beyond description.

The psalmist’s sense of awe leads him to consider the wicked and to reflect on himself. The Lord, as the examiner of all people, judges the wicked for their destructive acts and speech; thus, the psalmist prays that he will not be among them.
**I hate:** Rejection of evil is a mark of wisdom (see [1:1](Ps.1.1); [5:4-6](Ps.5.4-Ps.5.6)).
The psalmist’s prayer against the wicked leads him also to reflect on himself; he does not presume that he is righteous. This prayer has been repeated by believers over the centuries.
The **path** of wisdom leads to **everlasting life** (see [1:6](Ps.1.6); [Prov 4:18](Prov.4.18); [6:23](Prov.6.23)).

In this individual lament, the psalmist artistically sketches God’s enemies with all their evil intents. He prays for the Lord’s protection and rescue with confidence in God’s strength and justice. He foresees the evil as being judged by fire ([140:9-11](Ps.140.9-Ps.140.11)) and himself as being vindicated and dwelling in the Lord’s presence ([140:13](Ps.140.13)).
The psalmist prays for the Lord to rescue him from wicked people.
**sting like a snake . . . a viper:** These creatures depict the wicked as very corrupt people (see [Prov 23:32](Prov.23.32); [Isa 14:29](Isa.14.29); [Rom 3:13](Rom.3.13)).
The psalmist asks for divine protection (see [Ps 121](Ps.121.1-Ps.121.8)), praying that the Lord will keep him safe from the many schemes of the wicked.

The expression **Sovereign** **LORD** comes from combining the name *Yahweh* with the title *Adonai* (Master). See also [68:20](Ps.68.20); [69:6](Ps.69.6); [71:16](Ps.71.16); [73:28](Ps.73.28); [109:21](Ps.109.21); [141:8](Ps.141.8).
The psalmist prays for God’s judgment on the wicked.

The psalmist wants **fire** to descend on his enemies, and he wants them thrown into **pits** so they can never attack again. The language foreshadows the New Testament teaching on hell ([Matt 5:22](Matt.5.22), [29-30](Matt.5.29-Matt.5.30); [10:28](Matt.10.28); [18:9](Matt.18.9); [Mark 9:43-47](Mark.9.43-Mark.9.47); [Luke 12:5](Luke.12.5); [Jas 3:6](Jas.3.6); [2 Pet 2:4](2Pet.2.4)).
The psalmist prays for rescue and wisdom, and he envisions the end of evil. The principle of retribution ([141:10](Ps.141.10)) unifies the psalm.

The psalmist prays urgently for rescue. He does not have at hand either **incense** or an **evening offering** ([Exod 29:38-39](Exod.29.38-Exod.29.39)), but his prayers and devotion are the reality that those elements represent (cp. [Isa 1:13](Isa.1.13); [Rev 5:8](Rev.5.8)).
**Upraised hands** are a posture of prayer ([Pss 28:2](Ps.28.2); [88:9](Ps.88.9); [143:6](Ps.143.6); [Exod 9:29](Exod.9.29); [1 Tim 2:8](1Tim.2.8)).
Wisdom sometimes requires protection from oneself. One could say or think things that lead to the evil path ([Prov 13:3](Prov.13.3); [21:23](Prov.21.23)).
Wisdom opens itself to correction from **godly** people (see [Prov 3:11](Prov.3.11); [9:8](Prov.9.8); [15:31](Prov.15.31); [19:25](Prov.19.25)).
The psalmist faces severe persecution, so he cries to the Lord, and the Lord will rescue him.
**regarding his experience in the cave:** Cp. [Ps 57:title](Ps.57.1).
Though **overwhelmed** by his persecutors ([142:6](Ps.142.6)), the psalmist looks to the Lord for wisdom.

The psalmist reaches a point of despair (see [77:3](Ps.77.3)), and the Lord cares for him in his distress. The psalmist commits himself to the Lord’s wisdom (see [Ps 139](Ps.139.1-Ps.139.24)) but laments his entrapment by the wicked ([5:9-10](Ps.5.9-Ps.5.10); [140:5](Ps.140.5); [141:9](Ps.141.9); [142:3](Ps.142.3)).
Though he is alone, the psalmist’s trust remains in the Lord, who is his **life** (see [9:9](Ps.9.9); [16:5](Ps.16.5); [27:13](Ps.27.13)).
Though overwhelmed by loneliness and trouble, the psalmist focuses on the Lord’s goodness and protection. He knows that the Lord alone is his Redeemer, so he offers his praise.
His experience of confinement and duress is like being in **prison** (see [107:10](Ps.107.10)).

In this lament, the psalmist feels overwhelmed by constant harassment from his foes, so he turns to the Lord’s love, righteousness, and faithfulness. He remembers God’s acts in the past and yearns for the renewal of the Lord’s love. He opens himself to God’s wisdom because he knows that instruction will lead to life.
The psalmist prays for God’s love and mercy.
All people are guilty before God ([Rom 3:20-24](Rom.3.20-Rom.3.24)).
**I am losing all hope:** The psalmist confesses his desperation as his life slips away under oppressive and ruthless foes.
Remembering God’s acts from the past reassures the psalmist of God’s faithfulness ([42:4](Ps.42.4); [63:6](Ps.63.6); [77:3](Ps.77.3), [6](Ps.77.6); [119:55](Ps.119.55)).
The psalmist’s **thirst** is a deep longing for God’s redemption (see [42:1-2](Ps.42.1-Ps.42.2)).
The psalmist petitions the Lord for a renewal of his love.

The psalmist experiences **depression**. He feels that he is dying from anguish ([31:10](Ps.31.10); [119:87](Ps.119.87)), exhausted ([39:10](Ps.39.10); [71:9](Ps.71.9); [119:81](Ps.119.81)), fainting with longing ([84:2](Ps.84.2)), and overwhelmed by the weariness of life ([90:7](Ps.90.7), [9](Ps.90.9)).
**your gracious Spirit:** The Spirit brings God’s goodness (see [23:6](Ps.23.6)).
To **preserve** means in this case to restore from despair ([80:19](Ps.80.19); [85:6](Ps.85.6); [138:7](Ps.138.7)).
A prayer for vindication and renewal of life concludes the psalm.

This lament begins with an exclamation of love for the Lord. The community then reflects on the transitory nature of life ([144:3-4](Ps.144.3-Ps.144.4)). The psalmist prays for divine intervention and anticipates victory ([144:5-11](Ps.144.5-Ps.144.11)). A new song ([144:9-10](Ps.144.9-Ps.144.10)) and a prayer for rescue ([144:11](Ps.144.11)) open up the theme of the Lord’s blessing through his provisions and protection ([144:12-15](Ps.144.12-Ps.144.15)).
The psalmist’s descriptive names for the Lord reveal his deep love for him.

**what are human beings?** The same question in [8:4-6](Ps.8.4-Ps.8.6) elicits the answer that humans are mere mortals but are also glorious rulers. The psalmist depicts humans as having a transitory, empty existence (see [90:3](Ps.90.3), [7-10](Ps.90.7-Ps.90.10); [102:11](Ps.102.11); [109:23](Ps.109.23); [146:4](Ps.146.4)).
The psalmist prays for God’s intervention against his **enemies** (cp. [18:7-19](Ps.18.7-Ps.18.19)).

This prayer for the Lord’s blessing brings the laments of [Pss 140–144](Ps.140.1-Ps.144.15) to a close. It offers a vision of God’s provision and protection (see [Ps 127](Ps.127.1-Ps.127.5)), not only for the psalmist, but for his descendants and those of all the godly.
The psalmist compares **sons** and **daughters** to plants and pillars, which are images of strength and beauty.
**no enemy . . . no cries of alarm:** These images depict peace and security.

This hymn of praise is the last in this collection of the psalms of David ([Pss 138–145](Ps.138.1-Ps.145.21)). Praise continues in the last five psalms ([Pss 146–150](Ps.146.1-Ps.150.6)). This psalm celebrates the Lord as King of all ([145:1-3](Ps.145.1-Ps.145.3), [10-13](Ps.145.10-Ps.145.13)). God’s actions reveal his royal qualities ([145:4-7](Ps.145.4-Ps.145.7)). He cares for all creatures ([145:14-17](Ps.145.14-Ps.145.17)) and for those who fear him ([145:18-20](Ps.145.18-Ps.145.20)).
The psalmist praises God, the Great King who reigns over all other rulers (see [47:2](Ps.47.2)).
This litany praises God’s character and mighty deeds. **Each generation** will continue to testify to God’s power ([22:30](Ps.22.30)).
God consistently demonstrates his character toward **all his creation** (see [136:25](Ps.136.25)).
These verses form a description of the Lord’s kingdom.
The Lord cares for his creatures.

The Lord cares for those **who love him** and fear him. God-fearers love the Lord and find refuge in him ([5:11](Ps.5.11)); they seek him as their only true Savior ([40:16](Ps.40.16); [70:4](Ps.70.4)). They will experience a grand future ([69:36](Ps.69.36)), as well as God’s peace ([119:165](Ps.119.165)).
The Psalter ends with five hallelujah psalms, so named because each begins and ends with **Praise the** **LORD!** (Hebrew *haleluyah*).

The call to praise ([146:1-2](Ps.146.1-Ps.146.2)) leads into a warning against folly and false confidence ([146:3-4](Ps.146.3-Ps.146.4)). The psalm concludes with a blessing for all who place their hope in the Lord ([146:5-7](Ps.146.5-Ps.146.7)).
The fourfold repetition of the name of **the** **LORD** emphasizes that only he heals, unburdens, loves, and protects.
The psalmist calls for the Lord to be praised for restoring and blessing Zion, caring for the poor, displaying his power over nature, and revealing himself to his people.
This verse is a call to worship.
The psalmist recalls the restoration of Jerusalem and the Lord’s afflicted exiles.
The Lord created the heavens.
**He counts the stars:** God’s people can feel secure in knowing that the Lord attends to every detail of his creation; he knows all that belongs to him.
God measures out his justice on the poor and on the wicked ([55:22](Ps.55.22); [140:12](Ps.140.12); [145:14](Ps.145.14); [146:7](Ps.146.7)).
Human achievements fail to impress the God who commands nature; rather, he takes pleasure in those who fear him.

**human might:** Any physical or intellectual achievement is a gift from the Lord, just like the **strength of a horse**. These gifts are a reason to praise the Lord, not to boast ([Jer 9:23-24](Jer.9.23-Jer.9.24)).
The **bars** of the city **gates** symbolize defenses against enemies.
God **blessed** his people by empowering them with safety, prosperity, peace, and provisions (see [133:3](Ps.133.3)).
Simply by speaking **his command***,* the Lord can change the season from unbearable winter to refreshing spring (see [147:8](Ps.147.8); [148:5-6](Ps.148.5-Ps.148.6)).
**words . . . decrees . . . regulations:** The Lord gave powerful words to Israel so that they might obey him ([105:45](Ps.105.45)).
This psalm calls for the whole created order to praise the Lord because he has honored his faithful people.

During Jesus’ triumphant entry into Jerusalem, the crowds called out various blessings, including a phrase taken from this verse ([Matt 21:9](Matt.21.9); [Mark 11:10](Mark.11.10); [Luke 19:38](Luke.19.38)).
The created order is stable because of the Lord’s word (see [33:9](Ps.33.9)).

In the ancient Near East, people viewed different gods as having control over separate aspects of nature. The Lord, however, reigns sovereign over all natural phenomena; all the parts of creation are his servants, bringing praise to him through their obedience ([77:17-18](Ps.77.17-Ps.77.18); [104:4](Ps.104.4); [135:7](Ps.135.7); [147:8](Ps.147.8), [15-18](Ps.147.15-Ps.147.18); [Num 11:31](Num.11.31)).
The psalmist calls all humans to offer praise to God, regardless of status, age, or gender.
Universal praise of the Lord is fitting because he is glorious, and he has blessed his people (see [147:13](Ps.147.13); [Isa 46:13](Isa.46.13); [Eph 3:10](Eph.3.10)).
**His faithful ones** are his trusting and devoted servants ([Ps 86:2](Ps.86.2)).

This hymn of praise celebrates the Lord’s victory. He is the **Maker** of Israel ([149:1-2](Ps.149.1-Ps.149.2)) and the victorious **King** who shares his glory with his faithful ones ([149:3-9](Ps.149.3-Ps.149.9)).

God’s people, whom the world ignores and despises, will be vindicated ([Matt 19:30](Matt.19.30)). The **humble** will experience **victory** over their oppressors and persecutors (see [Isa 61:3](Isa.61.3)).
Everything that breathes is commanded to **praise** the Lord as he deserves. The whole Psalter describes the greatness of the Lord, so this psalm is a fitting conclusion.
The phrase **mighty heaven** alludes to [Gen 1](Gen.1.1-Gen.1.31) and to God’s glorious work in filling the emptiness.
The psalmist calls all people to praise God with instruments and dancing. **flutes:** These wind instruments are not mentioned as being used in Temple worship.
**clanging cymbals:** Temple musicians clapped two bronze bowls together as percussion instruments.
**Praise the** **LORD:** This refrain is a fitting conclusion to the entire book of Psalms.
